#6370. Fossil fuel emissions are down in 2026. Green energy isn’t the reason

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The decrease is probably temporary and a result of high gas prices from the Iran war

The disruption of oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz off the coast of Iran has raised oil and gas prices around the world. According to new projections, those higher fuel prices will decrease global carbon dioxide emissions from fossil fuel burning in 2026 by about 0.16 gigatons from 2025.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Scientists project that global carbon dioxide emissions from fossil fuels will decrease by 0.4 percent this year, after having grown by 0.8 percent each year on average from 2019 to 2025.

But the dip may not last. The lower emissions are probably driven by high oil prices stemming from the Iran war, researchers report November 9 in Nature Climate Change.

Global emissions probably would have grown again this year without the energy shock of the Iran war, says Glen Peters, a climate scientist at the Center for International Climate Research in Oslo, Norway. “So the energy transition that’s happening … it’s not quite big enough to get emissions heading downward yet.”

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

For the study, Peters and his colleagues used data on countries’ electric vehicle stocks and wind and solar energy generation to project those technologies impacts on global fossil CO2 emissions through 2028. The team used the generative AI model Claude to source data and write code for analysis.

By year’s end, global emissions will reach 38.24 gigatons, the researchers found, which is about 0.16 gigatons less than were emitted in 2025. For comparison, annual global emissions fell by nearly two gigatons in 2020 due to the COVID-19 pandemic and by about 0.5 gigatons in 2009 because of the global financial crisis.

If electric vehicle sales and solar and wind capacity continue growing at the rates they did in 2026, those technologies should counteract about 63 percent of the growth in emissions from 2025 to 2028 — or help avoid about 1.64 gigatons of added emissions.

The results indicate that the energy transition needs to accelerate if humankind is to realize consistently declining emissions, though EVs, solar and wind are already having a large impact. Without the offset in emissions provided by those technologies, global emissions would have risen by 1.9 percent each year on average from 2019 to 2025, the researchers note.

It’s very hard to say exactly how long it will take for humanity to reach peak emissions, Peters says. However, he notes, “the fact that we’re talking about this means that we’re close to that point.”

#6369. The 8 Best Home Generators Are a Big Investment. These Deliver Reliable Power During an Outage.

Our editor-tested and researched portable and whole-home options keep appliances and other essentials running during an emergency—no matter what.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Stronger and more frequent severe weather events are making a compelling argument for investing in a home generator. A large portable generator or a permanently installed standby generator can keep your entire home powered and operational for several days, or at least keep a few critical appliances such as a refrigerator running until the power comes back on. The cost of emergency power is never a small investment, though it is an increasingly important one.

The term “home generator” can be confusing. It’s an unofficial category that includes larger portable generators capable of powering several appliances or a few critical circuits using a transfer switch (not all portable generators are built for this task). It also includes permanently installed standby generators that can automatically switch to whole-home backup power when the lights go out. Choosing the right size generator primarily comes down to how much power you think you’ll need in an emergency.

There are many reliable home generators that deliver a great deal of power. Some offer you the choice of running on multiple different fuels, while other models use an inverter that can give you quieter and “cleaner” operation. There is a nice range of prices available, too, so you can easily find a generator below that fits your needs as well as your budget.

For the generators on this list that we tested, we considered the difficulty of unboxing, assembling, and starting each generator for the first time, because few things are as frustrating as buying a tool that turns out to be unnecessarily complicated from the get-go.

Once set up, the generators we reviewed were subjected to different load conditions, including things such as power tools, home appliances, and even recharging large power stations. We assessed the features that distinguish these generators from each other, including safety features, app connectivity, and portability, among other things.

A few picks on our list have not been tested, but we included them here after considerable research, taking into account the brand’s reputation, our knowledge of its product lines, various outside reviews, and our own experience testing similar models from those same brands.

The DuroMax XP11000iH is a powerful midsize dual-fuel inverter generator, capable of keeping most homes up and running for an extended period of time. Inverter generators are a step above traditional generators because they convert alternating current (AC) to direct current (DC) and then back again to AC. This process creates cleaner, more efficient power and enables the generator to run more quietly and fuel efficiently.

Having two fuel options—gas and propane—provides a big boost of convenience by allowing you to use whatever’s handy. No gasoline? You can use the same tank of propane you use for your gas grill. It’s also parallel-capable, so you can daisy-chain it with another generator if you need extra power.

The generator is enclosed in a large, sturdy plastic casing, which makes it durable and provides a fair amount of sound dampening. Of the many gas generators I’ve tested, it may be the quietest model that’s capable of backing up a whole home, especially when it’s running on propane, which trims it down by another few decibels. At 61 decibels on a 20 percent load, it’s about as loud as a dishwasher. Most comparably sized generators go up to around 80 decibels—about the same volume as a police siren.

In addition to a full suite of essential modern safety features such as a carbon monoxide shutoff and low-oil shutoff, it goes the extra mile with lots of little touches, like remote start. The integrated battery tender keeps it ready to start, no matter how long it’s been sitting, which can be a lifesaver, too. When you do run out to check it, an onboard display shows you key stats such as hours run, current load, and voltage output.

The only downside I could find was its weight. At upward of 200 pounds, it isn’t easy to carry. It does have wheels and sturdy handles, though, so it isn’t hard to wheel around on flat, paved ground—if you can push a loaded wheelbarrow, you can push this. Not that you’ll need to move it much; it’s a very sturdy generator, and it comes assembled with the wheels and handles attached (not all generators come with those pre-attached). —Reviewed by Nick Hilden

Technically, there are cheaper generators out there, but the Generac GP9500E offers an outstanding blend of capability, quality, and durability at a very reasonable price. As such, this is where I’d steer you if you’re trying to shave down your spend.

Its 9,500-watt running capacity is slightly higher than the DuroMax’s, and it’s capable of powering all but the largest of homes. It can get a little noisy under a heavy load, but that’s common with units this size. It let out a relatively moderate purr when it was just powering the lights and a few appliances, but it became more of a roar when the heat kicked on.

With three fuel options—gas, propane, and natural gas—you get about as much versatility as you could possibly expect from a generator. A relatively large 7.5-gallon gas tank delivers a long runtime between fill-ups. And, while I was initially skeptical as to the necessity of the third fuel option, having natural gas support showed its value when a storm knocked out the power, and I didn’t have gas or propane on hand. All I needed to do was plug it into the natural gas line, and suddenly my house was the only one on the block with lights on.

Beyond that, though, it’s a fairly basic model. It has essential safety features such as low-oil and CO shutdown, but lacks elements such as a fancy digital display, remote start, or app. I don’t necessarily think that’s a problem: It can be helpful to get a piece of machinery that doesn’t go overboard with features. Its control panel is about as straightforward as can be, and it’s a cinch to get up and running.

Like my top pick, the GP9500E is exceedingly heavy. It’s also quite sturdy, though, which feels like a fair trade. The outlet covers aren’t as flimsy and breakable as with many other models of a similar price point. It isn’t completely immobile: It has wheels and handles that make it easy to cart around short distances. Realistically, though, weight is almost always going to be an issue with any generator capable of backing up your house.

Ultimately, its selling point is the price. It’s hard to find a quality tri-fuel generator for around $1,100, and the GP9500E performs well if you don’t mind losing out on some bells and whistles.

When AC power isn’t available, the greenest way to recharge a power station is with solar panels. However, the panel’s maximum power output often exceeds the maximum solar input, so they just can’t recharge fast enough. In these cases, whole-home, battery-based backup systems need the help of a fuel-based generator to recharge, so you’re not left high and dry if the power’s still out. That’s where the EcoFlow Smart Generator 4000 comes in.

This dual-fuel (gas or propane) generator connects to select EcoFlow power stations via a DC charging and communication cable, including the Delta Pro, Delta Pro 3, Delta 3, Delta 3 Plus, and Delta 2 Max. (Note: If your preferred brand is Anker, it also makes a fuel generator that’s compatible with some of its power stations, the 5500 Tri-Fuel Inverter Generator, which we also tested and reviewed.) This DC connection allows autonomous operation, so when a station’s battery hits critically low levels, the generator automatically starts to recharge it.

You can also recharge non-DC-compatible power stations by simply plugging them into the AC output, though it’s a slower recharge. If it’s an EcoFlow station, you can still automate startup, too, by pairing over Bluetooth. But you won’t be able to do this with other brands of power stations.

Our test editor Bradley Ford noted that EcoFlow’s app is one of the best features of this generator. Connecting over Bluetooth or Wi-Fi, he used it to monitor fuel consumption and output, as well as set automated functions. He also tested how it can set the charging speed, monitor power output, and schedule times to start and stop the generator. He especially liked that the app provides a lot of useful information as well, such as generator fuel usage and estimated runtime.

Of course, it can work as a standalone generator, too, though there are some limitations. Ford notes that there are only two outlets: a 120-volt, 20-amp outlet and a 120-volt, 30-amp outlet. The latter outlet can connect to a manual transfer switch installed in your home, but it won’t be able to power any 240-volt circuits, and the total output of 3,200 watts is only enough to power a few circuits. However, he thinks it would work well for RV use, and because it’s an inverter generator, it’s better at safely powering sensitive electronics like TVs and computers. — Reviewed by Bradley Ford

Full EcoFlow Dual-Fuel Smart Generator 4000 Review

Whether you’re connecting devices individually, powering an RV, or running home backup power during a storm, this generator from Westinghouse (model WGen9500DF) covers all the bases. In addition to being dual-fuel (gas or propane), it includes both 30- and 50-amp outputs capable of powering 120- and 240-volt circuits. That means you could connect this generator to a transfer switch installed in your home using either option. And with 9,500 running watts of power, it’s enough for several critical circuits in your home, including the ones that run on 240 volts, such as a heating/ventilation/air-conditioning system, electric dryer, or well pump.

Several other features caught our attention, including a push-button electric start and stop (no need to mess with a pull cable), plus a remote start key fob. There’s an automatic low-oil shutoff, and the display provides the voltage output, frequency, and lifetime hours (this can run up to 12 hours on a 6.6-gallon tank of gasoline). The only drawback is the 74-decibel noise level. While that’s typical of generators of this type, if you're planning on using this to power an RV or camper, it may be too loud for some parks, as many limit generator noise to under 70 decibels.

While it does not offer as much power as some of the choices on our list, Champion’s 4,750-watt generator has enough capacity to run three or four critical 120-volt circuits in your home during an outage. It will also power small to medium campers and RVs via a dedicated 30-amp, 120-volt RV receptacle. Listed at around $600, this generator gives you a lot for the price you pay.

This generator uses a 224-cc engine with a 4.7-gallon fuel tank, enabling it to run for up to 14 hours (up to 10 hours using propane). A gauge displays a readout of the runtime hours and voltage output, and there’s an automated shutoff feature if the oil starts to run low. Since it’s dual-fuel, this generator can run off propane in addition to gasoline. For instance, if you are using it with an RV, you can run it off a camper’s propane tank without having to pack and haul a gas can. Likewise, with the included adapter hose, you can hook it up to a 20-pound propane tank.

There are a few drawbacks. Beyond the somewhat low wattage output for whole-home backup, there are no 240-volt outlets, so if you need that many volts to power circuits in your home for something such as a dryer or water heater, this model won’t be right for you. But if you just need something to keep some lights on and run a few appliances, this generator will get the job done and not cost you a ton of money up front to do it. — Reviewed by Bradley Ford

There are many reasons to opt for an inverter generator, but the two biggest ones are: cleaner, more stable power (important for powering electronics safely) and less noise. Loudness becomes a major factor with larger generators, as more power requires a more powerful engine. That’s why we were so impressed with this model (EU7000iS) from Honda. It delivers a lot of power but at notably low loudness levels.

It’s important to note that this is not a small generator. It weighs in at 263 pounds, making it one of the heaviest on our list. That said, we found it fairly comfortable to move around. The metal frame that houses the generator has a folding handle that locks into place and is capped with soft grips, while on the front of the frame there are strong 10-inch rubber wheels. This made it fairly easy to roll around, even up some gradual slopes.

It’s also quite sturdy. The outer casing is constructed of stamped metal and impact-resistant composite hard plastic, with two large, hinged maintenance doors that lock into place.

Once we fired up the generator, it was noticeably quieter than other models we’ve tested, even when outputting a 60 percent load. Using an app-based sound meter, we were reading around 70 decibels from 15 feet away, which is lower than you would see with a non-inverter generator. This is helped by an “Eco Throttle” mode that adjusts the engine speed to meet demand as different devices are added, but we found even the standard throttle mode was fairly quiet as well.

Other things we liked were an app that allows for remote operation over Bluetooth, ground fault circuit interrupter (GFCI) protection, a carbon monoxide (CO) sensor, and 240-volt output over a 30-amp connection, which will let the generator connect to a manual transfer switch for sending direct power to your home electrical box.

The two downsides are the cost (it’s very expensive at more than $4,000) and the fact that it can only be powered by gasoline; Honda doesn’t offer dual- or tri-fuel models for using propane or natural gas. But if those two considerations don’t bother you, the EU7000iS Inverter Generator is a high-quality machine that will keep you more quietly powered than some of the competition.

Full Honda EU7000iS 7000-Watt Inverter Generator Review

Battery-based backup systems are getting smarter and more powerful every year, making them an increasingly strong contender to fuel-based standby generators. This model from EcoFlow is one of the most powerful we’ve tested.

The power station combines a separate inverter unit with two 6-kilowatt-hour batteries for a total of 12-kilowatt-hour capacity. That’s enough to run power-hungry devices simultaneously—things such as heating/ventilation/air-conditioning systems, electric ovens and dryers, microwaves, and air-conditioning units. Add to this increased solar input, and you can recharge faster, too. For our tests, we connected this to a home electrical system in the home using EcoFlow’s Smart Home Panel 3, which acts as the automatic transfer switch.

During testing, our reviewer experienced two power outages, one for a few seconds and one for several minutes. This power station features an Emergency Power Supply (EPS) mode, which facilitates a 20-millisecond switch to backup power—without this set, it normally switches in about five seconds. During the longer outage, the switch from grid to backup power, and then back again, was seamless. It was fast enough that the lights never flickered and the internet never dropped.

Several advanced smart features stand out. The smartphone app enables you to view power usage, down to the circuit, preset what circuits get backup power during outages, manually turn circuits on and off, and schedule automated tasks such as charging and discharging. You’ll also receive notifications when the grid goes down and the backup power takes over. If you live in an area where electricity is cheaper during low-peak hours, it can also prioritize recharging from grid power by choosing those times of day.

Meanwhile, this system is highly expandable. You can add up to eight more batteries for a total of 10, and an inlet box that comes with the smart panel has three ports. You could plug a Delta Pro Ultra X, bolstered by extra batteries, into each port to increase the total energy storage up to a whopping 184.3 kilowatt-hours of capacity and 36 kilowatts of continuous output.

One of the biggest things our reviewer appreciates about the Delta Pro Ultra X and Smart Home Panel 3 is the peace of mind it gives. If the grid goes down, they know that their home systems will continue to run. — Reviewed by Bradley Ford

Pulsar is a relatively new brand in the generator business and doesn’t have a long track record. We first spotted it on Amazon and didn’t seriously consider its generators for testing. That was, up until our test editor needed a generator (with specific features and on a budget) after a generator failed at his solar-powered off-grid cabin. Happily, the Pulsar 7,250-Watt Dual-Fuel Inverter Generator showed up quickly and didn’t disappoint.

The generator was easy to assemble and prep, taking only 15 minutes. After adding oil, it was connected to a propane cylinder and was up and running on the first cycle of the starter. Our first task was to charge a solar battery bank during a wintertime period when there was not enough available sunlight, and it worked perfectly.

We have logged more than 20 hours of use so far, running it primarily on propane connected to a 100-pound cylinder (enough fuel to last a couple of months). This Pulsar puts out very clean power, with a claimed total harmonic distortion (THD) of less than 3 percent, which met the requirements of the solar inverter-charger I was using. Using the inverter to monitor the current frequency, we found that it was indeed very stable with minimal variance, between 59.97 and 60.09 Hz. All things considered, the Pulsar 7,250-Watt Dual-Fuel is a good value for the specs, capacity, and features. — Reviewed by Bradley Ford

True whole-home backup requires a professionally installed standby generator like Generac’s 22-kilowatt home standby generator. It’s designed to power a house that’s roughly 2,500 square feet. If you need to run specialized medical devices, work from home, or have kids who are learning from home, this model is a sound investment.

Another benefit of this bundle is that it includes a transfer switch, which is required if you’re planning to install this type of generator. It supports 200-amp electrical service, providing the backup circuits needed to power high-voltage appliances such as refrigerators and well pumps, along with air conditioning and heating systems. Plus, there’s built-in WiFi for checking the status of your generator and receiving maintenance alerts when you’re not at home.

You could just drive over to your local hardware store and buy a large portable generator to use as a home backup, but we wouldn’t recommend it. You want to make sure you’re getting a generator that can back up your home and power all the appliances, lights, and electronics inside. (Plus some extra watts in case you need them down the line.)

In addition, there are often state and local laws or homeowners association rules and restrictions around using them in residential neighborhoods. Choosing poorly or setting up your backup generator incorrectly could damage the generator or short out your house power at best, or lead to fire, electrocution, or carbon monoxide poisoning at worst.

Picking the best generator for your home starts with a little math. Ideally, you want to calculate how much energy you need to keep your house running, and buy a generator that can handle everything you want to power in an emergency, with room to spare.

The two key specs to pay attention to are the running wattage and starting wattage (e.g., 9,500 running watts / 12,500 starting watts). Running wattage is effectively your generator’s capacity: It tells you how much power a generator can produce steadily without any possibility of an overload. Starting wattage is the generator’s max output, or how much power it can produce for short, peak bursts when appliances first switch on.

When you are making your list, note what items are 120-volt and which ones are 240-volt appliances. It’s not hard to identify them. Refrigerators, small appliances, and most electronics run on 120-volt power and plug into standard outlets. Anything that requires 240 volts—electric dryers, well pumps, and HVAC systems—is either hardwired into your electrical system or has a dedicated 240-volt outlet. If you need to power the latter, the installation of a transfer switch and a generator that outputs at least 30 amps/240 volts may be required.

If you’re just looking to keep the fridge, lights, and a few modest appliances going through a short blackout, you can usually get away with a generator that supplies 3,000 to 5,000 watts. If you want to run the heat, hot water, and several appliances at once, plan on using at least 6,000 to 8,000 watts. If you think you’re going to be adding large appliances such as laundry machines and dishwashers, expect to need 10,000 watts or more.

A piece of advice we have: Once you figure out how much you need, opt for buying a generator that outputs around 20 percent more than that. It’s not uncommon to realize you need more than you thought you would.

It’s also important to consider that, while generators are certainly a hefty investment, they usually stand the test of time. Consumer-grade portable generators can run anywhere from 1,000 to 3,000 hours, sometimes more. If you run one for 100 hours per year, it should last for 10 to 30 years.

There are four basic types of generators, each with advantages and disadvantages.

The most traditional of the generator category, these run on carbon-based fuels like gasoline, propane, and natural gas. Some allow you to switch between them. Dual-fuel models add the option of either propane or natural gas, while tri-fuel versions offer all three fuel options. These generators can be small, offering as little as 1,000 watts of power output, or run very large, as much as 20,000 watts or more.

Different fuels offer different power capabilities. For example, a tri-fuel generator may offer 9,500 running watts and 12,500 starting watts with gasoline, but only 8,500/11,200 with propane and 7,500/9,500 with natural gas. Regardless of the fuel you choose, this type of generator must always be operated 5 to 20 feet away from the home or any window or door, because the carbon monoxide exhaust is deadly. Even a garage with an open door is not safe.

Often this type of generator is called portable, but that's a relative term: Almost all of them weigh more than 100 pounds, and many are upwards of 200. Many are on wheels, making them relatively easy to store in a garage and wheel outside when you need them, but actually moving one will likely require at least two people.

Inverter generators look and operate the same as other portable generators, but have an added component–a power inverter– that converts the alternating current (AC) power generated by its fuel source to DC (Direct Current), then inverts it back to AC before putting it out.

Generators without an inverter generate varying degrees of distortion in the sine wave of the alternating current, which can trigger power surges and other issues in some electronics. The inverter stabilizes the power, almost like a filter, “cleaning” it for more sensitive electronics like TVs and laptops.

So why doesn’t every generator have an inverter? Inverters are expensive, so the generators are, too.

Realistically speaking, you don’t need an inverter generator to power major appliances and your house power, but if you’re running a full home backup (or if you count a TV or laptop among your essential electronics), holding out for an inverter is a smart move.

While often referred to as “solar generators” because they can be paired with solar panels, power stations are not really true generators. They're advanced battery banks that store power, which you precharge using AC power or solar panels. They can’t generate electricity in real time.

But because they can offer many of the same electrical outputs as a fuel generator, they can function similarly to a traditional generator for as long as the batteries retain a charge. Some stations are very small and meant only for off-grid adventures like camping trips, but some are large enough to run whole-home systems that can produce 14,400 watts or more with expandable batteries.

Since power stations don't run on fuel or have an engine, they can be used indoors without the risk of carbon monoxide poisoning and operate with almost no noise.

The downside is that once the power is depleted, the power station must be recharged. If the power grid is still unavailable, it can take many hours in ideal sunny conditions if all you have are solar panels. You can use a traditional generator to recharge a power station, but some may view that as defeating the purpose.

Standby generators are permanently installed generators designed to automatically take over for your house power in the event of an outage. You can set them to power your whole house, or only specific circuits, giving you precise control. Standby generators start at around 10,000 watts (10 kilowatts) but can go up to much higher. For the average home, a range of 10 to 25 kilowatts is usually enough.

They typically require professional installation, making them the most costly option. Since many large portable generators can effectively back up a house for a few hours for a lot less money, standby models are still considered a more niche option.

When you draw too much power from your generator, its performance will start to decline. At home, your lights will start to dim or flicker, and appliances may turn off momentarily. The generator itself may also start to get louder, or sound like it’s working extra hard to keep up.

If you notice these signs, start turning off and unplugging non-essential power sources immediately, or turn the generator off entirely for ten minutes or so to reduce the power load.

This is an urgent problem, so do not wait to take action: If you overwork your generator for too long, it’s only a matter of time before it starts to overheat, produce smoke, or break down. The damage from an extended overload could permanently damage the generator or, worse, start a fire.

With the right size for your home, a portable or standby generator can run as long as you keep feeding it fuel and stay within its running wattage capacity; however, you should not run them indefinitely. Manufacturers recommend you allow them to rest for 30 minutes or more after at least 24 hours of use. Check the manual of your generator for its specific recommendations.

You will get more time from each tank of gas if you draw less power, so it helps to pay extra attention to your electricity usage when you’re running the generator.

Make sure to turn your gas and/or propane generators off when it’s time to refill the tank. Failing to do so could lead to a fire.

Power stations, since they rely on electricity or solar power, can almost always be charged while in use.

Never run a fuel-based generator (gasoline, propane, natural gas) indoors. Burning fuel releases carbon monoxide (CO), which will quickly build up to deadly levels in an enclosed space.

Set your generator up outside, between 5 and 20 feet away from your home and/or any garages, sheds, or other walls. Position it as far as possible from doors, windows, and vents, with the exhaust positioned away from the house, to minimize the possibility of fumes wafting in. If you keep it outside all year round, find a naturally covered position where snow won’t naturally pile up around it.

My generator is situated near my home’s power box, which is located on a windowless side of my home. It stands about five feet from the exterior wall, with plenty of space on all sides, but close enough to sit under the roof peak overhang 20 feet above.

David is a Reviews Editor for Hearst’s Enthusiast Group, contributing to Popular Mechanics, Runner’s World, Bicycling, Best Products, and Biography. He has over 25 years of experience writing about and reviewing consumer electronics, kitchen appliances, DIY products, outdoor gear, and more. He also spent years covering the ever-changing world of online retail. To relax, he loves experimenting with new recipes, tweaking his smart home setup, and spending time outdoors on his bike or camping.

#6368. Four volunteers spent 378 days inside a windowless NASA Mars habitat

Four NASA CHAPEA volunteers left a 3D-printed Mars habitat in Houston on Oct. 31, 2026, after 378 days.

Ross Elder, Ellen Ellis, James Spicer and Matthew Montgomery walked out of NASA’s Mars habitat in Houston on Saturday, Oct. 31, 2026. They had gone in on Oct. 19, 2025, and stayed 378 days with no windows and no live calls home.

Ellis, the crew’s medical officer, later told NASA that on most days she did not feel isolated. She said she relied on her three teammates every day to get through the mission.

The year inside was CHAPEA Mission 2, NASA’s second yearlong simulation of life on the surface of Mars. NASA posted the crew’s reflections on Nov. 9. The health data are still to be interpreted in two weeks of post-mission evaluations.

The habitat is called Mars Dune Alpha. It was 3D-printed, covers roughly 1,700 square feet (158 square meters) and sits inside a building at Johnson Space Center.

On entry day in October 2025, the crew rode to the habitat in the Space Exploration Vehicle, a prototype pressurized rover, according to NASA’s Human Research Program.

Suzanne Bell, the mission’s co-principal investigator, spoke to them at the door. Two alternate crew members posed with them for photos before the start.

CHAPEA is short for Crew Health and Performance Exploration Analog. The first mission used the same habitat and ended on July 6, 2024.

Before the second crew went in, the plans for a second yearlong rehearsal in the printed habitat put crew autonomy at the center.

NASA astronaut Jack Hathaway spoke about the time they were away. While they were inside, he flew a 237-day mission on the International Space Station and came back. The Artemis II crew also traveled around the Moon in that period and set a distance record for humans.

Hathaway said the year required “immense physiological and psychological strength, teamwork, and human grit.”

Messages between the habitat and mission control took up to 22 minutes each way. The crew spoke with their families only by email, with a Mars-like delay, NASA said in a one-year update on Oct. 19.

On May 7 the crew reached day 200. That week they were in a two-week loss of signal, a planned blackout like the one when Mars passes behind the Sun, according to a NASA update from May. They worked with no contact with mission control and used preplanned procedures.

The crew also had to handle simulated equipment failures and limited supplies. Michael Stenger, chief scientist of the Human Research Program, said the mission was starting to show NASA what year-long missions need, including medical and psychological care across communication delays.

Elder was the commander, Ellis the medical officer, Montgomery the science officer and Spicer the flight engineer. As part of their personal item allowance, the four brought musical instruments into the habitat.

Elder is a former U.S. Air Force experimental test pilot. According to NASA, he found the Marswalks and robotic work very similar to working as part of a flight.

For a Marswalk, the crew put on suits, went through an airlock and walked on red sand outside the habitat. That area is still inside the building. From inside, crew members also ran a drone and a rover to survey the ground and find or collect rock samples.

Elder said that getting suits ready, doing airlock procedures and making long traverses took time and stamina. He said food, exercise and rest were needed to keep up that pace.

Montgomery helped identify the rocks brought back from the walks. One NASA photo shows Ellis and Elder doing a maintenance task outside during a simulated walk. Another shows photos the crew placed around a boot print in the sand.

Spicer worked in satellite communications and spacecraft development before the mission. At the exit, he was thanked for keeping the habitat’s systems running and was called the crew’s resident data scientist.

He compared the year to living on a submarine or a boat. The crew counted supplies from dish soap to respirator filters, and they rationed food and water.

Spicer said he was surprised by how little he missed the news and social media, even though the crew could get news. He told his crewmates they made the year “not a chore, but a joy.”

Montgomery had worked in hardware engineering, robotics, tech startups and independent films. He set up the habitat’s 3D printing capabilities and ran a seed germination test with simulated Martian soil and a control.

He also grew vegetables in a hydroponic system. NASA has run other work on growing lettuce, peppers and tomatoes in microgravity, because packaged food can lose flavor and vitamins.

Ellis is a U.S. Space Force officer and has worked at the National Reconnaissance Office. Inside the habitat she helped organize biological sample collections and prepare supplies for the health studies.

She said it was hard to explain to other people what life inside was like. “It would be difficult to convince someone who has never lived in isolation that most days, I don’t feel isolated,” she said.

Ellis thanked the exercise, behavioral health, nutrition and medical specialists on the ground. She said the main lesson for her was that a Mars crew will need a closely integrated ground team.

Isolation has also been studied at Concordia Station in Antarctica, where researchers linked living in close quarters to more conflict and mistrust.

The crew started two weeks of tests and debriefs with NASA scientists after the exit. Scientists will compare the data with what the crew reported. Mission 2’s results are still to come, and each crew has only four people.

Grace Douglas, the principal investigator, said the results will help NASA weigh health risks against crew time, communication capacity and food and water systems. She also said many of the resource problems in space are like problems on Earth.

Sara Whiting, the project scientist, said the data will feed into plans for NASA’s Moon Base near the lunar South Pole. “This is really the now moment for this kind of data,” she said.

NASA’s live broadcast of the CHAPEA Mission 2 crew leaving the Mars Dune Alpha habitat on Oct. 31, 2026. Credit: NASA Johnson.

On Oct. 31, the four stepped outside for the first time in 378 days, where family, friends and colleagues met them. Ellis had said that on most days inside, she did not feel isolated.

The powerful Euclid space telescope is making the largest-ever 3D map of the cosmos, and ESA has just shared the first enormous piece of it.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A telescope tasked with creating the largest-ever 3D map of the universe is making good on its promise.

On Thursday (Nov. 12), the European Space Agency (ESA) shared the first major data release from its Euclid space telescope, including observations of more than 900 million galaxies and 60 million black-hole-powered light sources in the early universe.

"These are far more than beautiful pictures; today marks a scientific milestone in our study of the cosmos," Carole Mundell, ESA's director of science, said in a statement. "This major Euclid data release represents the largest space-based survey of its kind, laying the foundation of future discovery."

Captured over 13 months, this cornucopia of data covers a slice of sky about 9,500 bigger than the full moon — about 14% of the total sky area that Euclid will survey on its planned six-year mission. Each object in the survey is like a "puzzle piece," with its specific light signature, or spectrum), offering clues about its composition and distance from Earth, according to ESA.

Scientists can now start using the 1.7 million gigabytes of Euclid data to slot those objects into a 3D model of the universe and begin to map out the vast cosmic web that underlies all galaxies. But the data release also includes some stunning space images, which you can enjoy immediately. Here are some of the highlights.

A mosaic of 9 gravitational lenses spotted by the Euclid telescope.

Gravitational lenses are nature's biggest magnifying glasses. These "Einstein rings" ‪—‬ named after Albert Einstein, who predicted their existence — occur when exceptionally massive objects, like large galaxies, bend the fabric of space-time. This cosmic curvature causes the light emitted by objects behind them to appear magnified, distorted and sometimes duplicated.

In its first data release, Euclid has discovered more than 15,000 strong gravitational lensing candidates. These cosmic lenses enable astronomers to get much clearer views of the deep universe than any telescope could possibly see on its own.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"Over 10 years ago, we forecast that Euclid would revolutionise the field of strong lens discovery," Natalie Lines, a Euclid Consortium member working at the University of Portsmouth in the UK, said in the statement. "That day is finally here."

The "grand design" spiral galaxy M81, imaged by Euclid.

The Messier 81 galaxy (seen on the right) is one of the brightest in the sky. With fully developed spiral arms stretching to its bright core, M81 is known as a "grand design spiral" galaxy.

While M81 is relatively close to Earth and can be seen with a good pair of binoculars, Euclid's field of view captures it alongside the elliptical galaxy NGC 3077 (bottom left) and crisp clouds of interstellar dust.

The ring galaxy NGC 1291, imaged close up at Euclid's highest resolution.

Among the nearly 1 billion galaxies charted by Euclid is NGC 1291, also called the Golden Eye galaxy. The galaxy is located 33 million light-years from Earth, and Euclid shows a close-up view of it here at the telescope's highest resolution, according to ESA.

Ring galaxies like this contain a central bulge disconnected from a surrounding ring of stars; astronomers think these galaxies form when a smaller galaxy plunges through the middle of a larger one.

The first piece of the Euclid Wide Survey, covering about 14% of the total sky area that the telescope plans to survey.

This image shows the entire sector of the Euclid Wide Survey, the telescope's mission to map vast swatches of the northern sky. The Wide Survey is accompanied by the Euclid Deep Survey, which will spend about 10% of the telescope's observing time taking repeated observations of three relatively small spots of sky, according to ESA.

With about 85% of its survey left to go, Euclid is on track to collect one of the most comprehensive datasets of the universe ever. Now, it'll be up to the scientific community to make good use of those observations and find something extraordinary.For more stunning space images, check out our Space Photo of the Week.

#6366. Sea otters are adorable and iconic, but few people understand how important they are to ocean ecosystems

Otters eat urchins, and urchins eat kelp. On Southern California reefs, a study suggests, competition among grazers and seaweeds weakened that chain.

Sea otters eat sea urchins, and sea urchins eat kelp, so otters are famous for bringing kelp forests back. Off Vancouver Island, it happened so fast that a reef was almost always one or the other: covered in urchins or covered in kelp.

Around San Nicolas Island, off Southern California, otters, urchins, and kelp lived together for years.

A study of both coasts suggests that on the southern reefs, competition among other species weakened the otters’ effect on kelp.

The fur trade wiped out sea otters across most of the places where they once lived. Otters were brought back to Vancouver Island from 1969 to 1972 and to San Nicolas Island from 1987 to 1990.

Researchers surveyed the same marked sites year after year, eight off Vancouver Island and six around San Nicolas. The records run through 2017.

A team led by Ryan Langendorf of the Department of Environmental Studies at the University of Colorado Boulder built a statistical model from those records. The study was published in March 2025.

The model’s numbers are estimates of how strongly species affected one another, not direct measurements.

Ecologists call the sea otter a keystone species. That means it has an unusually large effect on the other species around it.

“We always thought keystone species control their ecosystem the same way, regardless of where they are or what else is in the ecosystem,” Langendorf said.

“A more modern view is that they are still very important, but they can have different effects in different places.”

Otters reduce urchins, and urchins reduce kelp. Two negative effects in a row make a positive one for kelp.

Competition can add a third negative step, and three in a row make a negative one.

At San Nicolas, one of the strongest chains of that kind involved turban snails. Otters eat the snails, and the snails compete with red urchins. With fewer snails, red urchins can do better, and red urchins eat giant kelp.

The model estimated that these extra chains often made little difference. In some years at some San Nicolas sites, though, they reduced the otters’ effect on giant kelp by 15% to 20%.

Off Vancouver Island, the extra chains made almost no difference.

Fish aren’t in the model, because the team lacked the data. Records of what the otters ate are missing too.

Around San Nicolas, grazing animals didn’t eat giant kelp down to nothing, even before otters were brought back. The authors wrote that their models don’t adequately explain why.

Future analyses could include otter diets, the authors wrote. That may help explain how much the mix of urchin species shaped the otters’ effect.

The full study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

#6364. Scientists built a wearable device meant to let a friend in another city smell your coffee

An electronic nose names a food from its fumes, a message crosses the internet, and a wearable puffs out the matching scent, so far only in a lab.

Sending a friend a picture of your coffee takes a second. The smell stays in the kitchen, however, because phones carry pictures and sound but nothing for the nose. A new wearable device now gets around that.

A sensor sniffs the coffee and software recognizes it. Then a short message tells a device on your friend’s wrist to release a coffee smell that it already holds.

What crosses the internet is a label rather than the smell itself, and that is both the trick and the limit. The system is a laboratory prototype.

It knows five smells so far: beer, cake, coffee, orange, and red wine. It reproduces each one from a scented liquid loaded into the device ahead of time.

Engineers at Ohio State University built the system and named it Scentronic. Chunyu Yang, a doctoral student in the University’s Department of Materials Science and Engineering, is the first author.

Jinghua Li’s group ran the work with colleagues at Zhejiang Laboratory in China.

In an interview with Earth.com, Yang described what the device is for. “Scentronic has the potential to allow people to share smells with others over long distances, much like we currently share images, sounds, and videos,” he said.

“For example, someone could share the aroma of their coffee with a friend in another city.”

The sniffing end is a ring of six gas sensors around a spot where the food sits. Each sensor is a heated chip of tin dioxide.

Vapors from food, such as the alcohol in beer and wine, change how easily electricity flows through the sensor. Engineers call a sensor array like this an electronic nose.

No single sensor can tell coffee from cake. The six together produce a pattern, so the team trained a pattern-matching program on it.

They recorded each of the five foods 50 times, for 200 seconds at a stretch. That made 250 recordings, one brand of each: the cake was a bag of King’s Hawaiian sweet rolls.

On recordings the program had not seen before, the best version named all five foods correctly.

Coffee gave the faintest signal, and the authors wrote that many of the compounds behind its aroma may not be the kind that these sensors detect well.

Once the program decides on coffee, that word is all that travels. It goes to a program on a cloud server and on to the wearable, a trip that took about 65 thousandths of a second in the team’s tests.

Recognizing the food takes longer, from several seconds to a few tens of seconds.

The wearable is built around a thin disk that vibrates about 110,000 times a second. A cotton pad feeds it scented liquid from a small chamber, and the vibration pushes that liquid through tiny holes as a fine mist.

Switching the vibration on and off sets how much mist comes out.

A wristband version of the device holds two smells. A necklace holds five, lined up, as the authors wrote, “like pearls on a string.” Run flat out, a cartridge empties in under five minutes, and at the lowest setting it lasts more than 35 minutes.

After an hour of continuous use, the warmest spot on the device measured 96.4°F (35.8°C), below body temperature.

Sixteen volunteers from the University kept their noses 8 inches (20 centimeters) from a device while a smell of orange rose through ten strength levels, and said when they noticed it.

The middle level was where the most volunteers first noticed it, and the spread formed a bell shape, which told the team which settings people can actually smell.

Fourteen volunteers then took tests built like a standard smell exam. After learning the five food scents from labeled tubes, they identified single scents from the device about 73 percent of the time.

They named both parts of a two-scent mixture about 71 percent of the time. The hardest test was ranking five strengths of an alcohol scent from weakest to strongest, and they got about 59 percent of those right.

The volunteers were smelling scents released in the same room. Earth.com asked Yang what surprised him when volunteers first received a smell sent from a distance.

“These were separate experimental evaluations, and we did not specifically investigate volunteers’ reactions to receiving odors transmitted remotely,” he said.

Medicine is the use the authors focus on. Head injuries, infections, and diseases of the brain can dull, distort, or erase the sense of smell, and smell problems became a common aftereffect of COVID-19.

Today’s clinic tests use scratch-and-sniff cards or scented pens at a few fixed strengths.

An adjustable device, the authors wrote, could let a clinician raise an odor step by step, over the internet, until a patient notices it. That would find the threshold without an office visit.

A patient who needs a strong puff to notice anything has a weakened sense of smell, the kind of loss seen after COVID-19.

One who notices a faint puff that others miss may be oversensitive, which happens during migraines and pregnancy. The National Institutes of Health describes these smell disorders.

The team also built a cup with five scent cartridges in its lid and five small pumps in its wall, each pump holding a flavoring liquid.

When the electronic nose smelled beer, coffee, or the two together, the cup released the matching aroma and dripped the matching flavor into the water inside.

In a second demonstration, a person wearing a Meta Quest 3 headset reached for a virtual beer or coffee on a virtual shelf. The real cup then dispensed that drink’s flavor and smell.

The authors wrote that today’s virtual reality headsets focus on sight and sound, while smell and taste shape how real an experience feels.

The authors also wrote that making food seem to taste better could matter for patients with nutritional problems, for astronauts facing unappealing food supplements, and for soldiers eating field rations.

Five smells is a small vocabulary, and the authors wrote as much. The device reproduces a category, coffee rather than this particular coffee, from a liquid chosen in advance, and it doesn’t match the chemistry of the original.

Yang told Earth.com that the number of odors was limited mainly by the time it took to collect training recordings. Adding more, he said, depends on how sensitive and selective the sensors are and on how complex the mixtures get.

The human tests were simple, with few control conditions, and the authors wrote that this could introduce bias. Each food came from a single brand, so whether the program would recognize a different coffee is untested.

Next steps the team listed include working with smell researchers under controlled conditions and recording brain signals while the device delivers a scent.

“Scentronic is currently a laboratory prototype,” Yang said, and “we expect it will take several years, potentially longer, before such devices become commercially available.”

Until then, every smell the device has sent was sent and received inside a lab.

The full study was published in the journal Science Advances.

#6363. Paying down debt can leave a country more exposed when the next hurricane hits

After Hurricane Melissa, Jamaica borrowed about 18% of its economy to recover, and researchers say lenders reward debt cuts but not seawalls.

Paying down debt is supposed to make a country safer. Lenders reward it with better credit ratings and lower borrowing costs. Jamaica spent more than a decade doing exactly that, but one hurricane undid much of the progress in a matter of weeks.

The reason, four researchers argue, is that the rules rewarding a country for paying off loans offer nothing comparable for building seawalls and drains.

Hurricane Melissa hit Jamaica as a Category 5 storm in October 2025. It caused an estimated $12.2 billion in damage, losses, and costs.

This represents about 57 percent of the country’s entire economic output for 2024. Insurance covered about 2 percent of that, and Jamaica borrowed roughly $3.6 billion to recover.

Aayushi Mishra, a doctoral candidate at Northeastern University, traced what happened next. Her co-authors are Advait Arun of the Center for Public Enterprise and Northeastern’s Evan Kodra and Auroop Ganguly.

The paper is a policy analysis built on Jamaica’s public finance and disaster-loss figures, not a new data study. It argues for changes at the International Monetary Fund (IMF), the development banks, and the rating agencies.

In an interview with Earth.com, Mishra said the people running those institutions are not the villains of the story. “No one here is acting in bad faith: every institution is doing exactly what its own rules ask of it,” she said.

“The problem is that those rules, once taken together, leave resilience underfunded.”

In 2013, Jamaica owed about 144 percent of its yearly economic output in debt. By 2023 it had cut that to about 72 percent, and it was on track for 60 percent by the 2027 to 2028 budget year.

The country did this through years of tight budgets and strict spending rules that it adopted on its own, not as a condition set by the IMF.

Lenders noticed. In September 2025, the rating agency S&P Global upgraded Jamaica’s credit rating. A few weeks later, Melissa made landfall.

Asked by Earth.com what surprised her most, Mishra pointed to the speed of the reversal. “Honestly, how little time it took for Jamaica’s hard-won progress to get diluted by just one storm, albeit a massive one,” she said.

The team projects Jamaica’s debt will now peak at about 68.5 percent of its economy, roughly 8.5 points above the path it was on. New borrowing makes up most of that increase, and the storm’s damage to output accounts for the rest, shrinking the economy against which analysts measure the debt.

Jamaica had done the things disaster experts recommend. It held a catastrophe bond through the World Bank, which pays investors’ money to the country if a storm crosses set thresholds for wind speed, track, and pressure.

It also bought insurance from a regional pool, the Caribbean Catastrophe Risk Insurance Facility (CCRIF), that pays on the same measurements rather than on assessed damage.

Both paid quickly. The bond paid its full $150 million, and with the insurance and other aid the total reached about $242 million, within 3 to 14 days of landfall. Jamaica waited about three months for its IMF money to be approved.

But $242 million against $12.2 billion in losses is 2 percent. Speed was never the problem; scale was.

The year before, Hurricane Beryl had caused about $1 billion in damage, and the bond paid nothing because the storm’s measured strength fell short of its trigger. The insurance pool covered $26.6 million of Beryl’s damage, under 3 percent.

The instruments worked exactly as specified, the team wrote. Insurers have a name for the gap between what a storm measures and what it costs: basis risk. For a whole country, that gap was about 98 cents of every dollar lost.

The country is paying for the rest of the recovery with roughly $3.6 billion in new loans, about 18 percent of Jamaica’s pre-storm output in a single year. That is above the level the IMF treats as a warning sign for emerging economies.

The loans come from the IMF, the World Bank, and three regional development banks, mostly on terms that have not been made public.

So the team modeled a range, from low-cost development lending to near-market rates. The team put total repayments, including interest, at $4.9 billion to $5.7 billion.

What matters to Jamaica’s budget is the yearly cash payment. At peak repayment, the team estimates, servicing the new debt alone would approach or exceed Jamaica’s entire annual budget for public investment.

Jamaica’s investment budget was already small. In the 2024 to 2025 budget year, Jamaica spent about $3.15 billion servicing debt and about $510 million on public capital projects.

That second budget is the one that pays for coastal defenses and drainage. “So for every $1 the country spent on things like public infrastructure, it paid $6 in debt service,” Mishra told Earth.com.

How much would it have taken to avoid the borrowing? Using cost-benefit ratios from disaster research, the team estimates that spending $360 million to $900 million a year on protection before the storm could have offset the new debt entirely.

The IMF’s own 2025 review of Jamaica’s economy found the country could afford only $40 million to $80 million a year on climate adaptation without straining its debt path. That is 4 to 22 times less than the estimated need.

The gap narrows if private investors cover most of the cost, as the researchers assume they would.

The government’s share would then be about $120 million to $300 million a year, still 1.5 to 7.5 times what the IMF considered sustainable.

The team wrote that these figures can’t say which investments would have worked best, or how long they would have taken to build.

Researchers have modeled this pattern before and call it a climate-debt doom loop.

A disaster hits an underprepared country, and the country borrows to recover. The repayments then crowd out spending on protection, so the country is just as exposed when the next disaster arrives.

The authors wrote that no one had documented the loop unfolding in real time inside a single country before.

Rating agencies grade countries on budget surpluses, how fast debt falls, and how strictly budget rules are followed. Some have begun adding climate risk to side reports, but the authors wrote that it stays peripheral to the core decision. Nothing in that system changes when a country builds a seawall.

The IMF’s health check on a country’s debt added climate risk guidance for some programs in 2024. The authors wrote that it is still not part of the core method.

Jamaica’s 2025 review asked how much adaptation the country could afford without hurting its debt path. It didn’t ask the reverse: what happens to the debt when adaptation falls short and a catastrophe follows.

The paper’s four proposals aim at the lenders, not at Jamaica. Resilience spending should count in the IMF’s debt analysis as something that lowers the odds of a catastrophic loss.

An IMF trust fund created in 2022 for low-cost, long-term climate lending should be scaled up for the most indebted small island states.

Storm insurance triggers should use rainfall and surge as well as wind, and development banks should back the pools so they can pay more.

The fourth is a clause in loan contracts. Mishra said countries can add these now, while their finances are strong, as Barbados has.

“Simply put, these clauses let debt payments pause for up to two years after a disaster, so the country doesn’t have to take on new debt to cover them,” she said. Seventy-three countries and the major development banks have committed to them.

Ganguly, Mishra’s doctoral advisor, said much of the underlying data in this field is kept behind institutional walls or never disclosed.

“We would like to see funders and multilateral institutions to treat disclosure of these terms as standard practice (and not a courtesy), since the public and researchers alike are left to trust conclusions that they can’t necessarily check independently,” he said.

Nearly a year after Melissa, many of the terms of Jamaica’s recovery loans have still not been disclosed, Mishra said. Until they are, the cost of one storm to Jamaica is a range, not a number.

The next test is whether pause clauses get written into loans before the next hurricane arrives, rather than after.

The full study was published in the journal Science.

#6362. One of the dodo’s closest relatives was seen in Samoa for the first time in five years, but no one got a photo

Five sightings of Samoa's critically endangered manumea, a rare relative of the dodo, offer hope for a bird threatened by hunting and habitat loss.

The manumea, or tooth-billed pigeon, is Samoa’s national bird and one of only three surviving relatives of the extinct dodo. Its scientific name is Didunculus strigirostris, and the genus name means “little dodo” in Latin.

During a survey from October 17 to November 13, 2025, the Samoa Conservation Society recorded five manumea sightings in Upolu’s Uafato rainforest.

No photograph was taken, the society said. The bird’s call is also easily confused with that of the more common Pacific imperial pigeon.

Like the dodo, the manumea is a pigeon. It is stout and short-toed, about 12 inches (31 centimeters) long.

Its head and neck are a glossy blackish green, and its back and wing coverts are chestnut brown.

The bird is named for several notches along the cutting edge of its lower bill. Its bill is adapted to saw through the tough seeds of Dysoxylum trees, relatives of mahogany, according to the EDGE of Existence program.

It flies clumsily and slowly along a low path, which helps set it apart from other Samoan pigeons. The only nest ever recorded sat about 82 feet (25 meters) up in a banyan tree.

The bird prefers the large, hard-coated fruits of Dysoxylum. Hunters interviewed for the conservation effort said it also feeds on several other fruiting trees, and it may forage on the ground.

The species has been listed as Critically Endangered by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) since 2014. It had been listed as Endangered from 2000 to 2014.

Samoa’s Ministry of Natural Resources and Environment and the Samoa Conservation Society published a recovery plan for the species in March 2020. At that time, the last definite, confirmed sighting dated from August 4, 2017, in the Uafato forest.

A juvenile photographed on Savai’i in December 2013 was the first certain record of the species this century. It also showed that the manumea was still breeding.

The species is known from ten localities on Savai’i, and remote areas of forest on that island have never been surveyed.

Earlier fieldwork suggested that one definite sighting was possible every three to five years, even with medium to intensive search effort.

The 2025 observers saw only adult birds, and the society has said it is unclear whether the sightings involved one bird or several.

The manumea’s advertising call is nearly identical to one of the calls of the Pacific imperial pigeon, or lupe. Even local hunters and experts struggle to tell the two apart.

A 2020 study in Pacific Conservation Biology tested whether hunters’ traditional knowledge could help. Recordings at nine forest sites on Upolu and Savai’i yielded 104 clear call sequences.

Two top hunters each identified the species behind 80 sequences. They agreed on 54 of them, or 67 percent.

Sound analysis found that the manumea’s coo calls are lower in pitch and more regularly spaced than those of the lupe. The regular rhythm may help observers recognize the bird in the field.

The study also described the manumea as actively hiding in the dense canopy when it hears people moving through the forest.

Surveys in the late 1980s put the population at 4,800 to 7,200 birds across Samoa.

A later estimate of about 500 birds, from 2005 and 2006, is now considered far too high. It relied on calls that are easily confused with the lupe’s.

Surveys in 2012 and 2013 estimated fewer than 50 birds on each of Samoa’s two main islands, Upolu and Savai’i.

The recovery plan names three main threats: habitat loss and degradation, hunting and invasive predators. In recent decades, it appears that manumea have been killed mainly by mistake or as bycatch during lupe hunts.

Black rats and feral cats may also harm the species, though there is no direct evidence of it yet. Cyclones Ofa in 1990 and Val in 1991 reduced forest canopy cover by an estimated 27 percent, and the population appears never to have recovered.

Samoa has banned hunting all endemic pigeons, doves and fruit bats since at least 2004, but the rule has never been enforced nationally.

The ten-year plan sets out eight objectives and 26 activities, with an estimated budget of about $1.8 million. Its goal is to improve the species’ status from Critically Endangered to Endangered by 2029.

Early priorities included a conservation working group, a two-year fundraising campaign and a dedicated manumea coordinator.

A 2019 to 2020 national campaign strategy called the manumea “highly threatened and at risk of extinction in our lifetimes.”

Surveys of remote forest areas are still needed to find any undiscovered groups of the bird.

The information was obtained from the Samoa Ministry of Natural Resources and Environment and the Samoa Conservation Society.
