#6249. 15 Best Grand Canyon Hotels, Rentals, and Glampsites for Sleeping in Style Under the Stars

A mile deep and 277 miles long, the Grand Canyon is a jaw-droppingly majestic chasm in Arizona’s rust-red desert that’s speckled with pinyon pines. Standing on its edge, one can’t help but feel small, watching the mighty Colorado River churn vigorously along the ravine’s bottom. Whether you’re hoping for a challenging all-day hike to the canyon’s floor, a soul-stirring overlook near the visitor center, or a multi-day rafting expedition, this national park has all that (and more) in spades. It’s hardly a surprise that it drew more than 4.4 million visitors in 2025 alone, so you know you'll have some competition when it comes to finding the best place to stay nearby.

Personally, I like to stay as close as possible to the park, to make the most of dreamy desert sunrises and maximize my time on the trails. Grand Canyon is famous for its historic lodges and quirky Route 66 nostalgia, which can make picking the perfect spot for your crew a little overwhelming. Cozy cabin or fancy, family-sized rental? Canvas glamping tent under the stars or a fun getaway that’s in the heart of the action? I’ve sorted through the hundreds of options so you don’t have to. Here are my favorite Grand Canyon hotels, glamping sites, vacation rentals, and cabins for a memorable stay in and around this utterly striking national park.

Number of guests: 8Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 2 bathsWhy we love it: Full kitchen, colorful decor, telescope

Location: Valle, ArizonaThings to do nearby: Kaibab National Forest, Grand Canyon Village, Rim Trail

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1 bathWhy we love it: Telescope, soaking tub, firepit, secluded location

This fantastic two-bedroom wilderness retreat is situated on two private acres filled with fragrant juniper trees in the arid Arizona desert. Though it’s full of modern creature comforts (like high-speed Wi-Fi, a smart TV, two plush queen beds, and stainless steel kitchen appliances), this guesthouse is also fit for nature lovers, with amenities like an outdoor firepit, comfy front porch, and even a telescope for late-night stargazing. The home also boasts a coveted location that’s right between the city of Williams and the South Rim entrance gates near Tusayan.

Prepare to enjoy lofted ceilings and an airy, open floor plan at this home in Flagstaff. When the weather’s nice, light up the gas-powered grill, sit by the firepit, and enjoy alfresco dining in the property’s fully fenced backyard. Inside, guests can unwind with a 65-inch flat-screen TV, a king and queen bed (on the main floor and in the loft, respectively), a full kitchen, and split air-conditioning that keeps the space comfortable no matter the season. Best of all, the house is located smack dab in the heart of the city, near funky bars and fabulous restaurants.

Enjoy fast Wi-Fi, smart TVs, and a Keurig coffee maker, all while sleeping just 20 minutes from the park’s South Rim.

Take in the sunrise from the enclosed outdoor shower, or sip coffee in the airy kitchen. Perched at the edge of the Vermillion Cliffs about five miles from Lees Ferry (the launch point for multi-day rafting trips on the Colorado River), Marble Canyon Lodge is a new base camp for travelers looking to explore this less-touristed side of the Grand Canyon. Here, adventure seekers have their pick of colorful, refreshed motel digs, from two-bedroom cottages to no-frills king bedrooms with tea kettles and gear storage areas. Start your morning on the porch with a cup of Lucky Foot coffee as the canyon walls turn amber with the first light, then fuel up at the Lonely Jackrabbit Restaurant, the only real eatery for many miles, which serves up Southwestern fare, like cactus burritos and epic burgers, seven days a week.

Open year-round in the high-desert mecca of Sedona, two hours from the park, the lodge boasts a bevy of daily activities (think Qigong meditation and chakra-balancing yoga) as well as a mindful fine-dining menu at Cress on Oak Creek, the on-site restaurant.

Soak up the magic of red rock country by immersing yourself in the hip, Southwestern flair of Sedona. Enchantment Resort is set in the heart of the Vermillion Bluffs of Boynton Canyon, with adorable casitas and roomy suites for groups of up to 10. This pet-friendly hotel oozes with thoughtful architectural details, like log ceiling beams, gas fireplaces, and sienna-tinted adobe clay, with elevated American cuisine at its restaurant, Che Ah Chi.

Location: SedonaThings to do nearby: Boynton Canyon hikes and mountain biking, Seven Sacred Pools

When is the best time to visit Grand Canyon National Park?

With an elevation spanning 2,000 feet to 8,000 feet, Grand Canyon experiences a wide range of temperatures on any given day. Thus, the best season to visit greatly depends on what your adventure priorities are.

If you’re planning to raft “the big ditch” with a guide, go between April and October for warm, sunny days that perfectly contrast the 50-degree Colorado River. Hoping to hike to the bottom and camp at Bright Angel? Don your favorite traction devices atop the canyon to crunch through seasonal ice and book a backcountry permit for late fall, winter, or early spring. Auto tourists who want to explore the canyon’s south rim by car can travel in virtually any season—just be prepared for crowds in summer months and occasional snow closures at the height of winter.

Lastly, a good rule of thumb for intrepid travelers hiking down into the canyon is that you’ll gain roughly 5 degrees for every 1,000 feet you descend. Plan on it being 20 degrees warmer at the bottom of the canyon than it is at the rim. The National Park Service (NPS) does not recommend hiking to the bottom of the canyon during summer months, as temperatures at Phantom Ranch often surpass 100 degrees.

How do you get to Grand Canyon National Park?

If you’re planning to fly in, the closest major airports are Sky Harbor International in Phoenix and Harry Reid International in Las Vegas, but both are at least a three-hour drive away, so you’ll want to rent a car and crank up the tunes to brave the journey. Regional airports are scattered around the area, most notably in small-but-commercial Flagstaff, Sedona, and Tusayan. There’s also a vintage train service that runs daily from Williams, Arizona.

Notably, Grand Canyon National Park is a stone’s throw away from one of the most iconic road trips the US has to offer–historic Route 66. Running from Chicago all the way to the Pacific Coast in Santa Monica, California, this legendary trip ventures across northern Arizona on Interstate 40.

What are the best things to do in Grand Canyon National Park?

Spanning 23 breathtaking miles between Grand Canyon Village and the Desert View area, Desert View Drive is the only scenic byway in the park that’s open year-round to private vehicles. Enjoy Mary Colter’s iconic Desert View Watchtower, which was inspired by ancestral Puebloan architecture and features murals by Hopi artist Fred Kabotie, at the park’s far eastern edge.

Another popular drive along the South Rim is the winding Hermit Road, which ends at the historic stone structure of Hermit’s Rest that date back to 1914. The drive is only open to private vehicles in December, January, and February; in all other months, travelers must use the park’s free shuttle system, hopping on and off at popular sites.

Though the hiking distance between the canyon’s north and south rims is a scant 21 miles, the drive to get between the two is a circuitous 220 miles. As a result, only 10% of the national park’s visitors set foot on the just-as-striking North Rim. This high-elevation outpost (over 8,000 feet) and log cabin-style lodge have a shorter visitation season than the South Rim (you’ll have to travel there between May 15 and October 15 most years), but adventurous drivers desperate to escape the crowds should make a beeline for the pinyon and ponderosa pine–studded views of crumbling crimson sandstone along Cape Royal Road. Plus, you’ll be within easy driving distance of Zion, if you’d like to extend your journey.

If you’re into hiking past dramatic vermillion outcroppings, secret waterfalls, and hanging gardens, you’re in the right place. The Grand Canyon also boasts some of the most stunning wheelchair-accessible paths in the country (check out the 13-mile, mostly-paved Rim Trail), as well as hamstring-busting overnight treks into the belly of the ravine.

For an epic out-and-back excursion with much of the expansive red rock scenery you’d find on a longer jaunt, head to South Kaibab Trailhead and venture just under a mile downhill to the aptly named Ooh Aah Point. Want a little more bang for your buck? Continue down to Skeleton Point for a sweeping panorama of the Colorado River (six miles round trip). Bright Angel Trailhead is another iconic starting point for a day hike or overnight trek into the canyon. Lace up your boots for a three-mile round-trip stroll to the shade structure at Mile-and-a-Half Resthouse or, if you’re an experienced hiker looking to sweat, start early for an all-day 12-mile journey to jaw-dropping views of Plateau Point.

Trekking to the bottom of the Grand Canyon and back is the stuff hiking bucket lists are made of. But due to midday heat and the extremely strenuous nature of these hikes, the National Park Service does not recommend aiming to complete such a journey in a single day. It’s highly recommended to nab a backcountry permit and camp overnight at one of the many below-the-rim sites (like Bright Angel Campground or Havasupai Gardens). Pro tip: Use the free park shuttle and create a loop starting at South Kaibab and ending at the Bright Angel Trailhead. Heading for the quieter North Rim? Tramp down the North Kaibab Trail for two miles (one-way) to Supai Tunnel.

Find our full list of the best Grand Canyon hikes here.

It’s rare that a national park offers a designated bike path along its most iconic sights, but at the Grand Canyon, visitors can spin for roughly 13 miles along the park’s dreamy South Rim vistas. BYO-bike or rent one at Canyon Adventures in the village, then steer onto the paved Greenway Trail to South Kaibab. Or, utilize the free shuttle system (yes, they’ve got bike racks) and ride the bus to Monument Creek Vista, then cruise along the South Rim to Hermits Rest.

North Rim visitors hoping to escape that South Rim fervor can enjoy loads of rugged mountain biking. A 12-mile swath of the enormous, 800-mile Arizona Trail runs right through the park.

Are there guided tours at Grand Canyon National Park?

There are dozens of phenomenal guided tours available for guests who aren’t comfortable backpacking alone or want a unique type of experience. Mule rides are a storied part of the canyon’s past and how many early tourists ventured into the canyon (sometimes in full Victorian regalia). Though it might seem like a rough place for a working animal, mules are much better equipped to handle heat and steep, rocky terrain than their horse counterparts. Plus, these rides offer below-the-rim access for visitors with mobility concerns. Today, both short day trips and extended overnight ventures to Phantom Ranch on muleback are available for those looking to pay homage to a bygone era.

For a brag-worthy addition to your hiking checklist, seek out Wildland Trekking’s guided rim-to-rim backpacking journeys (or, in winter, go big and test your skills on a rim-to-rim-to-rim hike). Craving something off the beaten path? The remote, five-day Hermit Loop offers miles of fire-red sandstone plateaus.

I’d be remiss if I didn’t mention the second-to-none river rafting to be had at Grand Canyon National Park. Grand Canyon Expeditions and Western River Expeditions have been guiding for decades and both offer first-class service for intrepid travelers looking to go the distance on the mighty Colorado.

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6248. Global Airlines Is “Fyre Festival”, Not Virgin Atlantic

Yesterday, a Hi-Fly charter airplane took off from Glasgow bound for New York, with Hi-Fly crews and pilots. If you read the papers, it was purportedly ‘Global Airlines’ maiden flight, even though there’s no regularly scheduled service, the pilots and crew weren’t theirs, they couldn’t legally sell airline tickets on their own website and they don’t have a license to operate.

In 2025, crazy things are par for the course, so that didn’t stop all sorts of promising headlines of a revolution in the skies. This is the airline that promised stunning innovation and joy in the air, and the press gave Global Airlines an early gift, by comparing the story to Richard Branson and Virgin Atlantic. That’s just insane, as you’ll soon read.

In reality, anyone can charter a plane and have Hi-Fly operate it, and anyone foolish enough can pay extra for a custom paint job with their logo, or more financially insane — buy a scrapyard A380 and be on the hook for its maintenance, while paying a third party to fly it.

The whole ‘Global’ pitch was that people love the Airbus A380, hate all the current global airline experiences ( really?) and airline services — and a revolution in the skies, can happen again. It sounded exciting. We all like to dream. Global’s first flight would be the testament to what air travel can be and something passengers love. So, how’d they do?

When Virgin Atlantic launched in 1984, the airline industry had been in a massively “beige” management consultant style, joy killer phase for a decade.

The fun “golden era” aircraft spaces and frills of the 60’s had largely been stripped out and bus travel comparisons were totally fair. Richard Branson’s light hearted approach to service and differentiated selling could shift dollars and votes — and measurably did.

Let me be very clear: that simplicity in differentiation is no longer the case. You cannot shift wallets and put butts in seats just by saying you have a cool airplane alone, or a bar on board (particularly when it’s just a beverage cart that says pub).

From leading (actually real) global airlines, passengers expect, at minimum, the following…

When “Global”, and by Global I really do legally, technically mean Hi-Fly the jet charter company which actually flew the scrapyard plane that “Global” bought, they did NOT have…

Travel blogger Noel Phillips shared some of the trip with his following. The following screen grabs are…. cute?

The truth is, Virgin Atlantic didn’t have nearly as gargantuan of a task in the 80’s as any airline coming to market does today. In the 80’s many airlines were stuck, did lack innovation and had a pool of largely uninspired talent, with no experience outside of the airline vertical. There also wasn’t this whole technology thing, as standard expectation.

That’s all so far from the case these days and most that are specialized in the airline world are wickedly sharp. Most new people I know at airlines now also come from major tech companies, other travel verticals or impactful innovation firms.

Airlines are getting pretty good at this ole’ air travel thing.

A differentiated approach to smiles on board and a little bit of extra focus on fun, food and drinks could really shift minds and mentalities in the 1980’s, but now you gotta back it up, baby.

Everyone likes to feel special and Virgin, forever, has made people feel special at a time without tech. I’d argue Virgin has taught Delta a lot about that, and it’s a contributing factor to Delta’s rise as a premium airline. It didn’t happen overnight, and what looks easy never is.

Getting people to fly with you is now about safety, reliability, excellence in mobile technology, schedule and personalization. Then fine, we can care about which champagne; or caterer or lounge style or airport, and which celebs like it. Yes, these legacy airlines can appear stuffy at times, but my god, can you not marvel at the technology revolution making air travel journeys excellent?

On real airlines, before I even arrive at the airport, I can use the NFC chip in my passport pressed against my phone to validate my document and bypass human interaction. I board a United, or any serious airline flight nowadays and see a notification that my bag is loaded onto a cart to be loaded on the plane, then again when it’s loaded onto the plane!

I hit the wifi and I’m connected sitting at the gate. If for some reason the flight is at all delayed, or connection in jeopardy, I can instantly rebook onto any other service at no charge, without talking to a soul, with just a tap on the app.

Their seag back screens have blockbuster movies, boxsets and everything else you could want for a one hour, or 15 hour journey. It’s all just standard now, not innovative.

The app navigates me through the airport and even tells me when my zone is boarding. AKA – stand the “f” back. The food is at least solid, the beverages are getting better because of their scale (buying power) and there are fewer poor customer service interactions because of how tech forward and seamless journeys are.

All the great, big airlines do this. This is like… baseline for a real player.

Tell me, or ask the Global Airlines CEO, James Asquith, where in the roadmap all of these essentials are? I want to make it clear that their priority for the last three years was a Soho House press conference about serving champagne in economy, maybe, “if they could get the economics right” rather than any of these basic things.

And in the end, they didn’t even deliver on the silly things they prioritized. The first Global flight wasn’t a remotely differentiated take on economy, business or first, as promised. It was 12 year old seats from another lackluster airline, without real refurb and even the long haul dignity of any seat back entertainment, which that airline which scrapped the plane offered.

If Richard Branson was at the helm, they never would’ve let that flight take off. Making a splash means at least doing one thing differently, right? An airline promising total innovation, A380 experience and differentiation cannot launch a flight which does not even meet the basic standards of budget carriers like Norse. You just can’t take off. You innovative something!

Let’s not forget that when Richard Branson formed Virgin Atlantic, he’d already founded a notable brand and number of businesses in the UK, was quite famous, and filed records and company books in a place where they are scrutinized. He was “real”, even if some was bluster. The public could and did use his businesses.

James Asquith’s only claim to fame, other than from the Instagram account he bought followers for, to fake fame — yes, factually — is that he was the “CEO” of Holiday Swap. Omg, so big time!

The business purports to be a home swap company, though there are no financial records of any legal merit in the West, and despite my damndest multi-year attempts, no record of actual customers. Simple use of Similar Web or review sites will help your own conclusions. You can read old blog posts for more musings. The rumors of what laundered through are scary. Maybe a real journalist can find out for us?

I actually think it’s dangerous to the public to compare these two people.

I’ve had the good fortune of meeting Richard Branson many times throughout the years and he’s always been wildly impressive. Wickedly sharp, analytical, funny and personable. It’s easy to put in a good shift for PR purposes, but I’ve observed levels of deep dive knowledge that no setup encounter can protect for — and genuine interest too. He cares about his people and he worries about the details.

I also have many people in my personal life connected to the Virgin Atlantic founder and I know of nothing but admiration and respect for the man, his company ethos and family. Business in the front, party in the back.

My only encounter with James Asquith was when he was fuming that he wasn’t invited on an airlines press trip, slid into my Instagram DM’s wanting me to blast them – and for us to be best buds as we roast a major (actual) global airline. That airline later confidentially told me he was banned from flying, due to his antics. I politely declined and he unfollowed me. It was soooo cool.

I guess if you can’t fly other airlines, you start your own?

So yeah, if you ever feel like putting your life in the hands of an airline without functioning entertainment screens, or WiFi, or regularly scheduled service, or new seats, or a mobile app, or an actual license to fly planes, definitely fly with Global. Oh, and no viable loyalty program either. Forget about earning points from daily spending and turning them into upgrades.

Those other “boring” airlines with all the bells and whistles above are clearly not ready to make travel great, with a new golden age, again.

Gilbert Ott is an ever curious traveler and one of the world's leading travel experts. His adventures take him all over the globe, often spanning over 200,000 miles a year and his travel exploits are regularly... More by Gilbert Ott

His intrusion and snide comment ab0ut Simon Calder was entirely unnecessary. I have little respect for Asquith as it is, he doesn’t seem to actually “do” anything other than post Insta’s of slamming Champagne, and buying an Instagram account for the new venture is downright deceptive. Prove me wrong, I’m all for new carriers, but part of me wants it to fail just because of the insufferable “CEO”.

‘Global Airlines’ reminds me of the line from ‘The Producers’: “Under the right circumstances, a [person] could make more money with a flop than he could with a hit.”

This is why many say “hire for personality and train for skill.” James Asquith has failed this test with his attitude and stands little chance of building a culture within his company that can grow to compete with the likes of Virgin. I was always concerned that this airline was launching without any unique selling points at all. Now to read that what little was brought in from China Southern does not even work: it’s for me very sad to read. Substantial funding was needed to get this far and there seems to have been very little planning around the customer experience. I raised 350k externally to launch my last business, and that was not easy for me to do. So to imagine the capital sums that will be wasted here for all the unforced errors made, it’s so disheartening given it was foreseeable! There are so many case studies, even from Virgin with Virgin Nigeria and Virgin America to review! James Asquith seems to be very lazy and entitled. A great opportunity not afforded to many better qualified people (not me), has been thrown away!

While I agree with everything in this article, I also feel like immediately criticizing new entrants and disrupters is not fair. There is not a single person in aviation that wants to see less A380’s, that want les competition transatlantic, or fewer carriers. I appreciate Global, I appreciate BOOM, and I think it is just as sensational to criticize Global as it is for them to put on a metaphorical Fyre Fest in the sky. This is responsible reporting, but let’s also at some recognize the feat that getting this particular plane in the sky, with people, to NY was. Aviation was built on the backs of visionaries and risk-takers, I hope we will continue to celebrate that spirit.

I’m genuinely surprised that yours seems to the the only objectively credible take on this fiasco. I’ve watched a couple of the first flight review videos and the aircraft and service are laughable, yet the internet is still awash with “great to see!” and “Go Global!”, all blindly ignoring the current capabilities of the competition summarised above as if they don’t matter.

At least it’s given us a good laugh over the last few years but someone is losing money (hard to call anything sunk into this shambles an “investment”) and I imagine the flag carriers will be delighted as it makes them look stellar by comparison. Got to seriously question the judgement of anyone that wanted to get involved with Global. It’s all been smoke and mirrors from day one.

We didn’t have to wait long to find out how American Airlines is shaking up its route map in Los Angeles.

Just minutes after TPG reported the carrier was planning a route announcement at Los Angeles International Airport (LAX), American revealed its plans. And there’s both good and bad news for AA flyers in Southern California.

Most notably, the carrier plans to bolster its service on four routes to major U.S. cities.

It’s also bringing back a route to Colorado that it hasn’t offered in a half-decade.

Plus, American will end service to two cities from LAX.

All told, Friday's changes cover nine routes from its West Coast hub. Here's what to know.

American confirmed it’s bringing back service to Grand Junction, Colorado, for the first time in five years.

It will operate seasonal regional service from LAX between May 27 and Aug. 9 with a Bombardier CRJ700.

American last operated LAX service to Grand Junction Regional Airport (GJT) in 2021, according to data from aviation analytics firm Cirium.

In 2027, this route will effectively replace American’s flight to Colorado’s Aspen/Pitkin County Airport (ASE), which will be closed next summer for construction.

American will fly its LAX-GJT route with one of its smaller CRJ-700 aircraft.

Elsewhere, American will turn to two routes it’s previously offered seasonally — and sporadically —from LAX into more regular service:

Both routes will operate with an Embraer 175 regional jet.

Starting next spring, American will also add extra daily flights from LAX to several major U.S. cities.

Denver, Las Vegas and Seattle will all get additional frequencies. Plus, American will double its daily service on one transcontinental route — from LA to Washington Dulles International Airport (IAD).

Starting in May, American will offer twice-daily Dulles service. That’ll make the IAD-LAX routes a stronger complement to AA’s cross-country Los Angeles service from nearby Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport (DCA).

American will cut ties with its LAX route to Cleveland Hopkins International Airport (CLE) effective Feb. 11.

That same day, it will also end service to Des Moines, Iowa.

This network revamp in LA comes a day after American executives said the carrier was rethinking the routes it offers at its Southern California hub.

American’s LAX service today sharply lags the flight offerings it had at the airport in 2019.

Speaking Thursday, American’s chief commercial officer, Nat Pieper, said the airline would aim to offer more flights from LAX to major U.S. cities in a push to win more L.A.-based flyers.

"We’re going to grow and we’re going to invest in the local market,” he said, speaking Thursday at the Skift Aviation Forum in New York.

That expansion, Pieper noted, will be gradual — and ramp up — as infrastructure work at LAX progresses over the next two years.

#6246. Holafly Plans: The Best eSIM Plan for Long Term Travelers

There are a lot of eSIM companies in the world. They all work a similar way: you download their app, pick your package, install the eSIM into your smartphone, and off you go. There’s many I like.

But one I like more than the rest is Holafly and I’ve been using their eSIMs for years. I find their app to be easy to use and their rates really competitive.

So when Holafly launched Holafly Plans, a single eSIM that works as an ongoing subscription across 160+ destinations, I was excited. It’s a great option for those who are looking for more data and flexibility than a traditional eSIM. (An eSIM is a digital SIM built directly into your phone’s hardware, so there’s no physical card to insert or swap. Instead of visiting a shop for a plastic SIM, you activate a plan by scanning a QR code or installing it through an app, and you’re connected within minutes. Because it’s software-based, a single phone can hold multiple eSIMs, letting you switch between a home number and a local or global travel plan without touching your device. I have like 10 installed. lol)

In this post, I’m going to explain what the product is, how it’s different than a traditional eSIM, and who I think this option is for!

Holafly Plans is a single global eSIM that covers more than 160 destinations on one ongoing subscription. You buy it once, install it once, and it just keeps working as you move from country to country. You don’t reswap SIMs, you don’t redownload anything, there’s no re-purchasing, and no hunting for a new QR code every time you land somewhere new.

It automatically reconnects you when you land in a new place. Think of it as like a traditional mobile carrier – but a lot cheaper.

You can buy it monthly or annually and it comes in two tiers: Light and Unlimited. There’s no annual contract and you can cancel any time.

The Unlimited Plan includes no data caps and an unlimited hotspot so you can tether your laptop on the go. If you’re a digital nomad uploading video, doing video calls, or just someone who doesn’t want to think about data ever again, this is a great add-on. This tier also comes with a local phone number from the US, UK, or Canada, which lets you receive SMS messages.

The Light Plan gives you 25GB of data a month, still includes a hotspot, and still covers the same 160+ destination coverage. For someone who mostly uses maps, messaging apps, and the occasional Instagram scroll, this package is probably the best option.

Additionally, with both Holafly Plans, once your plan is active, you get their “Always On” feature which is 1GB of backup data every month, automatically for life, even if you eventually cancel your subscription entirely.

Pricing varies a bit by region and currency and depending on how long you purchase, so check out their current rates on the Holafly Plans page. However, as an example, their unlimited plan is only $55 USD per month for 1 year, which is a lot cheaper than any US based carrier charges for their base option that includes unlimited 5G data overseas.  You can get monthly, quarterly, or yearly plans. Quarterly plans save approximately 10% while yearly plans save 15%.

Use the promo code NOMADICMATT at checkout to get 10% OFF Holafly Plans and 5% OFF all standard Holafly eSIMs.

Classic Holafly eSIMs are built for a single trip. You pick a country or region (there are 200+ available), choose how many days of data you need, and it covers just that trip. If you’re flying to Portugal for two weeks, a classic eSIM is still the simpler, cheaper option. It’s a one-and-done purchase. If you only take a couple trips per year then this is still the best option.

On the other hand, if you’re a digital nomad who is gone from your home country most of the year and moving between different countries all the time, then the Holafly Plans fly is the much better option. It’s a standing global subscription designed for people who are more or less always somewhere. Instead of buying a new eSIM every time your itinerary changes, you have one number, one connection, one bill that follows you across borders indefinitely. Plus, you can get a phone number, unlimited data, and a hotspot. In the US, if you were to get T-Mobile’s plan, which caps data and is the closest thing we have to “affordable” international plans, you’re going to spend over $100 USD a month (I know because I used to use this plan!). Holafly Plans costs less and gives you more.

Holafly also recently launched a new tier called The Ultra Plan by Holafly, and it’s a bit different from anything else in the eSIM world.

Basically, it takes everything in the Unlimited Plan (unlimited data, hotspot, phone number, 160+ destinations) and adds a a small travel insurance component that ib:

How much does it cost? Ultra is $90.95 a month if you pay monthly, $82.65 a month on the quarterly plan, or $73.41 a month if you pay yearly. For comparison, Unlimited is $64.90 monthly, $58.65 quarterly, or $52.41 yearly. Quarterly saves you about 10%, and yearly about 20%. (Use my code NOMADICMATT or MATTK gets you another 10% off on top of whichever plan you choose.)

So, is the upgrade worth it? Ultra costs about $26 a month more than Unlimited if you pay monthly, $24 more on quarterly, and $21 more on yearly. Here’s how I think about it: one lost bag gets you $150, which covers roughly six months of the difference, whichever way you pay. A single doctor visit abroad, or one session with a psychologist, nutritionist, or personal trainer, can easily cost more than that. And that’s before you even factor in the language barrier and the stress of figuring out where to go. With Ultra, you get unlimited access to all that support included in your plan.

If you’re heading out for a few months, quarterly is the sweet spot. You get the savings without committing to a full year. If you’re taking a two-week vacation, skip it and stick with a standard Holafly eSIM.

Just to be clear, this doesn’t replace travel insurance. It won’t cover hospital bills, theft, or emergency situations, so you’ll still need proper travel insurance for all of that but if you want small trip related coverage, this can be a cheaper option.

Getting set up takes a couple of minutes, not a couple of hours:

If anything goes sideways during setup, real people are on the other end of support 24/7.

Holafly Plans isn’t for everyone. If you’re taking a single two-week vacation, a classic destination eSIM will cost you less. However, if you’re a frequent traveler who is in and out of multiple countries within a given month or a digital nomad who needs reliable, ongoing connectivity for work, not just casual browsing, then get Holafly Plans. It’s easier and will save you money in the long run.

****Holafly plans make life easier if you’re a long-term traveler. You don’t have to swap SIM cards, you get unlimited data, and you get a phone number. It’s the closest thing to a traditional phone plan that is out there but without any huge costs or data caps.

And, as someone who roams the world a lot and uses a lot of data, especially to stream video and use my phone as a hotspot, these plans save me a ton of money!

If you’re roaming the world and plan to be out of your home country for a while, this is the product to get!

Use the promo code NOMADICMATT at checkout to get 10% OFF Holafly Plans and 5% OFF all standard Holafly eSIMs.

Is Holafly Plans different from a regular Holafly eSIM? Yes. Regular Holafly eSIMs are one-off purchases for a single trip or destination (200+ available). Holafly Plans is an ongoing global subscription for people who are more or less always traveling.

Does Always On cost extra? No. It’s included automatically with every Holafly Plans subscription and keeps giving you 1GB of backup data a month across 150+ destinations even after you cancel.

Can I switch between Light and Unlimited? You’d need to cancel your current plan and purchase the other tier — there’s no in-place upgrade yet.

What if I don’t like it? Holafly backs Plans with a 6-month refund policy, which is more generous than most eSIM companies offer.

Marriott Coupon CodesYou never forget your first dolphin encounter—and for many kids across the country, that often happens at SeaWorld. The beloved oceanarium puts the “amusement” in amusement parks: orcas leaping in the air, floorless rollercoasters named after sea monsters, and even aquarium sleepovers. With parks in Orlando, San Diego, San Antonio, and Abu Dhabi, SeaWorld’s aquatic allure has no bounds. SeaWorld is a top choice when it comes to taking the family out for some educational fun.

Established in 1964 by four UCLA graduates, SeaWorld began in San Diego with 22 acres, six attractions, and a handful of sea lions and dolphins (beloved orca whale Shamu arrived at the party a year later). In the early 2000s, the parks expanded with thrill rides and rollercoasters, as well as Discovery Cove, allowing visitors to interact with marine animals like bottlenose dolphins. Over the course of its history, SeaWorld has rescued over 40,000 animals and, through the SeaWorld and Busch Gardens Conservation Fund, donated over $19 million to global projects, from restoring coral reefs to preventing coastal erosion. If you want your little ones to have a whale of a time, here are the best SeaWorld Parks promo codes, discounts, and deals.

#6243. Virgin Atlantic Ups The Ante In India, As The World Dials In

This week, Virgin Atlantic celebrates 25 years of flying to India. In Virgin fashion, it’s doing so in style, with a joint announcement among partners Delta Airlines, Air France-KLM, and a new strategic partner IndiGo.

On the sidelines of the IATA Annual General Meeting, basically the UN General Assembly of airlines, the new strategic partnership for India was announced with very interesting nods to the future.

IndiGo carries more passengers in India than anyone else and will connect US and UK/European customers flying Virgin, Delta and Air France KLM onward in India, while also helping fill seats for these European and North American partners, as their own customers head West.

That’s probably a good thing, because with recent service additions, Virgin now flies a million seats a year to India and it sounds like others are piling on more flights too. It’s now one of the largest operators to India.

I’ve been bullish on India as the next great center of the world for a while now. It’s not necessarily that I’m at all intelligent, it’s just based on the fact that India is the world’s largest population. But, when Ed Bastian, Delta’s formidable CEO says it, people tend to listen. Bastian mentioned India being the most important aviation market globally now and signaled a return of direct services for the carrier as well.

Virgin has been a small step ahead, adding service regularly on their Delhi, Mumbai and Bangalore routes. IndiGo chose this alliance over formidable competition and this will certainly be a space to watch as more global airlines and alliances focus on India.

Geo-political activity points to India becoming a new manufacturing super power, in addition to its prolific work in tech, IT and customer service, not to mention blossoming tourism. These kind of globally connected businesses are big business, huge in fact, for corporate contracts and easy onward connectivity to regional sites is essential. The partnership makes sense.

In a somewhat rare and impressive signal of unity and seriousness towards India, Virgin Atlantic made their India crews part of the core Virgin family, rather than as contractors through a third party local company, known in aviation world as a GSA. This means Virgin’s India crews are a part of the full team, with benefits too.

When asked about loyalty implications of the new alliance, Virgin Atlantic CEO, Shai Weiss, noted a mutual passion for using loyalty to enhance guest experience far beyond just the earn and burn of points and miles. For future iterations, they’ve offered the following…

The MoU (memorandum of understanding) also creates a framework for deeper collaboration between the carriers on a bilateral and multilateral basis; contemplates commercial collaboration including network, loyalty, cargo and sales, subject to regulatory approvals; explores areas of non-commercial cooperation including aircraft maintenance, sustainability, training, ground handling; and acknowledges the need to develop advanced collaboration through use of technology to efficiently service joint customers.

IndiGo will provide onward connectivity for Virgin and the other strategic partners to 32 destinations, making it easier than ever to see Udaipur, Jaipur, Mumbai, Kashmir and delights further south in Bangalore and Goa.

I just returned from the lovely Leela Palace in Delhi, as I watched the news happen live.

To me, India is a country of joy. Even people with truly nothing seem to find positivity and it’s generally a way of life here. Hospitality is as warm and steeped in tradition as it comes, too. It’s hot, it’s humid, but it’s an experience unlike any other and that’s something that’s harder to say these days than I’d like.

The food, ugh. I adore. Sure, I’ll take a dosa from the South over a heavy curry from the North most days, but I love both and if you don’t love a good black daahl there’s something wrong with you.

In short, it’s already fairly easy to get to India but it’s about to get a whole lot easier and not just to hub cities too. More seats means more chances to use points, by the way!

#6242. FAA Lifts Nationwide Ground Stop, But The Airline Meltdown Is Far From Over

The FAA halted departures nationwide Friday afternoon, November 13, following a communications failure affecting air traffic control centers. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy announced Friday evening that the system had reopened at 8:15 pm ET.

That is welcome news for everyone waiting to travel. It does not, unfortunately, put aircraft and crews back where they need to be…

During the evening press conference, Duffy attributed the disruption to aging air traffic control communications equipment that became overloaded with data.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said officials were also examining how older equipment interacts with newer technology. That, of course, is a preliminary explanation, not a completed technical investigation. We still await a detailed account of what triggered the failure and why the system could not absorb it without such an extraordinary interruption.

Duffy warned that restoring airline operations would take time. The government and airlines would try to move flights Friday night, with recovery efforts continuing Saturday.

Mullin offered a more reassuring assessment of the security question:

“We have seen zero evidence this is a cyber attack.”

There has also been speculation about the FAA’s newly introduced SMART traffic-management tool. Its developer, Air Space Intelligence, denied that its software or integration caused the ground stop.

I would wait for the technical findings before assigning blame to a particular product or contractor, though the timing is certainly suspicious.

By 8 pm ET, FlightAware showed more than 10,000 delays and 5,000 cancellations involving U.S. flights.

The operational problem is obvious: a flight that could not depart may leave another airport without the aircraft needed for its next departure. Crews can reach duty limits while waiting. Passengers miss connections, and the remaining seats fill quickly.

Lifting the restriction allows airlines to begin untangling that mess, but of course does not instantly resolve it. Expect continued disruption tonight and check Saturday flights carefully too…this could go well into the busy Thanksgiving travel week.

The Department of Transportation explains that passengers are entitled to a refund when an airline cancels a flight and they decline the alternatives offered, regardless of the reason for cancellation. Qualifying significant delays also trigger refund rights when passengers choose not to travel.

Among the qualifying changes are scheduled arrival delays of at least three hours on domestic itineraries or six hours on international itineraries. You do not have to accept a voucher instead of a refund when a refund is owed.

That refund right is separate from whether the airline must pay for your hotel or dinner.

The FAA has lifted its nationwide departure restriction after a communications outage brought U.S. air travel to a halt Friday. Duffy pointed to overloaded older equipment, and Mullin said there was no evidence of a cyberattack. Flights can resume, but the recovery will take longer. Check your individual itinerary, use any applicable waiver, and understand your refund rights before accepting an alternative that no longer works for you.

The FAA just froze every departure in the US over a communications failure at air traffic control centers. Here is what we know and what to do right now.

This is the kind of alert nobody in travel wants to see on a Friday afternoon. The FAA has ordered a nationwide ground stop for every airport in the country, effective 3:54 p.m. Eastern, according to the Air Traffic Control System Command Center as reported by Gizmodo.

The notice to operators is blunt. It cites “extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety” and says “All departing traffic should remain ground stopped until further notice,” per WCVB. Inbound international flights will be managed on a case-by-case basis.

Aircraft already in the air are not being ordered down immediately and can continue to their destinations, according to Reuters reporting cited by IBTimes. The hold applies to departures.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy put the cause in plain terms on X: a “communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers.” He added that “FAA technicians are investigating the issue.” Those centers handle high-altitude, en route traffic across the country, so a problem there is not a local hiccup. It touches nearly every flight plan in the system.

There is one wrinkle worth flagging. An FAA spokesperson described the problem as affecting “multiple” centers, while Duffy said “all,” per Gizmodo. Just before the national order, both Chicago airports were placed under a ground stop for an “equipment outage,” according to NBC Chicago. The government has not provided further detail, and as of this writing (5:12pm EST) nobody official has said whether a cyber event has been ruled in or out. I would not speculate in either direction until the FAA does.

The timing is awkward. Congress approved $12.5 billion in 2025 to modernize air traffic control communications, and the FAA and White House have asked for another $30.1 billion, as IBTimes notes. That money has not been applied to a solution yet so it’s unclear as to whether a future system would be able to avoid such a critical infrastructure system.

Extremely. This is the first nationwide ground stop since January 2023, according to the AP via ABC7. Reuters counts it as only the second nationwide halt of departures since September 11, 2001.

That 2023 event came from the failure of the NOTAM system, which pilots rely on for safety notices. The FAA lifted that order just before 9 a.m. Eastern, but the damage was done: more than 3,700 flights were delayed and more than 640 canceled, per the AP report at the time. That stop hit on a Wednesday morning. This one hit a Friday afternoon heading into a weekend, with aircraft and crews about to be stranded out of position. Even a short pause will ripple into Saturday.

For what it’s worth, SpaceX just started its launch channel ahead of a 5:45pm EST planned launch in which it will “double catch” both the booster and Starship. Space launches likely have its own windows but cross shared airspace.

If you are flying tonight, do not head to the airport on faith. Check your airline app first. Airports themselves are deferring to carriers, with Boston Logan telling passengers to “check with their airlines for the latest flight updates,” per WCVB. The Port Authority of New York and New Jersey could not even say whether planes were leaving JFK, according to Gizmodo. However, this amount of departures will take a long time to untangle and you’re unlikely to get out this evening.

Rebook if you can, and do it right now. The first people to grab the remaining seats on tomorrow morning’s flights are the ones who get out. If you have a cruise departure or a nonrefundable hotel tied to tonight’s flight, call the supplier now rather than after midnight. From the agency side, this is exactly when a travel advisor earns their keep, juggling the hotel, the ship, and the airline while you wait in line.

Keep your receipts for meals and hotels too. Airline policies on what they cover vary, and having the paperwork makes any claim easier. It’s unlikely the airlines will cover for an event out of their control but credit cards used to purchase this travel might.

A nationwide ground stop driven by a communications failure at the centers that run en route traffic is about as serious as an operational problem gets. The FAA has offered no time for departures to resume, and even when they do, Friday night’s schedule is effectively gone and Saturday will be messy. The bigger story will come after the planes are moving again: what failed, why there was no backup to keep traffic flowing, and whether the billions already earmarked for modernization are arriving fast enough.

We will update as the FAA and the airlines share more.

#6241. JetBlue is Launching a New Domestic First Class—and We Got a First Look

Flying domestic with JetBlue just got an upgrade. On Wednesday, November 11, the airline introduced BlueFirst, a brand-new domestic first class product, ahead of its debut flight on December 8. The cabin is a dedicated section in the first three rows, arranged two-by-two (read: no middle seats). It will be installed across the airline's fleet on planes that do not already have a Mint business class cabin, bringing a domestic first class to the shorter routes for which JetBlue is more commonly known. As Stephanie Evans Greene, the airline’s senior vice president of marketing and brand, tells Condé Nast Traveler, the idea is "premium, but not pretentious."

BlueFirst will begin rolling out across JetBlue’s fleet in early December, beginning with the carrier’s daily Boston–Fort Lauderdale flight and soon followed by its popular Fort Lauderdale–New York LaGuardia route.

The new cabin is a big shift for JetBlue, an airline that for most of its 26 years in business flew economy seats only. The one exception is Mint, a lie-flat business class available on the airline's transcontinental and transatlantic routes, like New York to Los Angeles and London. To be clear: BlueFirst is not a version of Mint, and the two will never appear on the same plane. Mint planes keep Mint, and BlueFirst goes on every other aircraft. Where Mint is a bed, BlueFirst is a recliner, built for the shorter leisure routes that make up most of JetBlue's network.

To test out the BlueFirst product, we checked out the first aircraft with the new cabins installed on the ground at New York—JFK. Here's everything travelers should know before booking.

The first three rows of the plane will be dedicated to BlueFirst, with 12 seats in total.

As for the seat itself, the first thing that will stand out to travelers is just how much more space there is. BlueFirst has only three rows—12 seats total—and each seat is about three inches wider than a standard economy seat, with room to spare in every direction. The seat is spacious enough to hold a passenger and a laptop bag next to them (or a large purse, in my case), and the space in front is just as generous, with up to seven extra inches of legroom compared with JetBlue's regular Main seats. It reclines five inches too, though the recline takes a bit of pressure (hold the button and push back on the seat firmly). Press the button again, and the seat pops right back up. In true JetBlue fashion—this is, after all, the airline that built its name on being the un-stuffy one—there's no curtain cutting the BlueFirst cabin off from the rest of the plane.

Mattress company Tuft & Needle designed the seat cushion using T&N Flex foam.

The seat cushion is made with Tuft & Needle's T&N Flex foam (yes, the mattress company), developed just for JetBlue. It's squishy enough to comfortably sink into, and it responds as you shift, in both the bottom cushion and the backrest. The adjustable headrest also has wings that fold in to cradle your head. "I'll go on record and say I think they're some of the most comfortable recline seats that are out there in domestic first class," Greene says.

BlueFirst passengers receive a blanket and an amenity kit with socks, earbuds, mouthwash, and OSEA Malibu skincare products.

Aside from the bigger, more comfortable seat, BlueFirst gives travelers a slew of other perks. At every seat, there's a 13.3-inch screen with Bluetooth for personal earbuds, USB-A, USB-C, and a regular outlet, plus JetBlue's free Wi-Fi. The overhead bins above the cabin are reserved for BlueFirst passengers, so boarding doesn't come with the usual scramble for space, and each large bifold tray table has a stand for your phone or tablet. Travelers also get a blanket and an amenity kit with socks, earbuds, mouthwash, and OSEA Malibu skincare products, including a lip balm, hand cream, and the fan-favorite calming pulse point oil.

What's more, the perks start before passengers even get on the plane: BlueFirst comes with priority check-in, a faster security lane at more than 30 airports, and Group 1 boarding. Most BlueFirst fares come with two free checked bags—even BlueFirst Base, the cheapest of the three, includes one checked bag.

The dining options in BlueFirst depend on how long your flight is. A bento-inspired box is served on flights of 899 miles or more, with an entrée, a side, and a dessert. The exact menu changes based on the route. Dinner might be a tortellini pasta salad with marinated green olives, a pastrami sandwich with a citrusy cabbage salad, or sesame noodles with crispy wontons and a Szechuan dip. The desserts are a highlight: the pasta comes with a carrot cake with a caramel icing top that's deliciously moist (my personal favorite), and there are colorful macarons and a pistachio chocolate cake on other menus. Breakfast runs from hazelnut-ricotta crêpes to a sweet potato and bean bowl with guacamole and hot sauce, a poached pear, and blueberry chia pudding. There are also kosher, vegan, and gluten-free versions of the boxes.

Drinks in this section of the cabin deserve their own mention, because BlueFirst's come with a twist you won't find on other US airlines. Everything is ordered right from the seatback screen in Mixologist Mode, which lets you build your own cocktail (or mocktail) instead of choosing from a list. You start with a base—a spirit, a soft drink, coffee, a mixer—and add up to four items in total from the full drink menu. The crew then brings the ingredients right to your separate pop-out cocktail tray, and you mix it yourself. There's a limit of two drinks per order, but once the first round lands, you can start the next. The drinks come in real glassware from Fable, on handmade watercolor coasters by New York-based illustrator Danielle Rose Fisher. For anyone not playing bartender, there's also wine from Parcelle, coffee from Cometeer and Joe Coffee, and Smith Teamaker teas.

The new cabin will first roll out on JetBlue flights from Fort Lauderdale to and New York LaGuardia and Boston.

The retrofit should be nearly done by the end of 2027, covering every JetBlue plane that doesn't have Mint.

BlueFirst tickets are currently on sale for travel dates beginning in December. The cabins will be added to more than 30 routes throughout 2026; you'll start seeing the new seats on flights from JFK to Cancún, Liberia, and San Juan beginning in January. However, even on those inaugural routes, not every flight will have BlueFirst right away (it depends on whether a fitted plane is operating that flight). Just over a dozen planes will have the cabin by the end of this year, with the rest of the fleet following through 2027.

By the end of next year, the retrofit should be nearly done, covering every JetBlue plane that doesn't have Mint. Until then, it's worth double-checking before booking since JetBlue notes BlueFirst may only be available on select flights or dates, and planes can be swapped at a moment’s notice depending on equipment needs and maintenance.

#6240. This Is The Summer To Tick Santorini Off The Bucket List

It’s June, and for perhaps the first time in modern history, Santorini isn’t crowded. Those earthquakes a good few months ago? Not even a flower pot was tipped over, yet incessant clickbait headlines managed to have a lasting impact.

And that’s a shame, because there’s been a lovely tourism revolution brewing there, where local hoteliers are bringing back the kind of experience and hospitality that you want to come back for over and over again.

As someone who goes at least once or twice a year, and will again very shortly, I can only advocate to tick it off the bucket list this summer, because you’ll never find prices, availability or an experience quite like it again for a while.

In the last 20 years, Santorini got totally overrun. Cruise tourism and day trip mania somewhat ruined a once idyllic, low-key fishing island and then Instagram and TikTok lit the match.

But now the TikTok crowd is in Mykonos and Santorini, as unequalled in beauty as ever, is lovely again. Hotels like The Vasilicos and Santorini Sky bring wildly different, delightfully luxurious and hospitality driven experiences to the island.

Beach clubs, yes Santorini’s beaches are underrated, have made a nice little mark on quieter coasts with great effect too. Assyrtiko, the local grape has hit the world stage as a darling of sommeliers in top restaurants and vineyards like Vassaltis offer stunning tasting experiences.

And the food? There’s no Nobu, or Scorpios here, so there are plenty of places to feel the benefit of European pricing, including a personal favorite at Kantouni.

The trouble with Santorini has historically been that many of the best hotels are small, they fill up quickly, and as they do, they charge a fortune. For the best, like the ones mentioned above, it’s still worth it. But this season, all across the board, prices are lower and even if you don’t care about price, many of the best which might typically be sold out for the season have rooms.

As an additional tailwind for travelers, flights between the US and Europe are quieter this summer, which means there’s deals to be had with both points and cash from major markets to Santorini. If you don’t see cheap flights to Santorini, try a major hub and booking an onward ticket separately.

Naturally, precaution is a good thing in life. But fear mongering for the sake of clicks is another beast and I can’t help but be fairly appalled by the many weeks and months of coverage and follow up coverage, reiterating a narrative of fear… despite no damage to anything, anywhere.

If you do bag a great deal this summer and visit one of my very favorite places, and use this great Santorini guide to make the most of your time, you can thank the media.

Of note, Great Wolf Lodge Niagara is excluded from the deal.

If you’re planning a weekend trip (or a shorter mid-week trip!), use promo code MOREFUN to save 30% on two-night bookings for stays within 60 days of purchase. Again, this code is good for the rest of the year, so keep it tucked in the back of your mind if you’ve got a later-in-the-year trip brewing.

Special discounted rates on Great Wolf Lodge day passes are available for military members (active, retired, and veteran), teachers, fire and emergency medical service personnel, medical providers, nurses, 911 dispatchers, police, government employees, and correctional officers looking for a respite. If you work in one of these professions, use the Great Wolf Lodge discount code WPHEROES to access reduced pricing on stays. This code is good through the end of 2028, and you’ll need to verify your status using ID.me.

Proof of age is required at check-in to validate this Great Wolf Lodge discount code. More good news: It’s often combinable with other lodge perks to maximize savings when traveling with the whole family. Great Wolf Lodge Niagara is excluded from this deal.

Members of AAA, AARP, or other vehicle clubs can also save on lodge bookings. Enter your membership details to activate the Great Wolf Lodge AAA discount or Great Wolf Lodge AARP discount. Plan to bring your card with you, as membership cards must also be presented upon arrival. Right now, there is a promo code DRIVER that takes up to 30% off your bill.

One other reliable way to save: Join the Voyagers Club for free to earn points and exclusive members-only deals. Members get early access to Great Wolf Lodge promotion code releases and seasonal sales. They’ll also earn Voyagers Points for money spent at the lodge, which can be redeemed for future stays or on-site amenities.

You'll get a point for every $10 spent on bookings, package add-ons, cabanas, ancillary purchases like late checkout, and on-site spending charged to the suite, including food and retail. Points are not earned on any alcohol purchases, taxes, gratuities, fees, or on-site purchases not charged to the suite. You can check your points balance at any time in your Great Wolf profile, and redeem them by booking directly on greatwolf.com while logged into your account.

Having trouble with a promo code? There are a few things you can do to fix that. First, double check that the code is spelled correctly, with no extra spaces or typos. If all looks good, check the details of the promo code to ensure it's still active and hasn't expired. Some discount codes exclude certain locations, so make sure your booking meets any necessary criteria to qualify. If everything looks good and your Great Wolf Lodge promo code still isn't working, clear your browser's cache and give the page a refresh. When in doubt, contact the brand's customer service team for help (which varies by location).

Some of the most aspirational business-class award redemptions are increasingly hard to find, even for the most experienced points and miles enthusiasts.

Cathay Pacific is a prime example. It's harder and harder to find award availability in the Hong Kong-based airline's premium cabins, especially with partners.

But one trick still works: Look for award availability when airlines launch new routes or bring back old ones.

I was able to fly from Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA) to Hong Kong International Airport (HKG) for just 75,000 Atmos Rewards points. That is a screaming deal. But there was only saver-level availability for a limited time when the schedule was first loaded.

It turned out to be a fantastic redemption, with excellent service, delicious food and a comfortable lie-flat seat for the long journey across the Pacific.

I'll have more details later in this story on how to find some of these incredible deals in business class, but first, let's talk a bit more about this flight.

Here's what my experience was like aboard Cathay Pacific's Airbus A350-900 and how you can use a similar strategy to find these elusive business-class awards.

Cathay Pacific relaunched its service to Hong Kong from Seattle in March 2026, after suspending the route during the COVID-19 pandemic.

The route originally launched in March 2019 and was canceled in November of the following year. The airline's CEO told TPG that the carrier had always wanted to restore the route, which was Seattle's first nonstop service to Hong Kong since the pandemic.

The plane was a nine-year-old A350-900 with the ship number B-LRL, with 38 business-class seats, 28 premium economy seats and 214 economy seats.

It was a very comfortable way to cross the Pacific and opens up fun new ways to get to Asia from the U.S. West Coast. It also adds another way to use points and miles to fly to Hong Kong, though as you'll read below, it's no easy task to find the lowest-level award availability.

Business-class guests on Cathay Pacific are invited to use The Club at Seattle in the South Satellite area, which is connected to the main terminal by an underground train.

The Club SEA is an independent lounge that participates in Priority Pass. It offers a buffet of hot and cold food items and free drinks. It's basic, and it doesn't hold a candle to Cathay Pacific's own lounges in places like San Francisco and Hong Kong (no noodle bar here). However, it will do the trick for a quick drink and bite.

It was crowded during my quick visit, and I didn't spend much time at this lounge, since I'd had access to the beautiful Alaska Airlines lounge in the N Concourse. I grabbed a bite there before heading to the S Concourse, which is about to get a major, modern $2.5 billion renovation. It should be a much nicer place to hang out once the renovations are done.

Cathay Pacific has 38 business-class seats, split between two cabins. I was in the forward cabin with 30 seats arranged in a 1-2-1 configuration. There is a smaller cabin with just eight business-class seats behind a small galley/boarding area, which looked like a good option for a more intimate experience.

The seats fold down to 75 inches in length to become fully flat beds, though the footwell is a bit narrow.

Cathay Pacific gave out British lifestyle brand Bamford amenity kits that had moisturizer, cooling body gel, pillow mist, an eye mask, earplugs, a toothbrush and toothpaste and mouthwash. There were also noise-canceling headphones and a bottle of water at the seat.

The seat had lots of little storage areas, along with slippers (but no pajamas, as Cathay only has pajamas on select planes with first class).

Bathrooms are plentiful, with two in the front of the main business-class cabin and one more behind. The coolest thing was that the two bathrooms in front have windows — something you don't see that often on airplanes. Amenities were provided by Bamford and included a moisturizing spray and lotion.

The inflight entertainment was great, with an 18.5-inch HD touchscreen and plenty of movies and entertainment. I was able to choose from hundreds of movies and television shows (including a documentary on Cathay Pacific's 80th anniversary). There was also a tail camera and a moving map. A handheld controller is available to navigate the screen.

Cathay Pacific provides free Wi-Fi for business-class passengers, and I found it worked well on my flight. It's not as fast as Starlink, but it was still easy for me to get some work done.

I really like Cathay Pacific's business-class seats on these planes, though I'm excited to try one of Cathay's newer Aria Suite business-class products someday. Those suites are currently being installed on their Boeing 777-300ER fleet.

I'm especially hoping to see it on flights to and from John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK), which the airline has hinted could come as soon as next year. (The timing of that rollout remains to be confirmed.)

A friendly and attentive crew, delicious food and good bedding made for a great flight across the Pacific. I had especially good service with flight attendants Mei, Amanda and Elsa, all of whom were super friendly and chatty.

Service wasn't as formal as some Asian airlines I've flown, and the crew was fun to be around.

A predeparture beverage of orange juice or water was served during boarding.

Not long after takeoff, flight attendants served drinks. I went with a nonalcoholic Cathay Delight, the airline's signature nonalcoholic drink, made with kiwi, coconut and mint.

That was followed by a lovely amuse-bouche of a deviled egg. I could have happily eaten 20 of them.

The egg dish was served with a Betsy Free, Cathay Pacific's nonalcoholic version of its signature Betsy beer, in a vintage-style Cathay Pacific beer can.

That was followed by an absolutely delicious lunch: a roast carrot soup with a selection of breads, a hearty buffalo mozzarella and rocket pesto salad with grilled radicchio and toasted hazelnuts, and a roasted chicken breast in a maple-chipotle barbecue sauce, served with corn on the cob, creamed spinach and garlic mashed potatoes.

The dessert cart was filled with things like cheese and fruit plates, a yogurt panna cotta, ice cream, or a raspberry tiramisu and, of course, port or wine.

The flight attendants saw me snapping a ton of pictures, so they ended up letting me sample a little bit of almost everything. What a feast!

As if that weren't enough, flight attendants later brought around a chocolate sampler.

There were also snacks set out in the area between the two business-class cabins.

I was able to pre-select a second meal before the flight, and went with a classic beef burger.

There was a nice set of options available on the pre-order menu.

That meal was served after I'd gotten a few hours of shut-eye. Cathay Pacific is well-known for its burgers, and this one didn't disappoint.

I'm not sure how they managed to make a burger served at 30,000 feet taste good, but they did.

The flight attendants helped make my bed with a Bamford-branded mattress pad, duvet and large pillow. I managed to get about five hours of sleep — not too bad.

Before landing, there was yet another meal.

Breakfast was a more traditional Chinese meal of congee with shrimp dumplings and siu mai. Honestly, at that point, I was so full that I didn't eat much of it, but I did enjoy about four cappuccinos.

I'll tell you one thing: Come hungry when flying international on Cathay Pacific.

I was able to score that business-class seat on Cathay Pacific's newly resumed flight to Hong Kong for just 75,000 Atmos Rewards points and $5.60 in federal security tax. You can also book Cathay flights with American Airlines AAdvantage miles.

Unfortunately, low-level award space has been increasingly hard to come by using partners lately. That's why I always look when a new or newly resumed route goes on sale. I've often found low-level awards when the route first comes up for booking.

That also happened recently when American Airlines announced new service to Prague and newly resumed flights to Budapest,. The airline made business-class redemptions widely available for just 55,000 Alaska Atmos Rewards points.

So when a new route starts or resumes, check award availability as soon as the seats go on sale.

Related: 9 flight award booking hacks every traveler should know

Of course, you'll likely find more availability using Cathay Pacific's own program: Asia Miles. Cathay Pacific often releases more award availability to its own members. You can transfer miles 1:1 from multiple Cathay Pacific banking partners — including Bilt and Citi ThankYou Rewards, among others — directly to Asia Miles. American Express Membership Rewards also transfers to Asia Miles but at a reduced 5:4 ratio.

Award search tools are increasingly a big part of my deal hunt. Some of my favorites include Seats.aero, ExpertFlyer (owned by TPG parent company, Red Ventures) and Roame.travel. I also rely on the Points Path award tool, which runs in my browser, so I can see award availability when I search on Google Flights.

Flexibility is another key to finding award availability like this. You'll often need to travel whenever a seat is available, not on a specific date. If you're open to multiple destinations, you'll also have better luck finding the cheapest awards, especially to destinations like Asia. Consider using wherever you find the best redemption as a jumping-off point to see other destinations in the region.

Business class on Cathay Pacific's A350-900s may not have all the excitement of its newer Aria Suite, but it's still a super-compelling product, as my recent flight from Seattle to Hong Kong showed. This trip proved once again why Cathay Pacific is one of my favorite airlines, and the newly resumed service from Seattle adds another option for American travelers.

Friendly service, a great seat, and incredible food and beverages made this trip one to remember. The best part was getting all that for just 75,000 Alaska Airlines Atmos Rewards points.

Keep an eye out for newly launched (or relaunched) routes when you are looking for your next great redemption. You might get a happy surprise.

#6237. The Angry German On My British Airways Flight

I’ve written about the seat recline debate on many occasions, but finally experienced a real-life incident on a British Airways flight.

My position has been consistent over the years. Whether you recline your seat is your prerogative, not the prerogative of the person behind you. Even though a reclined seats often results in an uncomfortable position for the person behind you, that is the reason their seat reclines as well.

There are two exceptions. First, one should always recline their seat gradually. A sudden recline may result in a broken laptop. Second, seats should rarely be reclined during meal service (there are exceptions).

I was seated far in the back of the aircraft in 38H. Of course, my seat was up for the meal service. Of course, I reclined my seat gradually. But that wasn’t good enough for the passenger seated behind me.

He was a portly German gentleman, probably in his late 60s. He began cursing as I reclined my seat, then hitting it. I turned around and glared at him and he said nothing.

I turned back around and he began muttering to himself in German, cursing me out (assuming I was an Englishman and calling me some choice expletives). Zoning him out, I leaned back to go to sleep.

About 20 minute later he began shaking my seat. I got up and turned around. He made motions for me to put my seat up.

I proceed to lecture him, without expletives, in German that it was my right to recline my seat and that I had no choice when the person in front of me also reclined.

He was shocked that I spoke German and quickly shut up. I did not hear from him again during the flight.

When we landed, I offered him my hand and noted that economy class is difficult for everyone. He nodded and shook my hand back, noting that due to our late arrival he had missed his connection to Dusseldorf.

Tight seat pitch leads to air rage, but it is a reality of flying in economy class. I’m glad my own incident did not spiral out of control.

It’s one thing to have seats that don’t recline for short flights, say up to 3 hours – but quite another for flights longer than that, and especially for an overnight, long haul intercontinental flight.

The real problem is the continued insistance by airline managers who fly in premium cabins that NEVER, EVER have to worry about the indiginities and discomfort they intentionally create to better line their own pockets, yet whom seem to think its perfectly OK to create teensy-weensy seats packed into 31” pitch, no legroom rows that they never have to subject their precious, royal bums squeezing into.

Fact is, aircraft used for long-haul flights should be subjected to a minimum row pitch of 32”-33” and 18” wide seats.

Using high density confirgurations that were originally designed for short hops on domestic routes in Japan is one thing.

Subjecting adults to those types of seats and row pitches for flights lasting 3-16 hours is immoral and unconscionable – especially when the fat cats in the C-suite and greedy shareholders never, ever deign to sit in the awful seats that seek to profit so handsomely off of others from,

I’d love to see how long these shameful 31” row pitch seats remained at BA, United, American, Delta et al if the likes of Alex Cruz, Oscar Munoz, Doug Parker, Glen Hauenstein & all of those Wall Street “Analysts” actually had to sit in these despicable seats for their flights all the time as most flyers do.

If these seats are not good enough for the folks in the C-Suite, then they shouldn’t be sold at all.

Their hypocrisy and greed is shameful and disgusting.

On another note, I do like that you sometimes fly long-haul in economy, mirroring the experience of a lot of us who sometimes fly Business or Premium Economy only to fly in back on a later flight, Makes your content more relatable.
