#6224. 17 Best Airbnbs in Bangkok for Your Next Trip to Thailand's Capital

A vast metropolis where modern skyscrapers mix with antique wooden houses, Bangkok is, in my opinion, one of the best cities in the world. Whether you’re on the hunt for boat noodles or Thai massages, there’s so much to do and no bad time of year to visit. And when it comes to where to stay, travelers will find just as much variety among the excellent lodging options. While this Thai city delivers a sensory overload of epic proportions, there are plenty of peaceful pockets and quiet corners perfect for catching your breath after a long day of exploring. One of the best ways to get a bit of solitude is by renting a dreamy Airbnb in the area.

Over the years, I’ve spent months in Thailand’s capital city. I've visited for weekend girls trips, concerts, and trips with family, staying everywhere from Siam to Chinatown. I've experienced the city's endless ways to fill your days, from world-class museums to addictive street food to some of Asia’s best cocktail bars. If you're planning a stay and want a little more elbow room than the city's hotels might allow, there are plenty of charming rentals to lay your head down at, from studios with incredible river views to massive homes for the whole family to shophouses in Chinatown. Read on for some of the best Airbnbs in Bangkok.

We've vetted these listings based on Superhost and Guest Favorite status, ratings, amenities, location, previous guest reviews, and decor.

Number of guests: 8Bed and bath: 4 bedrooms, 3 bathsWhy we love it: Spacious design, hot tub, screen projector

Baan Konja sits at the end of a cul-de-sac in the café-crazed neighborhood of Ekkamai. This stylish four-story home is an ideal launching pad for families or groups of friends looking for a peaceful stay. Guests will love how well laid out and spacious the setup is, with elegant tiled bathrooms, a rare private hot tub, four plush bedrooms (three kings and a room with two singles), and a comfy outdoor balcony area. According to past guests, the host, Michael, goes above and beyond to address any issues, including providing toothbrushes and slippers if you forget yours at home. He’s also able to suggest great cocktail spots.

Neighborhood: EkkamaiThings to do nearby: Wat That Thong Buddhist temple; top restaurants, cafés, and bars

Number of guests: 2Bed and bath: Studio, 1 bathWhy we love it: Incredible river and temple views, Thai design, trendy location

Ideal for couples and digital nomads, this large studio apartment is high up in a residential building surrounded by some of the city’s best spots for eating and drinking. Outfitted with a comfortable bed and couch next to a floor-to-ceiling window, it's designed with local touches like Thai art, colorful throw pillows, and a hand-carved wooden headboard. But travelers are really booking this room for the incredible views over the river and the nearby temple. Just outside, Michelin-star restaurants, riverside cafés, and trendy boutiques are steps away.

Neighborhood: Talat NoiThings to do nearby: Talat Noi street art, Chinatown, Wat Traimit Buddhist temple

Number of guests: 3Bed and bath: Studio, 1 bathWhy we love it: Beautiful design, large soaking tub, open-air spaces

The Clay Room is one of six short-term rental units in this newly renovated apartment building formerly owned by the host’s grandfather. This studio-style room is cozy with a comfortable bed and couch area, a large TV, and floor-to-ceiling glass-block windows. But to me, the best part of a stay here is the glass-block bathroom that looks like it could be out of a ’70s design magazine. Separated by a large velvet curtain, it has handcrafted clay-colored tiles, natural mineral paint, a huge soaking tub, and two curved glass-block partitions separating the toilet area and shower. There’s also an outdoor kitchen and a washer and dryer in the leafy backyard area.

Neighborhood: Thon BuriThings to do nearby: Wongwian Yai Park, IconSiam mall, Wat Arun Buddhist temple

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 2 bathsWhy we love it: Quality craftsmanship, detailed design, first-floor spa

Located near the Jim Thompson House Museum, Chinatown, and Lumphini Park, this two-bedroom apartment is perfectly situated for exploring the best of Bangkok. Modern and stylish, its Scandinavian-style furniture is made with high-quality craftsmanship, according to past guests. The sleek style is accented with traditional pillows and throws woven with Thai patterns. Its main bedroom is huge with a king bed, while the second is smaller and has a set of bunk beds, making it ideal for a family with small children. When your feet get tired from exploring, walk down to the first-floor spa for a sublime Thai massage. (Of note, the apartment is on the second floor and there is not an elevator.)

Neighborhood: Hua LamphongThings to do nearby: Chinatown, Jim Thompson House Museum, Lumphini Park

Number of guests: 3Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Central location, high ceilings, historic design

Steps from the Chao Phraya River, this 130-year-old heritage shophouse is in the pulsing heart of Bangkok. The city's best bars, cafés, shopping, and public transport are practically at your doorstep, but the Airbnb’s effortlessly cool design makes it hard to leave. Fun yellow and white checkered flooring, a coral-colored spiral staircase and matching ceiling, painted cement walls, and retro Thai art are a few of the standout elements of this cozy one-bedroom. Although the listing says it can accommodate up to five with a king-size bed and a sofa bed in the lofted bedroom, as well as a king-size sofa bed in the living area, guests say the house is compact, so I recommend it for couples or small families.

Neighborhood: Bang RakThings to do nearby: Sathorn Pier, IconSiam mall

Number of guests: 8Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 2 bathsWhy we love it: Private driveway with EV charging station, 60" smart TV, large kitchen

After years of working in European hotels, host Chureerut moved back to Bangkok to live with her mother and open her own Airbnb. Located between Bangkok’s two airports, slightly outside the city down a quiet alley, it’s a great setup for a peaceful family escape. Chureerut lovingly combines Scandinavian tiles and lighting with traditional Thai design elements, such as teak and rattan furniture. The two-bedroom house (a king and a queen) sleeps up to seven and is fully equipped with everything you could ever need, from a washer and dryer to a fully stocked kitchen and a dreamy outdoor patio with traditional Thai windows. Should you need any Bangkok recs, Chureerut and her mother are right next door.

Neighborhood: Khet Lat PhraoThings to do nearby: Central EastVille shopping center, Crystal Design Center

Number of guests: 2Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Japanese-style design, pool, modern building

This full-service apartment on Bangkok's ​​Phahonyothin Road offers a quiet stay and easy access to the rest of the city. A seven-minute walk or a free tuk-tuk ride (provided by the building management) will take you to Sanampao Station, and from there, Bangkok is your fire-grilled oyster. The host has multiple one-bedroom apartments spread throughout the building, each with a subtle Japanese design: light timber, low beds (this one is a king), neutral tones, and large glass windows. Top-notch building amenities include a gym, outdoor swimming pool, and a massage parlor—a perfect tonic after a long flight.

Neighborhood: PhahonyothinThings to do nearby: Victory Monument, Jim Thompson House Museum

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1 bathWhy we love it: Stylish design, natural light, convenient location

This artfully curated apartment incorporates Scandi-chic touches throughout. Situated near Lumphini and Bechakitti Parks and just a short walk to the BTS, past guests have raved about the location. But its interiors are what really will catch your eye. The main living room has floor-to-ceiling windows with green views, rattan chairs, and a mustard-colored couch with colorful pillows. Find ocean-blue tiles in the kitchen for another fun pop of color. Its two king bedrooms have concrete floors, wooden furniture, and light pastel sheets. Black slate and white mosaic tiles adorn the bathroom, which includes a large tub. Keep in mind that it's located on the third floor and there is no elevator, so pack light!

Neighborhood: LumphiniThings to do nearby: Lumphini Park, One Bangkok, Benjakitti Park

Number of guests: 2Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 2 bathsWhy we love it: Outdoor bathroom, quiet workspace, tons of character

As soon as you check in here, you can tell it’s owned by an artist. Located in the historic center of Bangkok, chaotic Khaosan Road is a 10-minute walk away, but this two-bedroom renovated shophouse is a peaceful reprieve. Filled with fun art and an eclectic style, this cute and compact space includes a shared bedroom and living room, plus a second bed in a loft. Its large, exposed-brick dining room is ideal for a couple working remotely, and its outdoor bathroom is among the most unique I’ve seen in Bangkok.

Neighborhood: RattanakosinThings to do nearby: Khao San Road, The Grand Palace, Wat Pho temple, Loha Prasat “metal castle”

Number of guests: 2Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Lush garden, badminton court, brushed concrete interiors

Tucked into a local area in Samrong on the far outskirts of Bangkok (accessible via the BTS SkyTrain), this one-bedroom Airbnb is perfect for travelers who want to escape the chaos—at least for a little while. The owners have outfitted their backyard guesthouse with cooling brushed concrete, vintage wooden doors, and comfortable bedding, including a contemporary pullout sectional. Reach out to the hosts for help arranging a badminton game at the nearby court, a market tour, or a few other neighborhood experiences. Plus, the fridge is stocked with drinks and snacks to enjoy while relaxing under a banana tree in the large garden.

Neighborhood: SamrongThings to do nearby: Pak Nam fish market, Talad Rot Fai Srinakarin night market, Bang Krachao man-made island

Number of guests: 5Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1 bathWhy we love it: Great nearby food options, trendy tiles, access to hotel amenities

It’s all about coziness and convenience at this quaint two-bedroom (each with a queen) apartment near the SkyTrain and the Sathorn Central Pier. White walls, lofty ceilings, bamboo light fixtures, and handwoven wall tapestries make its newly renovated spaces feel airy and bright. Major brownie points go to the host, who can help with just about anything, including arranging an airport transfer, providing tips for the best local restaurants, and securing passes to use the neighboring hotel’s outdoor pool and fitness area (for a small daily fee).

Neighborhood: SilomThings to do nearby: Sathorn Pier, IconSiam mall

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 2 bathsWhy we love it: Sophisticated decor, powerful AC, designated workspace

Digital nomads flocking to Thailand—thanks to its visa—will love this fully-equipped house. During your stay here, you’ll find comfortable working areas, powerful AC, a stocked fridge, and even a printer. Located in a residential area outside the city center, the Ratchadaphisek MRT Station is just a five-minute walk away, connecting you to the city’s hotspots after office hours. Newly renovated, its trendy midcentury-modern decor is another stay highlight. Mismatched furniture, concrete floors, matte black fixtures, and pencil-strip bathroom tiles are all smart additions. It sleeps up to four with a queen in the bedroom and a sofa bed in the living room.

Neighborhood: RatchadaphisekThings to do nearby: Chatuchak Weekend Market, Jodd Fairs market

Number of guests: 6Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 2 bathsWhy we love it: Outdoor patio, eclectic design, tons of natural light

You'll find this delightfully eclectic three-bedroom respite on a quiet, tree-lined street in the residential Din Daeng area of Bangkok. Decorated with the owner’s paintings, parquet floors, and an eclectic blend of furniture, this homey abode is perfect for a young family or a group of friends. Its three bedrooms (two with kings, one with a queen) have unique styles, from wacky wallpaper to shiplap and fully tiled bathrooms. Each has a desk for working, but the peaceful patio with mango trees and ferns is a much better place to get the creative juices flowing.

Neighborhood: Din DaengThings to do nearby: Huai Khwang market, Ganesha Shrine, Thailand Cultural Center

Number of guests: 6Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1 bathWhy we love it: Beautiful design, luxurious bathroom, fantastic location

As far as neighborhoods go, Bangkok’s Chinatown is hard to beat. The city’s best street food, hippest bars, and most vibrant shops are all steps from your door. Inside an ornate shophouse, this two-bedroom, one-bath home offers more modern finishes than its exterior implies. Its bathroom includes a high-tech rain shower, luxurious soaking tub, and cool Oxford encaustic tiles. The bedrooms here are huge, with chic black and rattan furniture, handwoven decoration, king beds, and large TVs. It’s ideal for families, friends, or two sets of couples. Note that the stairs here are steep, but all the creature comforts are worth it.

Neighborhood: ChinatownThings to do nearby: Chinatown, Wat Traimit temple, Talad Noi historic neighborhood

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Sweeping city views, Nordic design, soaking tub

Situated on the 36th floor of the famous State Tower (you may remember the building’s rooftop bar from The Hangover 2), the unbeatable city views are enough of a reason to book this high-rise. A trendy royal blue kitchen, tropical wallpaper, and Scandi-chic furniture decorate the clean and compact space. Although the apartment is advertised as a one-bedroom (a king), there is an additional small space with two twin beds, perfect for little ones. If you like to be in the thick of it, the central location makes it the perfect jumping-off point to explore nearby night markets and the various neighborhoods along the Chao Phraya River, visible from your condo.

Neighborhood: SilomThings to do nearby: Sky Bar, Bangkokian Museum, River City Bangkok culture and lifestyle center

Number of guests: 3Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Fantastic lighting, standout bathroom, great location

Channeling the love den of Don Draper, this super-sexy, dimly lit studio is the perfect honeymoon rental. Inside an old shophouse, it’s a fourth-floor walk-up with midcentury-modern furniture, antique framed posters, a queen bed, and a small private balcony overlooking the buzzy Ratchathewi neighborhood. Dark wood and recessed lighting outfit the entire space, except for the striking bathroom, which is finished with olive green tiles and a large soaking tub (of note, there's no separate shower), perfect for bubble baths.

Neighborhood: RatchathewiThings to do nearby: Jim Thompson House Museum, Victory Monument

Number of guests: 6Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 3 bathsWhy we love it: Unique design, open-air living, stylish bathrooms

Neighborhood: RattanakosinThings to do nearby: Phra Sumen Fort, Khao San Road, The Marble Temple

What are the best neighborhoods to stay in Bangkok?

Chinatown and Talat Noi are always my go-to neighborhoods when I'm in Bangkok. They are full of fun, trendy bars, restaurants, and cafés worth spending some time wandering around. Sukhumvit is a great neighborhood for first-timers, with plenty of restaurant options, rooftop bars, and access to the MRT.

When is the best season to visit Bangkok?

Many people suggest that the best time to visit Bangkok is at the end of the rainy season—October through December—before the smog gets bad in January. March to May is the hottest time to visit, so it may be best to avoid if you don't do well in the heat, but I highly recommend planning a trip around Songkran (April 13–15), a.k.a. Thai New Year. It's known for hosting the world's largest water fight, and in my opinion, is one of Asia's best festivals.

#6223. Private Equity Is Buying easyJet. What Usually Happens Next?

easyJet shareholders approved Apollo’s £5.7bn ($7.6bn) takeover on November 11, with 97.07% of votes cast in favor at the court meeting and 96.67% at the general meeting. Apollo is paying £7.15 a share in cash, a staggering 81% premium to where easyJet traded before the bidding started in late May. Castlelake opened the tender and had a £6.25 offer rejected in June. Apollo reached terms on July 10 and the board recommended it on August 6.

Founder, Sir Stelios Haji-Ioannou and his family, held about 15.3% and is rolling the stake into the new private parent rather than cashing out. To satisfy European ownership rules, easyJet suspended votes on 233.9MM shares held by non-EU investors, and Apollo’s funds will hold no more than 49.9% of the new parent (similar to Delta’s ownership interest in Virgin Atlantic. Headquarters will remain in the UK, along with its air operator certificates in the UK, Austria and Switzerland. The deal is expected to close by the end of March 2027, ending more than 25 years on the London Stock Exchange.

In its July 10 statement, Apollo said it “believes in easyJet’s existing strategy,” naming three pieces: bigger aircraft, better ancillary and loyalty revenue, and “scaling Holidays into a structurally differentiated earnings stream.” The purchase is funded with Apollo equity plus debt that Barclays said it was highly confident it could arrange.

The three areas Apollo is targeting point to some common interests we have seen in the United States. More on that shortly.

The business it is buying is healthy. easyJet made £665MM in headline profit before tax in fiscal 2025, its third straight year of growth, with net cash of £602MM, per its annual results. easyJet holidays (alone) delivered £250MM of that profit and new targets have been established at £450MM by 2030. The gap Apollo will want to close is margin. easyJet’s top line EBIT of £703MM on £10.11bn of revenue in fiscal 2025 works out to 7%. Ryanair’s operating profit of €2.37bn on €15.54bn of revenue in its fiscal year to March 2026 is 15.3%, per its full year filing. Analysts quoted by Travel Weekly also count about 54 staff per aircraft at easyJet versus 43 at Ryanair. The aircraft capacity is roughly the same, though slightly higher with Ryanair.

Private equity in travel has produced some of the best deals ever made and some of the most spectacular failures, and the difference usually comes down to whether the buyer improved the business or just loaded it with debt.

The best example is Hilton. Blackstone put up $6.5bn of equity in 2007 in a deal that was about 80% debt, wrote the investment down by 70% during the financial crisis, restructured, took Hilton public again in late 2013 and walked away with roughly $14bn in profit, the most profitable leveraged buyout in history. Blackstone credited growth in Europe and China, not financial engineering. I would politely disagree.

Apollo has done this with an airline before. It bought Sun Country in 2018, kept CEO Jude Bricker and backed his shift toward a LCC model with denser cabins and ancillary fees, and took it public in March 2021, selling 9MM shares at $24 for about $218MM. This May, Allegiant closed a roughly $1.5bn acquisition of Sun Country. That’s a little less than 7x its initial investment so by percentage a better deal than Blackstone’s Hilton turn, but less nominal profit by a hefty margin.

Indigo Partners bought Frontier from Republic in 2013 in a deal valued at about $145MM (which seems really cheap in retrospect), with only $36MM paid in cash for the equity, and Frontier’s April 2021 IPO sold 30MM shares at $19, about $570MM. Bain Capital bought Virgin Australia out of administration (bankruptcy) in 2020, cut Tigerair (its wholly-owned ULCC), long-haul flying and freight, and re-listed the airline in June 2025 with a A$685MM offering, which Morningstar credits with lowering complexity and improving margins.

The failures look different. Greybull Capital took control of Monarch in 2014 through a £125MM recapitalization, and in October 2017 Monarch became the biggest airline failure in UK history, leaving about 110,000 travelers to be flown home by the government and 860,000 future bookings canceled. I had flown Monarch a few years earlier when I lived in the UK and had never considered that an airline might shut down to the extent that repatriation flights by the government would be necessary. For those who aren’t familiar, Monarch was a mid-sized leisure airline squeezed between Ryanair and easyJet, with no cost advantage and a buyer that could not supply one.

Of the five deals above, four created value and one collapsed. The winners bought businesses with a strong franchise and either grew them or simplified them. The loser bought a weak airline and hoped. easyJet is far closer to the first group.

Southwest was not bought out, but it went through the closest thing the US has seen to a private equity overhaul. Activist investor Elliott Management took a $1.9bn stake in 2024, reached about 16% at its peak and won board seats. Under that pressure Southwest started charging for checked bags on tickets booked from May 28, 2025, cut about 1,750 corporate jobs, added extra legroom seating and ended open seating in January 2026.

I expected that sameness to be the death of Southwest. I was wrong. Third quarter 2026 revenue hit a record $8.4bn, up 21.2%, revenue per available seat mile rose 21.6% on slightly less capacity, and net income rose to $270MM from $54MM, per its third quarter filing. Fuel has since forced a guidance cut, as it has for everyone, but the commercial changes are working. Elliott has already cut its stake to about 9% and given up two board seats, which is what investors do once the thesis has played out. I still have questions about how management talks about its plans, but becoming more like everyone else made Southwest more money.

The obvious Apollo playbook is to make easyJet look more like Ryanair: fewer staff per aircraft, more fees, tighter turns and a margin that closes in on Ryanair’s 15%. Some of that will happen. But easyJet cannot become Ryanair without giving up what makes it easyJet, which is primary airports like Gatwick and the slots that come with them. My bet is that easyJet becomes something else: a holiday company with an airline attached, closer to Jet2 than to Ryanair, where the plane is the distribution channel and the package is the profit. Apollo named Holidays specifically, the unit already earns more than a third of group profit, and a private owner does not have to explain to the market every quarter why it is growing a tour operator instead of an airline.

But it also named loyalty and in the case of Southwest, that changes the shape of the airline. Southwest is adding up to 15 lounges, introducing a premium card, and adding international partners (with redeemable awards coming eventually) which makes it far more like a legacy carrier. It makes sense that Apollo wants to add more loyalty revenue but Europe has challenges in this space as card fees are lower and credit cards are generally more strictly controlled than in the US.

It also mentioned larger jets and that points to something else altogether. That’s more like the Alaska’s move in acquiring Hawaiian and launching long haul via widebodies and the Southwest move that they *totally* deny is going to happen. If easyJet did something with long haul it would have to avoid the trail of dead carriers from WOW! to Nordic that shows it’s not such a good idea. I’d personally love to see what a trans-Atlantic easyJet operation would look like, but it’s also possible that the vague “larger jets” statement could just point to fewer A319s and A320s and more A321s.

History says private equity in travel works when the buyer gets a strong franchise and makes it better, and fails when the buyer gets a weak one and adds debt (though this is not always the case). Apollo is getting a strong brand with net cash, a growing holidays business and room for growth. There is risk in the debt Barclays is arranging landing on top of a fuel shock and the extent in which this fuel shock persists. If Apollo uses its time out of the public markets to build the holidays business rather than strip the airline, easyJet comes back to the market in a few years as a better company. Maybe. If it chases Ryanair’s margin with Ryanair’s tactics at Gatwick prices, it will learn what Greybull learned at Monarch. I genuinely don’t think that will be the case, but only time will tell.

#6221. How a Trip to India Helped Me Find Peace With a Life-Changing Diagnosis

After spending nearly 25 years away, Tina Aswani-Omprakash, 43, finally traveled back to India, confronting long-held fears about traveling with Crohn’s disease. Along the way she reconnected with her roots, her family, and the food she had spent years afraid to eat. Following more than 20 surgeries and years of debilitating illness, going on the trip was a hard-won milestone for Aswani-Omprakash, made possible through careful preparation and her doctors’ support. Involving everything from exploring historic palaces and temples to meeting some relatives for the first time, the experience reminded her how travel can help us feel connected to culture and live life to the fullest. Here is Aswani-Omprakash’s story, as told to health writer Katie Camero.

The tuk-tuk ride up the Chamundi Hills near Mysuru, India, took about half an hour. My husband, brother-in-law, and some of my colleagues were split between two rickshaws, winding our way up a massive hill toward the Chamundeshwari Temple. I used to love taking tuk-tuks as a kid, but at age 41 I found that the ride felt like so much more than a fun adventure.

I could feel the air on my face, and I remember thinking, I can’t believe it, but I’m really doing this. After over 20 surgeries and some near-death experiences, I had somehow worked up the courage to travel and live my life again.

Gopuram of Sri Chamundeshwari Temple, Chamundi Hill, Mysore, Karnataka, South India

Since childhood I’ve experienced a lot of what doctors call extraintestinal manifestations, which are symptoms that occur when an inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) affects parts of the body outside the gut. I dealt with issues like severe joint pain and eye issues alongside constipation and GERD, but at the time doctors didn’t think to refer me to a gastroenterologist. The discomfort and unpredictability of my condition meant I was always scared to travel, even if it was just a road trip.

The last time I visited my family in India was in 2000 at age 16. We took a day trip from New Delhi to the Taj Mahal and ended up eating street food because we were starving. We all got sick, but I fared so much worse than the others and lost about 20 pounds in the weeks that followed because I was so ill. I eventually was diagnosed with IBD—specifically, ulcerative colitis—in 2006. (Although later I learned I actually had a different type of IBD.) Nearly two years later, my husband, who was my boyfriend at the time, took me to Mexico and we both came down with traveler’s diarrhea after eating some sliced fruit. He threw it all up and recovered just fine, but it took me months to get better.

What followed was a lot of pain, shame, and silence. I worked on Wall Street at the time as a financial-services compliance officer, and it was very tough to figure out the diagnosis, accept it, and try to get on medication while navigating such a stressful career. I was on disability for many years before I eventually had to stop working. I didn’t know what to do with my life because I truly thought this disease and the complications associated with it would kill me.

Over two years, my condition went from mild to severe. During this time I experienced severe bleeding, weight loss, and other debilitating symptoms. I finally had my colon removed on July 4, 2008—which I often call my very own Independence Day. However, complications from this operation, as well as my IBD itself, required me to have dozens of additional operations including one to create a permanent ileostomy in 2011. It was through this process that I learned I actually have Crohn’s disease, another type of IBD.

It wasn’t until late 2024 that my doctors finally gave me the green light to travel to India—and I was terrified. The extra-long flight plus cuisines that include many trigger foods for my condition created a hurdle I worried was impossible to overcome. Although I had taken a few trips around the U.S. and Europe since my diagnosis, I had not conquered my fears of traveling back to India and enjoying the foods my family and I love without getting sick.

After all this time, I thought I couldn’t do this because of my Crohn’s disease. Yet there I was almost 25 years later. I did it—albeit with lots of preparation.

My doctors did an intestinal ultrasound and other tests to make sure nothing was brewing in my gut, and they gave me antibiotics, steroids, and probiotics in case I had a flare-up or bad case of traveler’s diarrhea. My husband and I also booked a hotel, which our relatives didn’t love, but it gave me easy access to filtered water (tap water could have been contaminated with harmful bacteria that could make me really sick) and a private bathroom in case I needed to make frequent trips overnight, along with other perks that kept us feeling safe and comfortable. I stayed clear of street vendors and only ate hot foods to reduce my chances of getting ill.

Even with those restrictions I enjoyed delicious, authentic food. In Mysuru, there’s a restaurant called MTR that offers South Indian cuisine like dosas, which I love. Though the lentil soup they come with can be a little spicy (a common IBD trigger), you can ask for a plain dosa with potatoes inside, which actually works pretty well for people with IBD. It’s a good way for us to enjoy the local cuisine while avoiding a flare-up.

Though it may seem like a lot of work, it honestly felt like such a huge accomplishment to go back to where my family is from and connect with my culture and relatives, some of whom I’d never met before, without getting sick.

However, it took a lot to get to that point. I faced many cultural challenges, not just during my journey to a diagnosis but also to starting treatment. My family survived the 1947 partition of India and Pakistan—my relatives were displaced from Pakistan and became refugees in India. As a result my family lost their trust in the West, and they certainly did not trust Western medicine. My condition got more severe than it needed to because my family was so against medicine or surgery. Marriageability and how others will perceive the family is also something my community worries about a lot. So I had to consider how my diagnosis would impact my sibling’s ability to find partners.

I felt a lot of fear as well because my dad died when I was 8 years old from Crohn’s disease that turned into colorectal cancer. Despite having this family history, I had to do a ton of self-advocacy to finally get the colonoscopy that started to give me much-needed answers and treatment options.

Through all of this I’ve learned that fear is just a mindset and we can accomplish whatever we want if we believe in ourselves. It also really takes a certain mindset to travel such a long distance and eat foods you haven’t been able to eat in so many years without feeling completely terrified you’re going to get sick.

Because of the stigmas I faced in my own journey with IBD, I co-founded, alongside other patient advocates and clinicians, the Strategic Alliance for Intercultural Advocacy in GI, a nonprofit that offers culturally sensitive resources for patients with GI conditions, caregivers, and health care providers to improve treatment and access to care. Many patients I speak with ask why I push past my comfort zone through my travels. My answer is simple: It makes me feel alive. With everything I went through in my 20s and 30s with this disease, I felt like I wasn’t really living. But when you go through so much disability, all you want to do is feel alive again.

Of course, trips like these aren’t feasible for everyone with inflammatory bowel disease. But if you start slowly, you might just surprise yourself. Growing with and owning your chronic illness is a process, and travel has helped me with that immeasurably.

#6219. Google Gets Spirit’s Data, But Not Its 97MM Customers

Spirit Airlines stopped flying its bright yellow planes earlier this year. The final flights landed on May 2, 2026 after 34 years, and the estate sale has been running ever since. The planes went, the LaGuardia slots went, and in July I wrote about the strange bid for Free Spirit, a loyalty program attached to an airline that no longer exists. The oddest asset of all turned out to be the paperwork.

Google won Spirit’s internal data at an August 14 bankruptcy auction for $10MM. The package covers about 500MM Microsoft Teams chats, 100MM emails from 80,000 accounts and roughly 30MM lines of code across 516 software projects. Google has said the data “can be helpful in improving our products and AI models” and that it “will not receive any personal information from this dataset.”

Small business owners have been inundated with emails and other unsolicited bids for their corporate data for training projects in what seems to be high amounts of free money that those training algorithms will turn into better models. There’s something incredibly valuable to companies in that data, which to me looks like very old “can you see my screen” messages on Teams.

But for Google to get what they have for just $10MM – which it earns in less than an hour every day – seems like a steal for Gemini.

Roughly 17,000 Spirit employees lost their jobs overnight in May, and their union was the only party in the room arguing for them while their HR files were being priced. Most companies would never have to face this question, because most companies do not die with their servers intact. It’s admirable, though, that labor reps continued to defend their members even after it was clear the airline would never be resurrected.

But the contract details are less comforting than the headlines. The August 14 agreement says the firm doing the scrubbing is one “acceptable to or designated by” Google, that Google pays for it, and that Google gets to review the work. The agreement also requires the de-identification to preserve “referential integrity” across the data set, meaning the links between one pseudonymous person’s emails, tickets and records stay intact. That is what makes the archive useful for training. It is also what makes anonymized data easier to unravel. Not to worry though, we haven’t seen any tech related data issues of late (wink.)

None of that is improper, and Google may handle it perfectly. My point is narrower. An airline’s emails are full of customers: complaint escalations, refund disputes, disability assistance requests, denied boarding cases. Excluding the customer database does not remove every customer from 100MM emails, which is why the scrubbing standard matters as much as the exclusion.

When I wrote about Free Spirit in July, the argument was that a dead airline’s loyalty program is less a currency than a customer file, and that buyers want the file without the liability of the points. The Google deal is the same lesson from a different angle. When an airline dies, the miles usually die with it. The data does not die. It gets sold. It also answers the question as to what value could be garnered from a defunct loyalty program.

Every airline and hotel program you belong to holds your travel history, your home airport, your spending pattern through the co-brand card and every complaint you have ever filed. Program terms reserve the right to change or end the program, and bankruptcy law lets an estate sell assets while leaving liabilities behind. The customer file is an asset and it may change the way both travel suppliers and its customers see each other. Had I known, I might have removed my details personally when the airline collapsed. I expect legislation at some point will learn from Spirit Airlines’ shut down and require a period for which consumers can remove or adjust their details.

Spirit was a low-fare airline with a loyalty program most frequent flyers ignored. If the data from that operation is worth $10MM to Google, the data inside a major US carrier’s program is worth vastly more to whoever is holding it if that carrier ever fails, or is sold in part or in whole.

The unions and the ombudsman did their jobs, and Google will most likely get a scrubbed archive it can use to teach software how airlines work. That is a reasonable outcome for a $10MM auction lot and make no mistake that Google will have to invest significant multiples of that amount to gain the end goal. The bigger takeaway is for travelers: the most valuable thing you give a loyalty program is not your spending, it is your information, and nobody is obligated to honor your points when the business behind them disappears. Use the miles while they are worth something, and assume your data will outlast them.

#6218. Half Cruise, Half Cargo Ship? What It's Like to Sail French Polynesia Aboard a Local Freighter

It’s certainly a romantic notion to hop a freighter and sail to the distant South Pacific. One could spend days at sea staring at nothing but seabirds and cargo pallets, waking up to the sound of those pallets being offloaded onto a tiny concrete wharf, meeting a community nestled among palms. One could take the day to hike or tour the island, or feast on fresh catches with the locals, while the offloaded pallets are filled with grapefruits, dried coconut husks, and flowers to be sold elsewhere—Tahiti, perhaps.

It might come as a surprise to know that one company has been offering dedicated cruises built around that very premise for over 40 years. In French Polynesia, the locally owned cruise line Aranui Cruises offers combination passenger and cargo services from Papeete, Tahiti, to the dramatically jagged volcanic pitons and pastoral scenes of the Marquesas Islands.

Fatu Hiva in the Marquesas Islands has no airport and is only accessible by sea.

The idea is simple: a ship operates a cargo service to the remote islands (two of them, Fatu Hiva and Tahuata, have no airport and are only accessible by sea), and while the inbound cargo of soft drinks, groceries, building supplies, and even racing canoes is unloaded in the port, the passengers can use the time to go touring. In March 2026, I joined one such sailing, onboard the purpose-built Aranui V to see exactly what the 12-night, nearly-thousand-mile journey to the Marquesas looks like.

I like to refer to the vessel as the “mullet ship”— cargo up front, cruise in the back. During the voyage, when I wasn’t swimming in the onboard pool, or enjoying a cocktail from the bar, I filled my days with lectures Dr. Carole S. Ivory, professor emerita from Washington State University, who specializes in the study of Marquesan culture and art.

I got to witness that culture up close on Aranui’s included shore excursions. The experiences were visits to archaeological sites and volcanic pitons by car on Nuku Hiva, or various organized hikes on several of the other islands. There are also optional excursions for an additional fee, like the scenic drive between two sides of the island on Fatu Hiva. The drive, which traced a narrow mountain road between villages, offered spectacular vistas from the sea cliffs and, to rejoin the ship, a bonus sunset barge ride—a worthy add-on.

The Aranui V ship is a passenger cruise in the front and a cargo ship in the back.

Local residents hired by Aranui guide passengers in their personal cars as these tiny islands have no buses. On tiny Ua Huka, our mahu driver (a person of third-gender common in Polynesia) wearing a red flowered dress and straw hat, spent the day chatting with passengers and eating. And oh, how we ate! Baguette sandwiches during a morning stop at a craft center. A plate of chow mein from the snack bar at the botanical garden. A tour-of-the-island plate from the buffet heaped with coconut milk-roasted goat, the raw fish salad poisson cru, steamed taro, rice, and magenta-colored mashed banana swimming in sweet condensed coconut milk.

On each of the islands, we passengers from the Aranui V were greeted with local musicians and artisans, typically in a community pavilion. The Marquesas are noted for their skilled carvers, working in both wood and bone to create intricately decorated bowls, decorative canoe paddles, and jewelry. Carvers also work in stone called te ke’a pua (flower stone), also known as garnet phonolite, a polished volcanic rock that has the natural appearance of being covered in crystalline flowers. The rocks themselves are found on the island of Ua Pou, and are worked into a variety of shapes: ornamental fish hooks, decorative whales and birds, and pestles used to smash taro called kea tuki popoi.

Unlike most cruise lines, which have multinational crews, Aranui instead runs a local cargo service that just happens to have a large international tourism component. This means all of the onboard crew are Polynesians, many of them originally from the Marquesas themselves. The service is friendly and informal, and I was often greeted on a first-name basis. A couple of the crew recognized me from my previous sailing to another island group, already some four years hence.

The passenger half of the ship has basic amenities like a pool and cocktail bar.

Aranui also doesn’t enforce the same separation between passengers and crew that is prevalent on other ships—passengers and crew can freely mingle. After dinner, many crew members and officers end up in the bar for nightcaps right alongside the passengers. On my previous voyage with Aranui, to the Austral Islands, I joined an impromptu card game in the onboard pearl boutique and watched the head of housekeeping handily clean out the ship’s captain over the course of several hands of poker, all while we and the silken strands of Tahitian Pearls in the display cases bore witness.

When my only pair of sandals broke alighting from the landing craft on Ua Huka, Aranui staff directed me to the ship’s French doctor, who fixed it with tape from his medical bag. “Come back later onboard,” he said, “and we’ll do surgery on the shoe.” While I waited, I took great amusement with a large notice on the door of the ship’s infirmary, warning that many of the fruits served onboard and in the islands have “diuretic and laxatif (sp) effect,” urging passengers to consume in moderation. I wondered how many passengers had visited the infirmary over the years with the same complaint before they felt the need to put up a sign.

At the end of our stop on Ua Huka, we all gathered on the deck of Aranui V. We still had calls on the islands of Rangiroa and Bora Bora scheduled, but it was time to bid our goodbyes to the Marquesas in a traditional manner. A member of the onboard staff invoked a prayer of thanks for the voyage and fond farewell to these magnificent islands, which we did with armfuls of local flowers and plants cast into sunset-dappled sea to watch float ashore.

That, however, wasn’t the lasting image of the Marquesas for me. For weeks after my trip, I awoke each morning in a home that seemed suddenly foreign, recalling the smell of the straw hats, the taste of the baked banana, the green of the mountains, the red floral dress of the snacking mahu, and the pallets of coconuts and grapefruits stacked on the tiny wharf.

#6217. The Week: Jensen Huang, Honeytrapped

Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang speaks with the media ahead of a meeting with the Senate Banking Committee on Capitol Hill in Washington, D.C., December 3, 2025.

• China has gained an edge in one of the world’s most dangerous technologies: the honeypot.

• Jensen Huang has resigned as CEO of the tech giant Nvidia, as news of extramarital affairs with multiple subordinates and a spy scandal engulfed the company. The “other woman” in the honeytrap has been identified in numerous reports as a Chinese national and executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company in the business of renting out computing power that relies on Nvidia’s advanced chips (which it has bought in huge quantities). U.S. intelligence has accused Megaspeed of smuggling contraband chips to China and identified the Nvidia CEO’s paramour as a Chinese spy, information that was passed on to senior officials in Washington. The FBI and Congress are taking a closer look. Nvidia’s advanced chips are absolutely critical for cutting-edge AI models, so handling this scandal will be complicated. We are ahead of China in the AI “arms race” to a degree that an effort dominated by the government would not match, but it’s a lead that Washington, if it mishandles its response to this mess, could all too easily undermine. We do, however, need once again to examine what chips U.S. companies may sell to China. The efforts that the Chinese appear to be making to get hold of a U.S. product make the case for not selling it to them. Huang has argued that if the U.S. withholds more advanced chips, the Chinese will develop their own. They will try to do so anyway. Beijing’s instincts are autarkic. There is no sense in the U.S. making that task any easier.

#6216. 10 Vacation Rentals Across North America For Your Next Family Reunion

Family reunions can be stressful. There’s much to consider, from dealing with a motley of personalities to making sure the kids are looked after. But things get much easier when you land on the perfect vacation rental, one in a crowd-pleasing location, with a spacious layout and plenty of amenities that will keep everyone happy. Whether you’re bringing the gang together for an outdoor adventure at Yosemite National Park, or seeking a laid-back sojourn in the Caribbean, the rentals on this list satisfy every kind of trip. Each featuring four bedrooms or more, these properties are sure to fit the entire clan with luxe amenities worth traveling for: think saltwater pools, golf simulators, and private beach access. What’s more, many are within the top 1% of guest reviews in their area, which means they’re loved by the people who have visited (and are often booked for return trips). Below, the best vacation rentals for family reunions across North America.

We've selected these listings based on ratings, amenities, location, decor, editor stays, and previous guest reviews.

Number of guests: 20Bed and bath: 6 bedrooms, 5.5 bathsWhy we love it: Private pool, proximity to beach, game room

Just steps away from Alys Beach, located on Scenic Highway 30A, this sunny and spacious six-bedroom home was designed for families: four king bedrooms with en suite bathrooms (one of which houses two extra twin beds); a bunk room with a double and four additional twin beds; and a queen with a trundle. There’s a game room, complete with ping-pong and Foosball tables, plus large-screen TVs. The little ones can enjoy amenities too, like mini cribs and pack-and-plays. If the family would rather swim at home, there’s a gorgeous heated pool for everyone to wade in, with sun loungers, an adjacent barbecue, and even a little tanning ledge for kids to take their first steps in the water.

Location: Inlet Beach, FloridaThings to do nearby: Seacrest Beach, Deer Lake State Park, Alys Beach

Number of guests: 10Bed and bath: 5 bedrooms, 4 bathsWhy we love it: Study area, in-unit washer/dryer, outdoor patio

Nantucket, with its pristine beaches and vibrant historic town, makes for an excellent family gathering. This classic, cedar-shingled home features an abundance of windows that bring in natural light, spotless interiors, and plainly chic furnishings. There are five bedrooms with high ceilings (some offer glimpses of the harbor), four full bathrooms, and a spacious kitchen. On the first floor, French doors open out to an outdoor entertainment area, with sectional seating, a dining table that seats 10, a gas grill, and an outdoor shower, all enclosed by a landscaped lawn—the perfect place for the group to kick back and relax.

Location: Nantucket, MassachusettsThings to do nearby: Nantucket Atheneum, Quaker Meeting House, Children's Beach

Number of guests: 20Bed and bath: 7 bedrooms, 6 bathsWhy we love it: Hot tub, proximity to ski resorts, golf simulator

This dreamy A-frame home in Pennsylvania’s Laurel Highlands offers adventurous family members proximity to the slopes at Hidden Valley and Seven Springs resorts. With seven bedrooms spread across three floors, there’s enough space for 20 guests to spread out, plus a fully equipped kitchen, dedicated theater area, game room, and even a golf simulator. After a long day of activities, there’s no better place to relax tired muscles than the hot tub outside, fit for six, or the firepit, surrounded by cozy loungers. Keep in mind the area does get icy over the winter, so 4WD is recommended.

Location: Somerset, PennsylvaniaThings to do nearby: Hidden Valley Resort, Seven Springs Mountain Resort, Ohiopyle State Park

Number of guests: 20+Bed and bath: 9 bedrooms, 8.5 bathsWhy we love it: Gazebo, valley views, fireplace

Located in the heart of Ohio’s Amish country, Hillside Villa is a bucolic escape for the extended family. While the entire villa can be booked (check for availability on the “Premier House” option), you can also opt for individual units, from a deluxe room for two with a jetted hot tub to a junior room that sleeps up to four. Each comes with scenic views of the hills, along with shared kitchen access (coffee and tea maker provided). There are 55-inch flat-screen TVs too, along with features like fireplaces and porches. In the backyard, you’ll find a gazebo with a firepit, perfect for watching the sunset descend over the farm-filled valley.

Location: Millersburg, OhioThings to do nearby: Country Acres Mini Golf, Pro Football Hall of Fame, Belden Village Mall

Number of guests: 14Bed and bath: 4 bedrooms, 3 bathsWhy we love it: Contemporary interior design, private lake access, barbecue

Offering 200 feet of private lakefront in Austin, this modern four-bedroom is a rare retreat. Ideal for a multigenerational family, it’s composed of a main house with two king bedrooms and a guesthouse with a king bedroom, plus a large bunk room with eight twin beds. Spend your days gliding along the lake on a kayak or paddleboard, floating on the 16-foot lily pad, or taking a hike through the surrounding Balcones Canyonland Preserve. End the fun on the two-story party dock, where you can enjoy a meal outside, with s’mores for dessert around the firepit.

Location: Austin, TexasThings to do nearby: Lake Austin, Sixth Street, University of Texas at Austin

Number of guests: 8Bed and bath: 4 bedrooms, 2 bathsWhy we love it: Hiking trail access, pool table, forest views

This Yosemite home, with its breathtaking cathedral windows and stone fireplace, will offer the family a stay they won’t forget. The perfect place to retreat to after a day spent at Yosemite National Park, this four-bedroom is wonderfully western, with its hanging deer antlers, wooden furniture, and tons of colorful textiles. Your group can spread out between two queen beds, two twin beds, and two bunk beds (one with a trundle). Prepare meals in the fully equipped kitchen, then enjoy some family time at the dining table, which seats up to 10. Up in the loft, you’ll find a mini arcade, a number of board games, and a pool table.

Location: Yosemite National Park, CaliforniaThings to do nearby: Yosemite National Park, Yosemite Valley, Yosemite Arch Rock Gate Entrance

Number of guests: 10Bed and bath: 4 bedrooms, 4 bathsWhy we love it: Mountain views, gym, wildlife sightings

Cozy, inviting, and lived-in, this Jackson Hole property is the ultimate mountain escape. Located in Spring Creek Ranch, the home is in a 1,000-acre ranch community, perched atop East Gros Ventre Butte, 800 feet above the valley floor. The first thing you’ll notice upon walking in is a kitchen and dining area that flows into the living room, with large windows overlooking the mountains. There are four bedrooms (three kings and one with two twin beds), each with views of the Tetons. Poke around the woods, watch a movie around the fireplace, and look out for elk.

Location: Jackson, WyomingThings to do nearby: Jackson Hole Valley, Jackson Hole Wildlife Safaris, Jackson Town Square

Number of guests: 8Bed and bath: 4 bedrooms, 1 bathWhy we love it: Scenic views, in-unit washer/dryer, beach access

In Quebec City, the Saguenay Fjord stretches over 62 miles and is surrounded by dramatic granite cliffs. This charming, four-bedroom home will place you right in front of the action. Settle back on the front porch with your loved ones and watch the tides roll in, or take sunset walks along the beach. The fully equipped kitchen has everything you need for meals at home, while the grand dining table looks out into the water. Outside, there’s a swing for little ones, plus a few Adirondack chairs for the adults to continue savoring the view.

Location: Saguenay, Quebec City, CanadaThings to do nearby: Saguenay River, Theatre du Palais Municipal, Okwari Le Fjord

Number of guests: 8Bed and bath: 4 bedrooms, 4.5 bathroomsWhy we love it: In-unit washer/dryer, chef available upon request, beach access

Dreaming of a family reunion across the border? At this bungalow in Placencia, Belize, you’ll have the Caribbean Sea right at your doorstep. Ideal for two families, the four bedrooms (one king and three queens) are spread out in such a way that two of them have their own separate entrance. Spend your days soaking up the sun, swimming in the saltwater pool, gliding along the water on a stand-up paddleboard, or preparing a fresh lunch in the outdoor kitchen. And if you truly want to leave your worries at the door, in-house chef services are available upon request.

Location: Placencia, MexicoThings to do nearby: Placencia Beach, Placencia Pier, Maya Beach

Number of guests: 18Bed and bath: 8 bedrooms, 7 bathsWhy we love it: Panoramic windows, hot tub, in-unit washer/dryer

For extra-large families with great taste, this eight-bedroom beach house is a no-brainer, with jaw-dropping, panoramic views of Lake Michigan and plenty of luxe amenities, from a hot tub and game room to a heated pool. There are gorgeous design details throughout, like vaulted wooden ceilings and circular ship-style windows. Rooms are split between the main house and guest house, with two separate kitchens. Just an 11-minute walk from Saugatuck Dunes State Park, the house provides access to endless scenic trails. Bonus: It’s pet-friendly too.

Location: Saugatuck, MichiganThings to do nearby: Kalamazoo River, Saugatuck Dunes State Park, Oval Beach

#6215. The Moment I Saw This Gorgeous Lake Como Airbnb, I Knew I Had to Plan a Trip to Perledo

Maybe it’s because I’m a dreamer, or maybe it's because I’m slightly impulsive, but whenever I'm planning a trip, I start by browsing Airbnb. I find it the easiest way to envision my time away, and I dropped the notion a long time ago that you don’t actually spend time in your accommodations. That's how I ended up finding myself in a teeny town called Perledo this past summer—my mom had always dreamed of visiting Lake Como for her birthday, so I decided to see what great accommodations I could find in the area for a visit in August, her birth month.

For a stay in Italy, if it’s sleek, minimalist, or modern, keep it away from me. I’m drawn to homes that feel like a reflection of the country I’m in—something uncommon with character and a story. So when I found this unbelievably charming rental in Perledo—a quiet village in the hills above Varenna, overlooking Lake Como—on the Airbnb platform, I booked it for my mom, sister, and I before we even had flights. I mean, look at it!

My family and I arrived in Lake Como on a scorching August day after spending seven days in Sardinia. After a flight, bus, train, and short taxi ride up and around the mountain, we were thrilled to land in our new home. A few days before our arrival, our host, Giulia (having the same name as her felt like a good omen to me!), helped us navigate getting to the apartment from the train, offering us multiple numbers for local taxis, as we hadn't wanted to rent a car. (I'm glad we went that route, because I wouldn't have wanted to deal with parking.)

Upon entering the home, after several trips up and down the stairs, we threw down our bags and immediately made our way onto the balcony. The sunlight beamed through the French doors with the mountains in the background, and the smell of crisp Alpine air made the three of us pause. Staring at the boats as they glided through the water, we all immediately forgot about the long journey it took to get there.

We discovered a bottle of red wine, taralli, and a bunch of Nespresso pods waiting for us on the kitchen table, and I was delighted to find the pantry filled with essentials—salt, pepper, olive oil, and vinegar. You know, those items you might need to complete a meal or a snack, but are annoying to buy on vacation.

The apartment felt warm from the sunlight, but also by design. The pearly walls, with green cabinets and warm wood accents, felt very grounding, like an extension of the atmosphere outside. The tile flooring in the living area reminded me of my cousin's house in Rome, and the pistachio-green-framed window in the bathroom opened wide for a clear picture of the mountains and lake.

After already spending a week with my mom and sister, I was ready for some space, so I opted for the sofa bed with a memory foam topper in the living room. The bed was already made, so it was easy to slip into the soft sheets for a nap after my shower. Throughout the stay, we were mindful not to let the hot water meter fall below a certain level, per Giulia's advice, but between the three of us, we rarely came close.

Giulia also gave us tons of information about the area, including ferry schedules, walking paths, and numbers for hairstylists (I'm always looking for a good blowout). Being able to communicate with her as a local resource felt like we had a personal tour guide with us at all times.

When we left the apartment on our first evening, we followed Giulia’s instructions to catch the complimentary Perledo Night Bus, a service provided by the town from 7 p.m. till midnight, to get to nearby Varenna, where we could grab the ferry to take us to other towns. Walking up and down the mountain, especially at night, would have been challenging and slightly dangerous, so we were happy to grab the shuttle, which was a 10-minute walk from our place.

Unlike Como town or Bellagio, Varenna is quieter, with restaurants that shut down around 9 p.m. Luckily, there are some places to eat and drink in Perledo too. For example, Bar Milano is where locals congregate for their morning espressos or evening nightcaps. For us, it was where we would grab our bus rides up and down the mountain, as well as breakfast (the apricot croissants are incredible).

The walk to Bar Milano was a deeply scenic experience for us—the sunlight glistening on the lake to our right; the lush green mountains dotted with homes to our left. We often noticed fountains and shrines to pray at on our journeys up and down, something consistent on most streets in the village. After arriving home with our breakfast every day, we would start our mornings slow, sitting on the balcony with our espressos and cornetti, taking in the postcard-perfect views of the lake. We often said hi to our neighbors just below us, families who were keen on enjoying the morning air too.

We made few plans for our days, except a reservation for my mom’s birthday lunch. We spent four hours indulging at Passalacqua, the boutique hotel in Moltrasio, and between the beauty of the space, the unhurried pace of the meal, and the kindness of the staff, it’s a memory we will all keep forever. Other afternoons were spent ferry hopping, exploring different towns. In Bellagio, it was imperative we walked down the most famous corridor—Salita Serbelloni. Filled with small artisanal shops and restaurants, it was here I bought a rosary necklace from a man named Filippo, the owner of Bellagio New Wave, a family business that has been in operation for over 100 years. He told me that he grew up above the building.

After days spent on our feet, ears buzzing from the large crowds, nothing was more serene than returning to the quiet of our apartment. Stepping off the shuttle and onto the street for our walk back to the Airbnb brought a sense of tranquility over our three days there, like we were truly going home. Being able to stare into the night sky, overlooking the stillness of the water while being hit with a slight breeze, offered a respite from the adventures of the day.

When I think of Lake Como, I think of two things: romance and luxury. Away from the noise but still close enough to the action, this Airbnb gave us a slice of that fantasy. I now recommend Perdolo to everyone. Safe to say, I’ll continue building my trips around great Airbnbs. The rest always figures itself out later.

#6214. Copa 737 Slices Open UPS 767 At Miami Airport After UPS Crew Fails To Yield

A Copa Airlines Boeing 737 carrying 172 people struck a UPS Boeing 767 at Miami International Airport after the cargo crew failed to yield as instructed. The resulting damage was substantial, but thankfully only two minor injuries were reported. The air traffic control exchange suggests that a runway change and cockpit checklist may have contributed to the error.

The collision occurred shortly after 9:00 pm on Saturday, November 14, 2026, at the intersection of two taxiways at Miami International Airport (MIA). Copa Airlines flight CM427, a Boeing 737-800 arriving from Panama City (PTY), was taxiing toward its gate with 166 passengers and six crew members onboard. UPS flight 358, a Boeing 767-300 freighter, was taxiing for departure to Bogotá (BOG).

According to the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), air traffic controllers had instructed the UPS crew to give way to the approaching Copa aircraft. Preliminary information from the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) indicates that the UPS aircraft did not stop.

The left wingtip of the Copa 737 subsequently struck the nose of the UPS 767, slicing open the freighter’s forward fuselage. Two passengers aboard the Copa flight were treated at the scene for minor injuries. Neither required transportation to a hospital.

Copa 737 left wingtip into the nose of a UPS 767. UPS was instructed to give way, crew acknowledged they went too far. Two treated for minor injuries on scene. pic.twitter.com/sB0kJamQ3J

— Fahad Naim (@Fahadnaimb) November 15, 2026

The air traffic control recording provides a remarkably candid account of what happened immediately after the collision:

Controller: “427, roger. UPS, you’re supposed to give way to the 73 there.”

UPS pilot: “Roger, we running checklist, runway change.”

Controller: “UPS 358, did you hit that aircraft?”

UPS pilot: “Yeah, we went too far, and then he clipped us with the wing.”

That final admission is clear enough: the UPS aircraft moved too far forward and entered the path of the Copa 737.

There may be considerably more context that we do not yet know. The NTSB investigation will examine the taxi instructions, cockpit recordings, aircraft positions, lighting, markings, and actions of both crews. But the reference to running a checklist following a runway change certainly seems like the cultist…how ways it to become transit (and one reason I dive a Tesla, but that’s another matter).

Photographs show a large opening in the nose of the UPS 767 and damage to the left wingtip of the Copa 737.

That UPS B767 looks pissed after clipping the winglet of that Copa Airlines B737! https://t.co/9vu34jsVkk pic.twitter.com/e0l5ergWei

— Turbine Traveller (@Turbinetraveler) November 15, 2026

The NTSB has characterized the damage to the UPS aircraft as “substantial.” An assessment of the Copa aircraft was still underway when the agency provided its initial update.

UPS issued a statement saying it was cooperating with investigators and would not speculate about the cause. Copa likewise said it would cooperate with authorities. The collision did not cause a wider shutdown at Miami. Other aircraft were directed around the affected taxiway while the Copa passengers were eventually brought back to the terminal.

A UPS Boeing 767 failed to yield at a Miami taxiway intersection and moved into the path of an arriving Copa Airlines 737. The resulting collision tore open the cargo jet’s nose, damaged the passenger aircraft’s wingtip, and left two passengers with minor injuries.

The UPS pilot’s acknowledgment that the crew “went too far” while handling a checklist and runway change offers an important clue, but the NTSB will determine what actually led to the mistake. Thankfully, this ended with damaged metal rather than a more serious tragedy. But two large aircraft colliding on a taxiway was a serious mishap.

#6213. The Real Reason Why The GE9X's 134-Inch Fan Beats Out The Diameter On Every Other Jet Engine Ever Made

Standing at an astonishing 134 inches (340 cm) in diameter, the General Electric GE9X is so massive that its front fan casing matches the entire fuselage width of a Boeing 737. It is an engineering milestone that instantly dwarfs every commercial turbofan built before it. Even so, the true marvel of this colossal design is not simply that it is the largest jet engine in aviation history, but why GE pushed the envelope to such unprecedented extremes in the first place.

For many years now, conventional wisdom in aerospace engineering linked massive size directly to chasing raw, record-breaking takeoff thrust. However, the 134-inch fan tells a fundamentally different story, one rooted in thermodynamic efficiency, bypass physics, and fuel burn reduction. This article explores how expanding fan diameter became the definitive master key to unleashing the true potential of long-haul operating economy, looking closely at the iterative evolution of the widebody power plant.

Moving a larger mass of air at a lower exhaust velocity needs significantly less energy than expelling a smaller mass at extreme speed, and this principle is at the very heart of widebody engine design, as detailed in publications from Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University. In large turbofan designs, the front fan functions as the main thrust-producing element, generating the vast majority of the total propulsive force while the core primarily provides power to drive that fan. The basic division of labor explains why widebody propulsion relies so heavily on volumetric airflow rather than raw jet exhaust velocity.

Expanding the fan diameter, reaching a massive 134 inches (340 cm), is the single most direct geometric lever available to engineers to scale this mass airflow. Through the widening of the intake area, the engine captures and accelerates a vastly greater volume of ambient air around the hot engine core. The deliberate scaling drives the bypass ratio up to approximately 10:1, maximizing propulsive efficiency and greatly changing the thermodynamic performance of long-haul flight.

The direct operational payoff of these high-bypass mechanics is a decisive reduction in Specific Fuel Consumption (SFC). Because the enlarged fan handles a greater volume of air at lower rotational speeds, it minimizes the kinetic energy wasted in high-velocity exhaust plumes while delivering the smooth thrust required for transoceanic routes. The aerodynamic foundation then removes excessive fuel burn, giving way to that volumetric expansion that is the absolute master key to unlocking long-range operating economy.

Reaching the milestone 134-inch (340 cm) diameter was not an overnight conceptual leap, but the result of an aggressive, multi-year iterative design trajectory during the evolution of the Boeing 777X family. When General Electric initially laid out the propulsion design to succeed the legendary GE90 family, early studies contemplated retaining the proven 128-inch (325 cm) fan casing of the GE90-115B. However, as Boeing refined the aerodynamic profiles, maximum takeoff weights, and ultra-long-range operational targets for the incoming 777-9, engineers realized that minor tweaks would fall short of the radical efficiency leaps demanded by modern airline economics.

Through successive design iterations, GE incrementally pushed the outer fan containment casing outward. The development path saw the diameter step up to 132 inches (335 cm), before briefly testing configurations at 133.5 inches (339 cm), and ultimately locking in the record-breaking 134-inch envelope. Each fractional expansion of the fan face resulted in measurable gains in bypass ratio and mass airflow, which helped to show that in the specialized world of widebody turbofan design, every additional inch of intake diameter can make exponential dividends in overall fuel burn reduction.

The GE9X's step-by-step upscaling necessitated a total rethinking of fan dynamics, as a larger diameter compounds both centrifugal stress and aerodynamic drag if not meticulously managed. So, through carefully tailoring the fan tip velocities and expanding the casing boundaries through advanced computational fluid dynamics, GE made a brand new geometric baseline. This careful stretching of the fan envelope paved the way for unprecedented bypass efficiency that did not lead to a destabilization of the core mechanics of the engine.

Unravel the secrets of the massive GE9X, a jet engine that redefines scale and efficiency in the skies.

Building an engine fan wider than a 737 fuselage is a huge problem for runaway rotational weight. Scaling a conventional metal fan to a massive 134 inches (340 cm) using traditional titanium or heavy alloys would create massive centrifugal loads, needing exponentially stronger containment rings and heavier shafts. It would instantly cancel out any thermodynamic or fuel-burn gains achieved by high-bypass geometry. GE solved this profound engineering problem through advanced material science, with the help of fourth-generation carbon-fiber composite fan blades.

The breakthrough came in the aerodynamic efficiency and material properties of these advanced composite structures. Each fourth-generation blade is stiffer and capable of managing a vastly greater aerodynamic workload, so engineers were able to slash the total blade count from 22 on the legacy GE90 down to just 16 on the GE9X. Furthermore, these blades incorporate specialized steel leading edges and impact-absorbing fiberglass trailing edges to handle foreign object damage, all while maintaining an ultra-thin profile that keeps aerodynamic drag to its very minimum.

Such a radical reduction in blade count, paired with a lightweight carbon-fiber composite fan case that saves roughly 350 pounds (158.8 kg) per engine relative to traditional metal casings, strips away massive amounts of dead weight. By shedding structural mass despite the record-breaking physical envelope, the low-pressure spool can rotate with optimal efficiency. The GE9X is just the latest example of how crucial advanced composites are to the modern widebody power plant design ethos.

The relentless pursuit of fuel efficiency naturally tempts propulsion designers to dream of even larger fan diameters, but the GE9X’s 134-inch (340 cm) envelope is seen as a strict, practical ceiling for direct-drive commercial turbofans. Pushing fan dimensions significantly beyond this threshold triggers immediate, almost uncontrollable structural and geometric penalties that threaten to offset any thermodynamic gains. Chief among these barriers is aircraft ground clearance; when fitted to the 777X, the massive nacelle leaves a tight static clearance above the tarmac, as noted by Jalopnik. Scaling the fan any further would result in substantially taller and heavier landing gear legs, bringing further structural weight penalties that would instantly prevent high-bypass fuel savings.

Furthermore, swelling the fan casing beyond 134 inches leads to crippling aerodynamic drag and frontal cross-section penalties during high-speed cruise. As aerodynamic studies consistently demonstrate, the external drag penalty of an oversized cowl eventually eclipses the internal thermodynamic efficiency gained from a larger bypass ratio. For direct-drive turbofan designs, 134 inches hits the absolute mathematical sweet spot, balancing maximum propulsive mass flow against the rigid constraints of modern airframe integration.

It is quite clear that the GE9X’s monumental fan diameter stands as a definitive milestone in conventional engine design, though even the most impressive engines have caveats. It extracts every available fraction of efficiency from a direct-drive layout, creating the absolute outer boundary of what is physically and operationally feasible for widebody propulsion before radical new architectures, such as open-rotor or geared systems, must take the stage.

A closer look at the GE9X's troubled development.

One of the most counterintuitive realities of the GE9X program is that despite possessing the largest fan diameter in commercial aviation history, it is not engineered to deliver the highest raw takeoff thrust. While its predecessor, the GE90-115B, is rated at up to 115,000 pounds (511.5 kN) of max thrust, the GE9X is calibrated to a nominal 105,000 to 110,000 pounds (467.0 to 489.3 kN), as per Simple Flying analysis. Ultimately, the deliberate reduction in maximum rated thrust highlights a key shift in how modern widebody propulsion is conceptualized and optimized.

The justification for this lower thrust rating rests in the aerodynamic brilliance of the 777X airframe itself. Featuring a high-aspect-ratio composite wing, the 777-9 and 777-8 generate exceptional lift and cruise efficiency compared to the 777-300ER. Due to the airframe being inherently more efficient during climb and high-altitude transit, it does not need that raw, brute-force runway thrust to hoist heavy loads across intercontinental routes that was seen on the GE90-powered predecessor.

Rather than chasing higher poundage ratings, GE engineers channeled every ounce of headroom into slashing Specific Fuel Consumption and mitigating thermal stress across the core. The goal was to tailor engine output precisely to the aerodynamic profile of the 777X, and therefore, the propulsion system achieves elite fuel economy without needing to match the maximum raw output of older, heavier power plants.

The GE9X’s 134-inch (340.4 cm) fan is far more than a showroom spectacle; it is the definition of what thermodynamic optimization should look like. Prioritizing bypass ratio and mass airflow over raw, unneeded pounds of thrust, GE successfully resolved the conflicting demands of modern long-haul aviation, and did so without falling into the trap of brute-force escalation.

Now, with the Boeing 777X family moving closer to full commercial entry, this monumental fan has made the definitive benchmark for widebody efficiency. It proves that the future of jet propulsion lies not in burning more fuel to create raw power, but in mastering the physics of air on an unprecedented scale. Delays have pushed its entry to service way out of initial projections, but when it does finally take to the skies in customer colors, the world will finally be able to see the full power of GE Aerospace's most radical creation yet.
