Flight cancellations are on the rise in 2026. Since Jan. 1, U.S. carriers have canceled roughly 2% of all flights, according to FlightAware, putting this year on pace for the highest cancellation rate since 2022. And delays remain common: About one in four departures nationwide was delayed between Memorial Day and Labor Day, according to data from aviation analytics firm Cirium.

While most flights leave on time, delays and cancellations remain a reality of air travel — whether due to bad weather, mechanical issues, scheduling problems or other unforeseen circumstances, including the recent nationwide ground stop.

In case you experience flight delays or cancellations, here are tips on how to decrease your chances of getting stuck and increase your odds of arriving at your destination as quickly as possible. Plus, check out our advice on how to potentially get reimbursed for unexpected expenses due to your flight delay or cancellation, depending on the reason that caused the delay.

In this era of full flights and easily available information, don’t wait for the airline to tell you there is a problem. You can keep an eye on general flight trends across the country by using FlightAware, which gives you a good overview of how a day in the sky looks.

FlightAware’s “MiseryMap” focuses on delays. In the 24 hours before travel, you can manually check the status of your flight on your airline’s website. If possible, be sure to check the plane's origin. Even if the conditions are clear where you are, there’s a good chance your plane won’t get to you on time if it’s sitting in a snowstorm somewhere else.

It’s also a good idea to sign up for flight notifications from your airline. Here are details on how to opt in to that process with American Airlines and United Airlines.

You can also get flight status updates sent directly from FlightAware. TPG staffers are also fond of the Flighty app, which offers a reliable "Where's My Plane?" feature to track your plane starting 25 hours before your flight.

Be sure to download your airline’s app on your phone, too. Many airlines will show you where your incoming plane is currently. In fact, your airline’s app often has more up-to-date flight departure information than what’s on the departure and arrival boards at the airport.

This can be a tricky one. If your flight is still listed as “on time” in the app, leave for the airport according to the original schedule.

Even if your flight shows as delayed in the app, that status is subject to change. So, in most cases, it’s best to be at the airport ready to go at the originally scheduled time. We’ve certainly heard stories of flights being delayed only to depart sooner than expected, leaving some passengers behind.

Sometimes, you’ll receive confirmation well in advance, letting you know if your flight will be significantly delayed. Say you are at an airport that isn’t a hub for the airline you are flying (meaning there's less chance of spare planes and crew), and the plane that's supposed to operate your flight is nowhere close to arriving at the airport. In that case, it's likely that your posted delay will be a real delay. However, it’s still safer to be at the airport, just in case.

Bad weather can sometimes cause a temporary ground stop at the airport. As soon as the weather improves and the stop lifts, airlines will try to get their flights off the ground ASAP. So, it’s best to be close by should things change on short notice.

Related: 3 things to do if your flight is delayed

It’s important to know your rights as an airline passenger, which have been changed in recent years.

For instance, if your flight is canceled or significantly delayed and you choose not to travel, you’re entitled to a refund, no matter the reason for the disruption. According to current rules from the U.S. Department of Transportation, passengers on domestic flights that are significantly changed, including arriving three or more hours late, and international flights arriving six or more hours late are entitled to automatic refunds if they choose not to travel and don't accept alternative transportation or travel credits. Those refunds must be issued within seven days for credit card purchases and 20 days for cash payments.

However, if you get stranded overnight, you may also be able to recoup costs for extra meals, hotel nights and ground transportation, depending on the reason for the delay. A widespread FAA ground stop, for example, is unlikely to be a covered reason.

You’ll find these and other passenger rights guarantees on flightrights.gov, the DOT’s dashboard.

On that website, you’ll find a rundown of what airlines guarantee in the event of “controllable” delays and cancellations — disruptions within an airline’s control. Keep in mind that these controllable situations typically exclude weather-related problems.

When looking at the dashboard, you’ll quickly see that some airlines promise to do more than others regarding overnight hotel stays, ground transportation, credit vouchers and rebooking on partners. Give that list a look not only when you’re deciding which airline to book with but also in the event of a long, controllable delay or cancellation. This way, you’ll know what the airline has promised to do in those situations. You can file a complaint with the DOT if the airline doesn’t hold up its end of the bargain.

Monitor weather patterns a few days before your flight to see if any major systems are anticipated. It’s vital to check the forecast the night before and on the day of travel to see how any issues could affect your departure and arrival airports.

Again, be sure to opt in to receive updates on your flight’s status. If you know bad weather is coming later in the day, ask for an earlier flight if you can. Alternatively, leaving the night before the weather arrives is a good idea if you want to minimize the risk of delays.

Many airlines will issue travel advisories during (and ahead of) severe weather, such as blizzards, ice storms or even heavy thunderstorms. These advisories allow travelers to make changes even when flying on a restrictive ticket that typically can’t be altered — like some basic economy fares. In some cases, the airline may even proactively change your flight.

If you know bad weather is on the horizon, visit your airline’s website and look for an advisory notice or call the airline to discuss options. If an airline gets ahead of weather issues, you may be able to reschedule your flight by a few days in either direction with no fees. Additionally, you can try asking for a nonstop flight if the weather jeopardizes your connecting flight.

However, if the airline hasn’t issued its own advisory, you might need to pay out of pocket for any fare differences if you really want to be proactive in changing plans.

Standing in a long line at the airport or waiting on hold by phone is usually no longer the most efficient (or most enjoyable) way to rebook when a flight is canceled or delayed.

Most major airlines will allow you to rebook yourself using a mobile app. You may be able to rebook for a new time or even to a new nearby origin or destination city. For that reason, the airline app should probably be your first stop when you learn of a hiccup in your travel plans.

United will even let you standby for up to three flights if something happens to your originally scheduled flight, while maintaining your original seat.

That said, there are times when automated rebooking systems are not your best option. Sometimes, the only automated option is a red-eye flight or a flight several days later that will head to your destination. That’s especially true when many flights are full.

If you can’t locate what you need on the app, find an airline employee who can work the ticketing desk. Check their uniforms and name tags to ensure you get a ticket agent, versus a baggage handler or a similarly outsourced contractor who is less likely to be able to help.

If the U.S. call center has long hold times (which can happen during widespread issues), you can try dialing an international number for faster service. You can often find those numbers on the airline’s website. You might also find success reaching out to an airline on the social platform X or other social media channels when customer service lines are busy.

For example, when the first leg of an American Airlines flight from New York to Arkansas, scheduled just before Christmas, was delayed, TPG Managing Editor Madison Blancaflor missed her connection. She contacted American Airlines on X to help ensure she was rebooked on the earliest possible flight. She still had to endure a long layover in Charlotte, but it was better (and less stressful) than rushing to the customer service desk to try to rebook upon arrival.

Additionally, some airlines offer live online chat or text options that can be quicker than calling.

If there are no reasonable booking options left with your carrier, ask whether there are options available on another airline. If the delay is weather-related and you are on a basic economy ticket or are flying on a low-cost carrier, there might not be other airline options at your fingertips. Still, it’s worth asking — and, if possible, presenting options you have researched yourself.

Related: Don’t wait on hold: Here’s how to reach airline customer service quickly

If you have airline lounge access at a United Club, a Delta Sky Club or something similar, you can head there for help from experienced agents with potentially shorter lines. Use it as a spot to gather your thoughts, charge your phone and make level-headed decisions. The agents there might be able to help you change or track your flight, as there are usually agents with that knowledge and ability in the airline lounges.

In third-party lounges, such as an American Express Centurion Lounge, you won’t be able to get that type of airline-specific assistance, but you’ll probably be in a better spot to wait out the storm than in a crowded terminal.

Related: Best credit cards for airport lounge access

Sometimes, if you really need to get home, you may need to do the work and pay for a new flight yourself.

In some of our prior experiences, the airlines we originally booked with couldn't get us home within 24 hours of our flights being canceled. In cases like these, you may be able to book a nonstop flight with at least one last seat available on another carrier.

Keep in mind, though, that rebooking yourself is typically not covered by any insurance provider or carrier. Still, you should be able to get a refund for your original ticket, which will at least offset some of the pain of a new one. The extra work may be worth it to control your own destiny and avoid being stuck as options narrow.

Your credit card’s built-in trip delay or trip cancellation coverage can help with many unexpected expenses in the face of delays and cancellations, but a brand-new flight home isn’t likely to be one of them. Still, in some cases, it may be the only way home for a while, so you’ll have to weigh the pros and cons.

Fortunately, many airlines now allow you to cancel main cabin tickets and, at the very least, get airline trip credit; you can use this credit to book a future flight — even if you are being proactive to try and avoid possible delays and, ultimately, your originally scheduled flight does not experience a delay. (This does not necessarily apply to basic economy fares or low-cost carriers' flights.)

Related: Should you get travel insurance if you have credit card protection?

While thinking through what to do in case of a flight delay or cancellation, consider your options at airport hotels; they can fill up during major delays and cancellations. Sometimes, it is best to call it a day, get some rest and try again in the morning.

Airport hotels are generally pretty affordable on points, but cash rates can skyrocket when demand surges. Accommodations are typically covered by trip delay protection in the event of cancellations or very long delays via cards like the (see rates and fees) and .*

*Eligibility and benefit level vary by card. Terms, conditions and limitations apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by New Hampshire Insurance Company, an AIG Company.

Related: Why my favorite use of Hyatt points is a Category 1 airport hotel

If you know in advance that your flight will be canceled or delayed, heading to the airport early could score you a same-day standby flight that gets you to your destination on time.

For example, one TPG staffer used this strategy to avoid getting stuck overnight when a hiccup with his flight from Austin to New York would have caused him to miss a connection in Dallas. He arrived at the airport a bit early and was placed on the standby list for an earlier flight connecting to a different city.

Getting on the standby list isn’t foolproof, especially if the earlier flight is almost full. This is a case where having elite status can help since you’ll have priority over non-elite travelers. Additionally, some airlines charge non-elite travelers a fee to be added to the standby list for an earlier flight.

Related: The best credit cards to reach elite status

The hard truth is that in the event of airline delays and cancellations caused by weather, the airline itself is not going to help you out with the extra expenses you incur due to the change in plans, since the weather is outside its control. Travel insurance may have your back if you purchased it, but beyond that, the credit card you booked your flight with may also be able to reimburse you for unexpected expenses due to your flight delay or cancellation — even if it was caused by weather.

Many rewards credit cards confer valuable travel protections when you have a delayed or canceled flight (if you used one of them to book your flight). Below are just a few examples of cards that provide some built-in coverage:

*Eligibility and benefit level vary by card. Terms, conditions and limitations apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by New Hampshire Insurance Company, an AIG Company.

Related: Best credit cards with travel insurance

To highlight how valuable this can be, a couple of years ago, one TPG staffer's flights home from Colorado during the busy winter holiday season were canceled due to a snowstorm.

She was faced with an unexpected $1,100-per-night hotel stay during peak season in a pricey ski town, based on what was still available at the last minute. Ultimately, her eligible Chase card covered not only the $1,100 unexpected hotel stay but also the unexpected car service and meals during the delay. Within 26 days of the unexpected cancellation and delay, she had a check for $1,401.74 in her hand, thanks to using the right credit card to book the flight.

Unfortunately, some situations are not covered by the built-in trip delay and trip cancellation protections that commonly come with some rewards credit cards, but it never hurts to save receipts and try.

Last but not least, we recommend being decisive when making travel decisions amid delays or cancellations.

The longer you wait to switch flights or book a hotel, the greater the chances you’ll be at the mercy of whatever dwindling options are left as hundreds (or thousands) of other passengers rebook their plans.

Most of the time, your flight will get you where you need to be, close to when you want to be there. Still, flight delays and cancellations are a reality of air travel. If your flight is delayed by an hour or two, there’s not usually much to do other than be patient. However, when facing a long delay or cancellation, it’s good to have a plan to reduce the odds of getting stuck.

Given the common theme of full flights these days, acting quickly, researching options and making a speedy decision will put you ahead of the pack.

#6211. 9 Chefs on the Meals They're Traveling For in 2027—From Korean Soups to Peruvian Ceviche

Any professional chef can confirm that while menu development, staffing, interior design, and operations are all part of running a restaurant or kitchen, finding the time to travel in search of different flavors often feels like a rare luxury. But spending time in a different city or region is key to staying inspired. Even a quick weekend getaway can lead to incorporating new ingredients in familiar dishes, serve as an opportunity to learn a new culinary technique, help forge a connection with one’s own heritage, or connect with peers who are pushing the industry forward.

As the end of the calendar year draws near, we spoke with some of our favorite women chefs about where they’re most excited to visit in 2027—from a sushi counter in Tokyo to the oldest restaurant in Beirut—and what they’re hoping to eat and learn from those travels.

A table at ARREA!, Almuerzo Otoño's restaurant in Álava, Spain

“I went [to the Basque Country] for the first time in 2013, but it was such a quick, rushed trip that I left feeling like I’d barely scratched the surface. I’ve been wanting to go back and really do it right ever since. At the top of my list of spots is Arrea!, Edorta Lamo’s restaurant in Kanpezu, a small village in the mountains of Álava. I’ve heard such wonderful things about it. What excites me is that it’s not the Basque Country most people think of first—as in, San Sebastián with its coastline and all of its pintxo bars. It’s inland cooking, built on what’s hunted, foraged, and grown right there in the mountains. And I'll be eating my way through plenty of pintxo bars too, of course. — Katie Button, chef/co-founder of Cúrate Bar de Tapas in Asheville, and author of Spanish Accent cookbook

“I’m in love with Erin French’s new cookbook [Seize the Supper], and wildly enough, Maine is one of the few states I've never been to. So, I'm plotting something for next summer. I love that it's a mostly female crew, a standout (unfortunately) in our industry. Erin’s focus on local produce and connecting to the earth speaks to my own regenerative cooking and inspires me constantly to dig deeper and deeper. I also admire her ethos of humble simplicity, distilling dishes to their core, filled with soul and properly honoring ingredients, with a nod to her family's heritage. I dream of her play on sweet and savory—like the soft polenta with honey and ricotta.” — Camilla Marcus, chef and founder of Westbourne

The seafood platter at the new Casa Juani in Boulder

Casa Juani's Spain-inspired sea urchin dish

“I am most looking forward to traveling to Boulder to visit my friends Kelly Jeun and Eduardo Vallelobo at their restaurant Casa Juani. Both are accomplished chefs who are experts in Italian and Spanish cuisines, and they recently made Bon Appétit's Best New Restaurants list. I am most excited to try everything on their menu, which is entirely Spanish. Eduardo is very proud of—and from!—Madrid, and the menu celebrates Spanish cuisine and culture.” —Melissa Rodriguez, Chef & Partner at Crane Club & Bar CC in New York City

For cookbook author Rebekah Peppler, edomae-style sushi is a must-eat in 2027.

“[Sushi Meino], a six-seat counter in Tokyo’s Azabujuban neighborhood by Chef Mei Kougo, one of only a few female sushi masters in Japan, has been high on my list since it opened in 2023 and I haven’t yet had the luck of securing a very-difficult-to-get reservation. I'm heading back to Tokyo in the spring and hoping 2027 will be my year! If I don’t get in, I’ll still be heading to Makimaki, her takeout-only hosomaki shop that opened nearby earlier this year.” — Rebekah Peppler, recipe developer and author

Baekyangsa Temple, where Buddhist nun and chef Jeong Kwan hosts meals

Freshly foraged ingredients, including mushrooms, herbs, and greens, used by chef Jeong Kwan

“Eating at venerable Jeong Kwan’s table has been high on my list for years, and I was devastated to be out of town when she and Chef Esu Lee were cooking together at his excellent restaurant Orson in Paris recently. It lit a fire in me to finally prioritize booking a trip to Baekyangsa Temple [where she cooks] to attend one of her demonstrations in 2027.” — R.P.

Street bread Ka'ak is the reason chef Mary Attea will be headed to Lebanon in 2027.

“I'm dying to try manakish and shawarma straight from the source. Plus ka'ak, the ring-shaped street bread with sesame, along with all the spreads from the market. And [I want to pay a] visit to El Soussi, one of Beirut's oldest restaurants, famous for its Lebanese breakfast, especially msabbaha, the warm mashed chickpeas with lemon and tahini. I'd be sure to get an order of beid ghanam as well, which is lambs testicles cooked in lemon and olive oil, served with fattet hummus. Growing up in the US with Lebanese heritage, we often ate many Lebanese meals as a family. But the dishes we prepared and enjoyed were such a small sliver of everything Lebanon has to offer. I've been wanting to go for such a long time so I could experience the vastness of this incredible cuisine and the country's beauty. I was meant to travel there this past March, which was postponed, so it's top of my list for 2027!” —Chef Mary Attea, executive chef of Musket Room and Raf’s in New York City

A ceviche dish at Lima restaurant Al Toke Pez

“I’m especially excited to explore Nikkei cuisine and experience Peruvian ceviche firsthand. In Mexico, we make wonderful ceviches, but I believe Peruvians have truly mastered the art of preparing this dish. I want to experience their approach to seafood, acidity, and flavor in its place of origin, while exploring the broader culinary traditions of Peru. I believe there are many shared histories and points of connection between Latin American cultures that we don’t always recognize, and I want to explore those connections through food. I’m also drawn to the opportunity to experience traditional Mesoamérican markets that are still operating throughout Peru, not only in Lima but in other regions as well. Markets reveal so much about a place: its ingredients, its people, its traditions, and the ways food connects communities. I’d also love to experience Inca culture firsthand and better understand the country’s rich cultural and culinary heritage.” —Norma Listman, chef and co-founder, Masala y Maíz in Mexico City

Traditional Assamese food items on sale at the annual Bhogali Bihu Festival in Assam

“I’m particularly interested in Assam’s distinctive use of black sesame and wild greens. During a trip to Mumbai, I had the opportunity to taste Assamese food prepared by two sisters who cook and preserve traditional Assamese foodways. Their food completely blew my mind. I would love to travel to Assam to learn more about the region’s culinary traditions and experience its food culture firsthand. As a chef who cooks both Indian and Mexican cuisine, I feel a responsibility to keep learning and exploring the vastness and richness of India’s food traditions. India is incredibly diverse, and there is still so much for me to discover. Now, as the mother of a mixed child with Indian heritage, I feel an even greater responsibility to expose him to his culture. Traveling to Assam would be an opportunity to continue learning for myself while creating a meaningful connection between my son and his cultural roots.” — N.L.

“I hosted a pop-up at ADI last year, and was able to witness firsthand the ways in which chef Kanchan [Adhikari] is doing the most incredibly inventive things with food within the South Asian diaspora while also marrying it with a Japanese omakase-style sentiment. One of my favorite restaurants of the past year and I am counting down the days until I can eat a meal in that gorgeous dining room again!"” —Samah Dada, chef and creator of recipe platform DADA Eats

A bowl of pollock soup, a dish local to Inje in South Korea

“Inje is the smallest county in South Korea and is most famous for hwangtae guk (dried pollock) soup. You can find many restaurants clustered together there that serve this regional specialty, but my absolute favorite is a place called Song-yi Sikdang. The brief menu basically comes down to the hwangtae jungsik—a set that includes pollock soup, a whole grilled pollock, an assortment of 12 perfectly seasoned namul banchans, and a warm bowl of rice. Inje is located in the Taebaek mountains alongside rivers and basins, so when you get there, you’re surrounded by stunning landscape and flora, which is absolutely gorgeous year round—ranging from verdant mountains, to golden and crimson foliage, to snowy tree tops. Inje is a short and tranquil two-hour drive from Seoul and feels similar to that of driving upstate on the Taconic from Manhattan. The geography and climate makes it the perfect environment for preparing dried pollock and also foraging for diverse wild greens and herbs (namuls), rare ones that you can only find there and are seasonally available at local farmers markets. —Clara Lee, co-author of Korean Soups and co-founder of food company Queens

I have been wanting to travel to Italy for many years, and Puglia has been top of mind. It feels like a place where food is still very much connected to the culture and deeply rooted in the abundance of the land. Since the provenance of things is our ethos, this feels particularly aligned for me. Anytime I travel (but specifically Europe). “I am really drawn to the simplicity of the cuisine. A beautiful local grilled fish with olive oil, handmade pasta, regional cheeses—these are all things that truly excite me as a chef because their beauty is in how uncomplicated they are. Local, fresh bounty, cooked well: to me this is what makes food memorable.” —Abigail Dahan-Kramer, pastry chef at Provenance in Philadelphia

#6210. US Flights Have Been Grounded Nationwide

The United States Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued a rare nationwide ground stop Friday afternoon, with all outbound flights from the US being directed to halt ground operations. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin stated in a press conference that there was “no indication as of yet” that anything “nefarious” caused the ground stop, and suggested that it was due to a broad was a telecommunications outage.

“There has been a temporary telecommunications outage - out of an abundance of caution all flights have been halted,” the FAA said in a statement on X. “Every flight has been accounted for and international flights will be handled on a case by case basis.”

Department of Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said in a statement that the ground stop was due to a "communication issue" and that “FAA technicians are investigating.”

The halt on take offs and landing is in place for both domestic and international flights operating within the US. United Airlines, one of the four largest airlines in the nation, said that the order did not apply to in-transit aircraft: “United Airlines is responding to a nationwide ground stop issued by the FAA. United flights that are already airborne will continue. New domestic flights will not depart while the FAA ground stop remains in place,” United Airlines said in a press release. “United will work with our customers to get them to their destinations once this issue is resolved.”

The last time a nationwide ground stop occurred in the US was in January 2023 following a computer outage in the Federal Aviation Administration's (FAA) pilot notification system (NOTAM).

CNBC reported that the widespread server outages affecting telecommunications over the past 24 hours were to blame, citing internal information from Alaska Airlines.

According to Cirium, an aviation analytics company, there are 26,284 flights scheduled to depart on November 13 from the US. As of 5:50 p.m., 600 flights have been diverted so far, with 496 of those 600 flights (82.7%) returning to their origin airport and the other 104 diverting to a different airport. At this time 481 have been canceled or no fly nationally, representing 1.83%. This will grow today,” a company spokesperson said. “After 4 p.m. Eastern time today, there were still some 11,000 flight scheduled to depart from US airports today.”

#6208. Rocket Failure Destroys 40 Amazon Leo Satellites And Complicates Delta Air Lines Wi-Fi Plans

Delta Air Lines made a calculated bet when it chose Amazon Leo over Starlink for its next-generation Wi-Fi. That bet became a little riskier on Sunday when a rocket carrying 40 Amazon satellites failed before reaching orbit.

A United Launch Alliance Vulcan rocket lifted off from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station on November 15, 2026, carrying 40 satellites for Amazon Leo, the low-Earth-orbit network Amazon is building to compete with Starlink.

About 10 minutes after launch, the rocket suffered what ULA called an “anomaly” and failed to deliver the satellites into orbit. The entire payload was lost. ULA, a joint venture between Boeing and Lockheed Martin, issued the following statement:

“Based on data received by our Launch Director, we confirm that the Vulcan vehicle launched from Space Launch Complex 41 suffered an anomaly 10 minutes into the flight and failed to deliver the Amazon mission to orbit.

“Every flight generates data, and every flight teaches us something. Since the anomaly just occurred, we don’t have any specific data yet to understand what occurred today.

“We will work closely with our customer and other appropriate organizations to find the cause, determine the appropriate corrective action, and return to flight as quickly as possible.”

This was the first complete mission failure in ULA’s approximately 20-year history and the first Amazon Leo launch aboard a Vulcan rocket.

The loss of 40 satellites is significant, but it certainly does not destroy the Amazon Leo project. Before Sunday’s failure, Amazon had already placed 398 satellites into orbit across 14 launches. The planned constellation calls for 3,236 satellites to provide global coverage, meaning Amazon had deployed about 12% of the initial network before this launch.

Amazon also has hundreds of satellites reportedly ready for launch and is not exclusively dependent on Vulcan. Its next mission, using an Ariane 6 rocket to carry 36 more satellites, is scheduled for November 23 from French Guiana.

So this is not necessarily a case of the entire Leo launch schedule stopping while ULA investigates. Amazon has contracts with several launch providers and can continue expanding its satellite network using other rockets. Still, Amazon planned to use Vulcan for dozens of missions. Any lengthy investigation or redesign could slow the deployment schedule and place more pressure on its other launch partners.

Delta has committed to installing Amazon Leo on an initial 500 aircraft beginning in 2028. The carrier promises download speeds of up to 1 Gbps and upload speeds of up to 400 Mbps through a purpose-built antenna, with service remaining free for SkyMiles members.

But unlike Starlink, which is already operating on hundreds of commercial aircraft, Amazon Leo remains a system under construction. Delta chose a product based on what it is expected to become rather than what passengers can use today.

That choice was defensible. Delta has a broad relationship with Amazon Web Services and wants to integrate connectivity with Delta Sync, its loyalty program, seatback entertainment, and broader customer data strategy. I have defended the logic behind that decision: Delta was choosing a technology and commercial partner that would allow it to retain more control over the passenger interface and potentially build a much broader digital ecosystem. I’d rather have Delta retain contorl over its system than Elon Musk do the same…

> Read More: Is Starlink A Trojan Horse For Airlines? New Musk Report Makes Delta’s Decision Look Smarter

But choosing an unfinished network carries execution risk, and we just received a vivid demonstration of it. One Mile At A Time puts it well: “One of the risks with picking a service that’s still in development is that the timeline is really quite fluid, and this is an example of that.”

United Airlines is already installing Starlink throughout its fleet and expects to complete the project by the end of 2027. Delta does not plan to begin installing Amazon Leo until 2028. In theory, United could finish bringing Starlink to its entire fleet before Delta installs Amazon Leo on its first aircraft.

Delta is not leaving passengers without internet in the interim. Free Delta Sync Wi-Fi is available across most of its fleet, and in my experience it generally works well on most flights. Delta also says it is adding Viasat capacity and deploying Hughes Fusion technology as it works toward full fleet connectivity.

The suggestion that Delta passengers are flying around without functioning Wi-Fi is simply not accurate. But Starlink is better than any inflight internet system I have used. It is fast, low latency, and remarkably consistent. I increasingly choose United flights where I know Starlink will be available because it allows me to work in the air almost as easily as I can on the ground.

Delta CEO Ed Bastian has defended passing on Starlink, citing disagreements over the business model and customer access rather than any personal dispute with Elon Musk.

Fair enough. But every delay to Amazon Leo gives United more time to widen its lead.

One failed rocket does not prove that Delta made the wrong choice. Amazon has the resources, technology, and launch contracts to build a serious Starlink competitor, and Leo may ultimately deliver an excellent onboard product. But Delta selected a network that does not yet exist at the necessary scale. Sunday’s launch failure is precisely the sort of development that can disrupt a carefully constructed timeline but is also hardly unique to getting new technology up and running.

Delta understood that risk when it passed on a proven product in favor of a deeper relationship with Amazon. Now it needs Amazon Leo to recover quickly and keep its 2028 installation promise. Ultimately, passengers will not be amused if faster Wi-Fi remains years away.

No longer do you need to head to a store in person and battle it out for the last jacket on the rack: REI’s online outlet has tons of great gear to save on, all shoppable from the comfort of your own home. From shoes and socks to helmets, boots, and bags, expect huge savings on something for everyone. One of my favorites includes 27% off Smartwool Active Fleece Wind pants. There’s also plenty of other deals on travel gear worth calling out, like 30% off the CamelBak All Around travel tumbler and 41% off the Osprey Arcane small crossbody bag. On REI’s outlet page, shop top brands like Arc’teryx, Hoka, Keen, Osprey, Patagonia, Salomon, and Columbia, all in one spot.

For something a bit more consistent, sign up for an REI lifetime membership to score an estimated 10% off every year on all eligible purchases. Memberships are a one-time payment of $30, and last the rest of your life, so you’ll be able to score benefits for years to come. To get your rewards, simply shop as you usually would, and earn back an estimated 10% Co-op Member Reward annually on eligible full-price co-op purchases. Your reward will automatically be uploaded to your account in the following month.

Members get more benefits, like free standard shipping on every order (5–7 business days)—a convenience that non-members can only reap the reward of when they hit the $60 minimum spend. Members also save 20% off on bike and snow shop services, have extended return windows of up to a year rather than the usual 90 days, get free ski and board wax and a flat tire tube with repair, and up to 33% off gear rentals. All of these benefits more than make up for the $30 fee.

As an added bonus, those who sign up by November 12, 2026, will also receive a $30 gift card, which they can use on whatever they please for 30 days after they sign up. To be eligible to receive this gift card, all you have to do is make a $50 purchase at REI and buy your membership in the same order. This means your $30 one-time membership fee is basically free once you take advantage of the gift card.

Give your gear and clothing a second life when you trade in gently used products to REI’s Re/Supply platform—and receive a gift card for eligible items. Simply fill out the trade-in form to get an estimate on your product’s eligibility and credit value. Then drop your products off at your nearest REI store. Once your trade-in is complete and your product has been evaluated, you’ll receive an email with an REI e-gift card that you’ll be able to use to purchase more of your favorite gear.

Your used products will head to REI’s Re/Supply shop. Not only is this a great way to keep textiles and other items out of landfills, but you’ll get money back to spend on something else. These gently used secondhand products are shoppable as well, and at great discounts, so if you’re open to taking home a pre-loved item rather than springing for a new piece, expect to find some excellent savings. The brand is closing its online version of the shop, but customers can still purchase gently used items in its brick-and-mortar stores.

One final way to keep to your budget and still get some great deals is by signing up for the REI credit card. Customers who open an REI Co-op Mastercard get a total of 15% in REI rewards (5% card rewards on all REI purchases and 10% Co-op member rewards). Cardholders also earn 1.5% in rewards on all other purchases when not shopping at REI. As a bonus, there is no annual fee, and the rewards no longer expire.

REI credit cards are only available to members, so you’ll have to complete the one-time sign-up and $30 membership fee, but once you do so, you’ll be able to sign in online and validate your Co-op membership to join and start racking up rewards. All rewards are ready to be redeemed online and in stores at REI as soon as they pop up in your account. As a bonus, customers can expect a $100 REI gift card after their very first purchase outside of REI, but use it quickly, as the gift card expires 60 days after your account is opened.

#6206. Inside 'Grand Theft Auto VI'—and the Real-Life Florida Locations That Inspired It

Set to be released on November 19, 2026, Grand Theft Auto VI is expected to be the most profitable piece of media ever created. Pre-sale estimates suggest the game has made a staggering $476 million in revenue already.

Dreamt up by Scottish developers Rockstar Games, the GTA series has been big business for some time now. The previous instalment, Grand Theft Auto V has reportedly made a whopping $11 billion since its release in 2013. Not bad for a game in which you essentially steal cars and shoot guns.

If you haven’t played the games, you should know that they take place in a sort of shadow version of the US, with each game taking place in a new city inspired by a real-world counterpart. For me, they’ve been a fascinating companion to my travels in America. When I’m in New York, walking among towering skyscrapers, I can’t help but be reminded of Liberty City, the location of 2001’s dark and atmospheric Grand Theft Auto III. On holiday in Los Angeles, driving along the Pacific Coast Highway, the long, ocean-view roads of GTA V’s Los Santos were front of mind.

It works both ways. Red Dead Redemption 2, an open-world cowboy game released by Rockstar between GTAs V and VI, is perhaps the most immersive video game to date. In it, you can wander everywhere from dry, open deserts to lush forests where you can kick back with your horse, camp, and look for rare herbs and flowers. For me, it’s inspired trips to the deserts of the American Southwest and served as an interesting entry point into learning about US history. Now when I’m abroad, I’m thinking of these games, but also learning more about the real-world events and cultures that inspired them. It’s a full-circle moment that only enriches my travels.

These gaming vacations, or ‘gami-vacations’, are becoming increasingly popular. Fans are traveling to Tokyo to visit real-life locations from the Yakuza series and role-playing classic Persona 5, to Paris to see locations featured in the Assassin’s Creed series, to the Pacific Northwest to soak up the vibes of zombie classic Day Gone, and to Iceland to walk dramatic black sand beaches like those in the Hellblade series.

“Santa Monica, the Sunset Strip, and Griffith Observatory from GTA V,” one Reddit user replied to a post asking about video game locations fans wanted to visit in real life. “Old town Tallinn feels like a very fairytale environment to me. If you went in winter, it would feel like a set from Assassin's Creed,” suggests another Redditor.

Far from being confined to their rooms, crouched over consoles, gamers are increasingly inspired to get out into the world. It’s a beautiful tradition, and one that GTA 6 looks set to continue. Set in the fictional state of Leonida, GTA 6 is set to be the franchise’s largest map to date. With six key locations, there promises to be something for every type of traveller. Here’s what you need to know, along with the real-world inspirations for each game location.

“We’re a long way from the ‘80s, but Vice City is still the sun and fun capital of America,” reads Rockstar’s official guide to GTA VI’s base of operations, Vice City.

As fans are aware, the new game returns to the setting of the 2002 release, Grand Theft Auto: Vice City. Set in the 1980s, that game borrowed pretty heavily from the story of Brian De Palma’s brace of crime films Scarface and Carlito’s Way, giving players the ability to control one Tommy Vercetti as he rises from the streets to build a narcotics empire. As expected, disco, perms, neon signs and flared trousers were the order of the day.

Updated for 2026, GTA VI’s Vice City is a modern cityscape full of high-rises, trendy rooftop bars, nightclubs. and more. It sounds pretty idyllic, but this being GTA, there’s a shadier side, too. “When the sun fades and the neon glows, everyone has something to gain—and more to lose,” the official longline reads.

The recent Netflix preview of the upcoming game gave us a bit more insight into the locale, including shots of BASE jumping from city bridges, a jewelry store robbery and subsequent high-speed escape, and a shootout through a drug den in a down-on-its-luck neighbourhood. In other words, as the main large city in the game, it looks like there’s plenty to keep Vice City residents occupied—on both sides of the law.

Inspiration: While Rockstar doesn’t explicitly explain that ‘game location X equals real world location Y’, it’s pretty obvious that Vice City is based on South Florida’s party capital, Miami. Despite the criminal element of Vice City, the real-world city has been keen to play on the connection. A New York Times story suggests the city is keen to embrace its fictional twin due to a drastic drop in real-world crime recently. Which is, of course, great news for tourists. For the full GTA experience, you can enjoy Miami’s beaches, bars, and car culture, alongside iconic EDM nightspots like Club Space and E11EVEN Miami.

In Leonida Keys, the dress code is casual and the bars are loaded. “Life in this tropical archipelago isn’t flashy, but it’s easy,” runs the official description. In game, the Keys look like an ideal place to hit pristine tropical waters for a dive, jet ski, or scuba trip. Naturally, there seems to be a strong party boat presence too, with a Spring Break vibe. While we’re sure some absolute in-game carnage will take place there, at present, it actually looks like quite a nice place to unwind and escape the more criminal elements of the game’s plot.

Inspiration: The obvious IRL comp here is Key West, nestled at the very southern tip of Florida. In fact, here you can see the southernmost point in the continental US, just 90 miles from Cuba as the crow flies. As well as a plethora of luxury hotels, casual bars, and seafood spots, you can kick back on white beaches, or enjoy a glass-bottomed boat tour.

For a break from all of this, you can visit the Hemingway Home, where Ernest Hemingway finished books including A Farewell to Arms and To Have and Have Not—that is, when he wasn’t out big-game fishing. The house is home to the first-ever swimming pool built in the Keys, as well as descendants of Hemingway’s famous six-toed cats.

Fans don’t know much about GTA 6’s Grassrivers yet, although the official synopsis does suggest some intrigue: “You never know what lies beneath the surface of this primordial expanse. The gators may be the most famous attraction, but there are far deadlier predators and weirder discoveries among the mangroves.” So far, all we’ve seen is an airboat tour and a birdwatching tower, suggesting a heavy emphasis on encounters with the natural world. Watch this space.

Inspiration: Clearly inspired by the Florida Everglades, Grassrivers will surely have a feel and flavor all of its own. The real Everglades has a rich cultural history. Yes, there are airboat tours catered to tourists during which you can spot ‘gators and learn all about the invasive pythons that are terrorising the ecosystem. And yes, you will be able to try deep-fried gator afterwards. But the real treasure is traditional foods like thick and chewy fry bread, swamp cabbage, or sofkee, a thin porridge made from corn.

And, at the Ah-Tah-Thi-Ki Museum near Fort Lauderdale in the north of the Everglades, you can learn about the Seminole nation, a group made up of Native Americans moving south to escape the British, mixed with escaped formerly enslaved peoples from the area’s plantations.

If GTA 6 were represented on an old-timey naval map, Port Gellhorn a “failed resort on the edge of the map" might be marked “here be monsters.”

We know very little about the area yet, except for the fact that it’s rooted in poverty, with locals pushed to extremes to make ends meet. According to Rockstar, “Cheap motels, shut-down attractions and empty strip malls won’t bring the tourists back, but there’s a new economy in this once-popular vacation spot. It’s fuelled by malt liquor, painkillers and truck-stop energy drinks. Jump on a dirt bike and hold onto your wallet.” In other words, it sounds like a great place for a video game, less so for a holiday.

Inspiration: Again, Rockstar hasn’t been open about which area of Florida Port Gellhorn is based on, but fans and Florida locals think it takes inspiration from Panama City and the surrounding areas in the Florida Panhandle. Off the beaten track of most holidays, Panama City nevertheless has a strong reputation for seafood and water sports. Given its deepwater port, there’s also a strong maritime history. St Andrews State Park might be your best bet for snorkelling, swimming, kayaking and a calm and safe designated tidal pool.

Ambrosia sounds, possibly, like the least appealing locale in GTA 6. It’s reportedly a factory town, overseen by vicious biker gangs. “In the heart of Leonida, American industry and old-school values still reign supreme – whatever the cost. The Allied Crystal sugar refinery provides the jobs, while the local biker gang provides almost everything else,” runs Rockstar’s official primer on the place. The Netflix preview didn’t help. We saw a shootout in a dilapidated house, backyard wrestling, and possibly some mud-wrestling too. Mark this one as the biggest unknown of the game.

Inspiration: Florida locals think Ambrosia is based on Clewiston, Florida and the surrounding agricultural area around Lake Okeechobee. The main crop here is sugar, with Clewiston known as "America's Sweetest Town.” The irony in the in-game depiction is pretty obvious here, but the IRL location is well worth a visit if you’re a fan of fishing, with the local largemouth bass on Lake Okeechobee a particularly sought-after prize.

Mount Kalaga National Park looks like a truly beautiful in-game location, teeming with wildlife and activities from bicycle riding to kayaking. What’s not to love? Well, this bucolic utopia may actually prove to be too good to be true. In the Netflix preview, a televised advert for the ‘Prairie Sandwich’ seemed to take place in the park, suggesting that rather than enjoying the park’s animals in their natural habitat, your main goal might actually be to shoot them. If so, hunting will be an interesting addition to the game, and one that worked well in Red Dead Redemption 2. Of course, players will probably be able to opt out of the bloodshed and just enjoy a nice stroll among the trees instead. Here’s hoping.

Inspiration: While there’s no one-for-one comp for Mount Kalaga National Park, the Southern US States in particular are well known for their stunning national parks. Fans think this one takes inspiration from North Carolina’s Table Rock Mountain, Georgia’s Providence Canyon State Park, and the Suwannee River, which runs through Georgia and Florida. Whatever the real inspiration, if you are visiting Florida, it’s a reminder to get off the beaten path and out of the cities into lovingly preserved wild areas.

#6204. Introduction: I Crossed The Atlantic Six Times So My Kids Could Spend A Month In Germany

Taking my kids to Germany for a month should have required one flight across the Atlantic and another flight home. Instead, getting them there, returning to the United States, flying back to pick them up, and inserting one especially circuitous journey along the way meant I crossed the Atlantic six times…including a memorable detour through Greenland.

I realize I will certainly not win any accolades for my environmental stewardship, but my wife and I are trying to create a comfort with Germany for our kids which includes both the culture and the language. They are German citizens too after all.  And so what I did this summer, as I did last summer and as I will do next summer, was take them over to Germany in mid-July and pick them up in mid-August.

That was a lot of travel for me, but I’m not going to lie: I loved (just about) all of it.

I booked a round-trip economy class ticket in spring to get us home from our ski trip and then back in the summer, which included SWISS economy class ticket from Zurich – Chicago and Austrian economy class from Los Angeles – Zurich via Vienna and was even able to squeeze in an overnight in Vienna at the Park Hyatt, which I booked for 25,000 Hyatt points.

The week I booked (the last week in February) was the week the conflict in Iran broke out and I was very happy I booked when I did because I got the tickets for $764 r/t. I also booked before United cut off awarding mileage on basic economy tickets. Since I booked on United ticketing stock, I received PQPs (status points) and RDMs (redeemable miles) for these flights. I also figured the lack of advance seat assignments would not matter because I was traveling with two young children.  That gamble paid off well and we were seated together at check-in on each flight.

That got us to Germany, but I had to find a way back to the USA and then back to Europe the following month to pick them up, plus a ticket home for all three of us.

Flying Blue came through with a perfectly-timed last minute 60K redemption on Air France from Basel – Paris – New York, plus €453 in taxes. It was such a pleasure to fly on Air France and I look forward to sharing all the details from my A350-900 business class flight.

Recall I landed in JFK around 10:00 pm and drove overnight to Pittsburgh, which itself was a journey. Then from there I flew home via Lisbon, Frankfurt, and Washington, DC…as one does.

But then I had to get from Southern California back to Basel and decided to fly via San Francisco, Denver, Newark, Nuuk (Greenland), and Copenhagen. That was three tickets, including:

I found SAS Business Class saver award space to get the three of us back to the USA, which has to be one of the best deals out there at 60K EuroBonus miles for me and only 30K miles for the kids, which included business class from ZRH-CPH as well. Taxes were €214.59 total for the three of us.

The flight availability forced an overnight in Copenhagen, but a late arrival so we used 36,000 Marriott Bonvoy points to stay at the AC Hotel Bella Sky Copenhagen near the airport, a towering property that was perfect for the overnight layover.

I won’t review the JetBlue A220 flight to Burbank since we all fell asleep right away after too much Taco Bell in Times Square…

#6203. Ryanair Cancels All Flights In Europe On Christmas Day

Christmas Day is fast approaching. On that festive day, airlines around the world will collectively cut 16% of flights, with Europe especially affected (-37%). Generally, it is much more common for carriers to scale back activity significantly than to cut flights completely.

One of the exceptions is Ryanair, Europe's largest carrier. OAG data shows that the ultra-low-cost carrier will have zero services on December 25. This is not unusual, as that's the same every year. This could be to give staff a break or because the airline does not think that it'd be worth flying.

Analysis of Ryanair's schedule for Saturday, December 19, to Sunday, December 27, shows that the pan-European operator plans 25,936 movements. Compared to the equivalent period in 2025, activity has jumped by a substantial 24%. Europe's already-largest operator grew by virtually a quarter in 12 months.

What is unchanged is that no flights will operate on December 25. 2,090 movements will exist on Christmas Eve 2026, which has jumped by 19% year-over-year. The volume will surpass the 2,000 services milestone for the first time. Ryanair will continue to have the most short-haul flights in Europe on that day.

It'll operate one in eight of Europe's short-haul flights on December 24. Naturally, flights will be down substantially compared to the prior Thursday, at 22% lower. As easyJet's Christmas Eve offering will be virtually unchanged (-1%), the gap between the two European behemoths will narrow significantly.

On a typical Thursday, the ultra-low-cost carrier's first flight of the day is usually around 5:45 AM. On Christmas Eve, schedule analysis shows that 63 routes are scheduled to leave between 5:45 AM and 5:55 AM. Covering 1,599 nautical miles (2,961 km), the longest link will be from Milan Malpensa to Tenerife South. At just 167 nautical miles (309 km), the shortest service will be from Leeds Bradford to Dublin.

Things will be very different in the evening. On the prior Thursday, the last departure of the day is down to be the 11:45 PM service from Seville, in southern Spain, to Rabat, the capital of Morocco. Not so on Christmas Eve. It'll be FR305, which is due to leave Salzburg, Austria, for London Stansted, Ryanair's top airport — including on December 24 — at 6:00 PM.

Ryanair's Top 5 Airports: Movements On Thursday, Dec. 24

Usually, Ryanair's final arrival of the day is at around 1:15 AM, which is based on aircraft that took off the day before. On Christmas Eve, the latest scheduled arrival time is at 6:55 PM, with 31 routes due then (shown in the map above). Once the crew (and everyone else working for the airline) have finished their duties and gone home, there will be enough time to celebrate before midnight.

One of the airlines has cut more routes than the other two carriers combined. Find out which here!

The airline will return to the air on Saturday, December 26, the so-called Boxing Day. 78 departures are scheduled to leave between 5:45 AM and 5:55 AM. 26 of them will be from UK and Irish airports, including some short legs, such as Edinburgh to Cork. It is likely that some passengers will be worse for wear from the festive day.

Ryanair plans a total of 3,448 movements on December 26, up by 27% compared to Boxing Day 2025. 1,175 routes will be available: 1,054 international and 121 domestic. With 11 outbound flights, Dublin to Gatwick will have the most activity.

Ryanair's movements across its entire network will increase from December 27, before dropping slightly for New Year's Day. But while the carrier's flights on Christmas Eve, Christmas Day, and Boxing Day will be higher than in 2025, New Year's Day will have fewer services than on January 1, 2026.

#6202. A TikToker Went Viral for Kayaking 500 Miles of Congolese River—and Started an Even Bigger Conversation

Last month the Welsh adventurer and self-described extreme athlete Ash Dykes was paddling along the placid waters of the Sangha River, a tributary of the Congo River flowing through Cameroon, Central African Republic, and Republic of the Congo, when something stirred underneath his vessel, kicking up bubbles. Dykes, with the local guide Obed Temba Tuyumvire and cameraman Will Perez, had just pushed off on a kayaking trip through the Congo Basin, the world’s second-largest rainforest and a critical ecosystem for humans and wildlife alike. The team knew they might encounter lowland gorillas, or perhaps forest elephants, as they made their way nearly 500 miles down the river. Perez then brought up another possible cause for the sudden ripples: a hippo. If the travelers had happened upon a hippopotamus, as many locals had warned them about, they were in immediate peril.

In October, adventurer Ash Dykes, local guide Obed Temba Tuyumvire, and cameraman Will Perez embarked on a 500-mile kayaking trip in Republic of the Congo.

When Dykes posted the minute-and-a-half-long video of this “encounter” in the Sangha—cause still unknown—the post racked up over 8 million views on TikTok. The thousands-deep comments section, full of viewers hooked as to what might happen next, burst with theories: Some swore that Mami Wata, a water spirit said to frequent the riverbanks, had caused the sudden movement. One user mused that the three men were in “a real game of Hungry Hungry Hippos,” while others zoomed in on Perez’s visibly tense expression. Another user quipped: “I quit my job to focus on this expedition.”

Though intended as a joke, the latter reaction succinctly illustrates the attention this trip has garnered on social media. For weeks millions of viewers were glued to the team’s frequent TikTok dispatches—which they later fleshed out into a longer YouTube series of deep dives. The videos documented the logistical hurdles in reaching the Sangha; their trudging amid the heat and threat of parasites and disease; their day spent with the Ba’Aka people, a seminomadic Indigenous tribe in Dzanga-Sangha Protected Area, where they foraged for wild coconut and joined a traditional hunt; and extended stretches of the three bobbing through calm waters. Those following online celebrated alongside the men when they spotted forest elephants, and their pulses quickened when they outran a swarm of bees chasing their kayaks. When the team went abruptly silent for a prolonged stretch, following a power bank failure, viewers worried that something catastrophic had happened.

The Congo Basin is the world’s second-largest rainforest and a critical ecosystem for humans and wildlife alike.

The Sangha expedition—or “mission,” as Dykes has dubbed it—was the first leg in an ambitious undertaking called Project 6. The venture involves the Welshman—who’s made a career of adventure travel and breaking world records (such as becoming the first person to walk the length of the 4,000-mile-long Yangtze River, which took him nearly a year)—traverse “extreme” parts of the globe by performing intensive feats of athleticism. He will soon cross Kyrgyzstan on horseback in subzero temperatures for the second installment of the project; he is revealing ensuing stops one by one.

“I'm fascinated with corners of the world that I am unfamiliar with and learning from the people there that call it home,” Dykes says. “Then [it’s] mixed in with the challenge of: Can I do what is deemed impossible, or can I do what people have tried to do before but failed to complete?”

Aside from accomplishing the athletic challenge of constantly paddling down the Sangha every day for weeks, Dykes says he aimed to showcase the beauty of the Congo Basin, and its inhabitants, in a responsible way—stressing to viewers that “you can go to places like this as long as you put the right preparation in,” he says.

Video on TikTok and Youtube showed the trio of Tuyumvire, Perez, and Dykes on their river adventure.

Dykes is quick to credit those who made the Congo Basin excursion possible—especially Tuyumvire, who works in conservation advocacy and ecotourism through his Kigali-based company, Kumbukumbu Tours. Born in a forest village near Virunga National Park in the Democratic Republic of Congo, he fled the region following the civil war and lived in a refugee camp for over a decade before founding his tour company in 2015; he says those experiences shaped his belief that responsible tourism can be a means of helping make a local impact, particularly for young people. Tuyumvire agreed to join Dykes’s excursion because he saw an opportunity to tell meaningful stories about the Congo Basin for a larger audience.

“Because we have been surviving these out-of-context stories or even more exaggerated stories,” says Tuyumvire. “I myself feel the responsibility to always say yes to someone who has the microphone, and I tell the right context.”

Ahead of the excursion Tuyumvire worked with Dykes to pick the specific location for the journey and scouted out the upper headwaters of the Sangha. Tuyumvire offered context and commentary in videos throughout the trip, speaking about the critical endangerment of forest elephants, the deforestation threatening the Congo Basin, and noting that women were on the front lines of hunting when they met the Ba’Aka people.

Yet straddling the line between education and entertainment for a predominantly TikTok viewership resulted in unexpected tensions. Internet connectivity posed a challenge due to the forest canopy; still, Dykes insisted the journey be “as live as possible” online. “I can’t be claiming that this is a lifetime expedition and then we use either recycled content or we go dark,” he says.

Forest elephants are among the wildlife that inhabits the Congo Basin through which the team traveled.

While a plurality of viewers seemed genuinely fascinated by the three-week-long trip, even during less-exciting moments, Dykes noticed that some expressed a morbid glee for destructive content. Dykes says that some online commenters even started to bet money on how the trio might die in the Congo Basin, perhaps at the hands of a hippopotamus or a crocodile. “I think people are lost or confused as to what is a video game and what is a movie, and then what is reality,” he says. “So it's almost like this disconnect where people just wanted to be entertained: ‘If I'm going to the Congo, I want to see you escaping wildlife, wrestling.’” Tuyumvire saw the conflicting responses from viewers as “another kind of challenge for me to…create a story that will continuously be fed to the audience, but that will not also be overcrowded by too much exaggeration.”

Others have criticized Dykes, drawing parallels between him and other foreigners entering so-called forbidding places and, intentionally or not, reinforcing outdated tropes. Guy Dieudonne Moukandi N'Kaya, a lecturer and researcher at Marien Ngouabi University in Brazzaville, Republic of the Congo, says that Dykes’s trip through the Sangha felt honest in that it showed the “tense coexistence” between humans and wildlife in the region. Yet the way Dykes framed the expedition gave N’Kaya pause: Leading up to the trip, Dykes noted in a TikTok teaser that he would be “dropping into the heart of darkness,” a phrase culled from Joseph Conrad’s controversial, turn-of-the-20th-century novella about a Belgian trading company siphoning resources from the Congo River. N’Kaya says that descriptors such as “heart of darkness” and “unexplored,” which Dykes has also used in some of his posts, erase the presence of those who have long lived within the region: “The Sangha is not empty,” N’Kaya writes over email. “For centuries it has been traversed by people in dug-out canoes—fisherfolk, traders, and families.”

The water of the Sangha River, a tributary of the Congo River, is tranquil—but the threat of disease-carrying bugs, dangerous wildlife, and the physical challenge of traveling 500 miles on human power made this one of Dykes' six missions.

While Dykes emphasizes that he wanted to raise awareness of the Congo Basin, which is under dire threat of deforestation, some viewers have questioned whether the adventure has truly benefited the region—or whether it’s more of a boon to his Project 6 venture. The Congo Basin has long grappled with interlacing issues including extreme poverty, corruption, and illegal mineral mining, which Tuyumvire says stem from the legacy of colonialism and slavery. “People are poor in the sense that they are ready to sell anything they are able to, to be able to just survive,” Tuyumvire says. “People seeing a white person in this region, it brings memories of the past: ‘This guy’s coming for timber. This guy’s coming for minerals.’ Things that really don't give them any kind of hope to develop the area. And that itself, the mindset, is a threat to the forest.”

After returning from the trip in late October, Tuyumvire has been resting and resuming his routine following the physical demands of kayaking. He’d never kayaked at length before a few weeks ago; he says his real motivation was to “share the stories and to try to transform the adventure into something impactful.” The widespread interest in the videos hasn't translated to bookings of his tours, but that was never the goal: “The audience we had is not an audience of travelers, to be honest,” he says. He has been reflecting on how, in hindsight, he wishes he had created a stronger call to action so that TikTok viewers’ curiosity could have a direct impact on the region. (Alongside his tours Tuyumvire helps run the Congo Rainforest Fund, a local NGO that works with local communities to understand threats to the forest and create solutions, such as shoring up educational efforts and job opportunities.)

But he believes that broadcasting the journey did help viewers further understand a place that they may not have been familiar with. “[The] Congo Basin has been represented as a difficult place to access, a difficult, complex place to understand,” Tuyumvire says. “So people were saying, ‘Finally, someone is going to give us the real information’…we want to see them in the reality."
