#6195. Walking the Peaks of the Balkans, a Trekking Route With Community At Its Core

I'm awoken by the sound of cowbells clanging outside my bare-boned wood cabin in Dobërdol, a high mountain settlement in northern Albania. Through the window, slightly fogged from the chilly morning air at 5,700 feet, I see the culprits: five chestnut-colored cows munching on grass just feet from my bedside, their bells and tails swinging away.

The Albanian Alps are one of our Best Places to Go in 2027.

I make the short and frigid walk across the guesthouse lawn to the breakfast room, maneuvering around a dozen or so hikers' tents pitched in the grass. Yesterday’s 10-mile trek from Çerem to Dobërdol is still fresh in my mind: dusty dirt trails edged with wild blueberries I couldn’t resist picking and patches of willow gentian, their petals so intensely purple they matched the berry stains on my fingers. The forests of pine, beech, and spruce in these parts are thick enough that the daylight dims inside of them; the valleys dizzyingly deep as they fold in on themselves.

The Peaks of the Balkans trek is a 119-mile inn-to-inn circular trail across the long-disputed borderlands of Albania, Kosovo, and Montenegro.

Local-owned guesthouses welcome trekkers with included meals, like fresh vegetables, homemade dairy, and cured sausages and meats.

It’s mid-September, and only 7 a.m., but breakfast is already in full swing, not an empty seat left at the tables squeezed into the cozy timber-framed room. The Kurmekaj brothers, our hosts, are frantically grabbing four plates apiece from the kitchen, loaded with fried eggs, sausage, fresh sheep cheese, and cucumber-and-tomato salad, a fixture on the Balkan plate. I do my best to duck out of their way as the door behind me swings open and more trekkers pile in.

This is my fourth day of ten on the Peaks of the Balkans trek, a 119-mile inn-to-inn circular trail across the long-disputed borderlands of Albania, Kosovo, and Montenegro, through what’s called the Accursed Mountains—a name whose ominous origins supposedly lie either with the devil, war, or travelers cursing the range’s unforgiving terrain, depending on who you ask. Conceived in the early 2010s as a cross-border peace and tourism project, this trail was meant to reconnect mountain communities that had been splintered by war, create livelihoods, and give residents a reason to remain—or return—to villages hollowed out by conflict and emigration.

The Peaks of the Balkans trail offers both busy sections and quiet side trails where your only companions may be a single hiker or group of grazing cattle.

By those measures, it has been remarkably successful. A late 2025 study published in the Journal of Outdoor Recreation and Tourism estimated that roughly 43,000 hikers now walk the trail each year—up from regional estimates of roughly 20,000 in the pre-pandemic era—injecting more than €25 million ($27.7 million USD) annually into mountain regions where family homes, shepherd settlements, and seasonal villages have increasingly become guesthouses for trekkers. But that success is also beginning to crowd some of the places that the trail was created to support, as a growing number of travelers takes interest.

Ricardo Fahrig of the Albania-based adventure travel company Zbulo, which has been running Peaks trips since the trail’s early years, helped me piece together my own self-guided route on these trails. He says the contrast between busy Dobërdol and the quieter terrain I’m soon to enter after breakfast gets to the heart of the issue. “It’s not the number of travelers on the Peaks of the Balkans trail,” he tells me, “but rather the distribution. Some sections remain sparsely visited, while others, like Dobërdol, struggle with volume during a relatively short season”, a period from roughly June through September, with some hikers continuing into early October.

After breakfast, just a few steps down the trail from the guesthouse in Dobërdol, the clatter and congestion of the morning fade immediately. So do the other trekkers, flowing like a stream up the steep green lip of the expansive bowl-shaped valley we all woke up in, then onward to Milishevc, Montenegro, the usual stop after Dobërdol.

Stepping off the primary Peak of the Balkans trail—which the writer did with a self-guided itinerary from Zbulo—allows for quieter moments and a greater sense of solitude.

All except two. Stef Van Dam, a seasoned Dutch thru-hiker I’d met on my second day on the trail, falls into step beside me on the cattle-worn traces of the route we've chosen to take instead. He, too, is detouring off the official trail. Whereas I’m headed for the heart-shaped lake below Gjeravica, Kosovo’s highest peak, he will peel off later to summit it—“the peak of the Peaks of the Balkans,” he calls the mountain.

At the empty pass marking the Albania-Kosovo border, 1,600 feet of ascent later, we collapse onto the same rock—for all we know, Van Dam is munching his apple in Albania while I air my blisters in Kosovo just next to him. From up here, this border is steeped in irony—a line so invisible we have to guess at where exactly it’s drawn, yet a matter that has been fought over, fortified, closed, and redrawn for more than a century.

Ahead, a narrow dirt track just below the Kosovo side of the pass continues along the contour line, snaking through the treeless and boulder-strewn landscape. To our left and many mountain miles away, we spot the village of Junik where we’re both planning to sleep that night, me in a gueshouse and Van Dam in his tent somewhere nearby. As if marking the spot, a golden eagle circles in the unblemished autumn sky above it.

“This is exactly what I came to this trail to find,” Van Dam says, the first to interrupt the silence. “I wanted something quiet, more remote than other trails in Europe. I’ve found it here.”

Having myself walked a few of the more notably crowded European trails, including the Camino de Santiago, I know what he means. Besides the two of us and the eagle riding the thermals overhead, there isn’t another soul in sight.

Along the route, small guesthouses warmly welcome trekkers, who have created a reason to stay—or return—to communities once disrupted by conflict and emagration.

By late afternoon, after Van Dam and I part ways below Gjeravica. What appeared as a scattering of rooftops no bigger than a thumbnail now reveals itself in the distinct forms of summer homes and traditional katuns, seasonal shepherd settlements composed of simple huts and stone-walled livestock pens.

The family has only recently begun welcoming trekkers into their home, and they radiate the kind of excitement that comes from still being delighted by every single arrival. Renaja leads me to my room for the night, tucked on the third floor beneath the A-frame eaves. Downstairs, pizza bakes in an old wood-burning stove while Renaja's mother and grandmother set a long table for the dozen or so guests still dribbling in.

The old highland idea of besa—that a house belongs not only to its owner, but to God and to the guest—is coming to life before my eyes. Or, as Fahrig, who first came to these mountains in 2012, later puts it: bukë, kripë, zemër, an Albanian expression meaning “bread, salt, and heart.” “The material offering may be simple,” he says. “The welcome is what makes it memorable.”

The following morning, I continue deeper into Kosovo, eventually rejoining the main Peaks of the Balkans route. Now, it’s Montenegro on the other side of the invisible line I keep crossing. Over the coming days, the trail shifts between empty mountain passes and occasional stretches of asphalt—the latter one being a reason, Fahrig says, that many trekkers truncate this section entirely. He estimates that places such as the Rugova Gorge—a river-carved passage whose 2-3,000-foot-deep limestone walls bear stone-blasted tunnels, a frothy emerald river, and viewpoints at every turn—currently receive around 30 percent or less of the traffic funneled through Dobërdol.

The Peaks of the Balkans stitches together sections that include dirt paths, country roads, and sometimes asphalt—but even the less photogenic portions lead to impactful destinations.

In Drelaj, where this dramatic gorge opens into a wider pastoral valley, skipping Kosovo begins to feel like missing the point. This quiet highland hamlet is embraced on all sides by forested mountains. Across its green curves and garden plots are chalet-like summer homes built out of wood and stone, each boasting a balcony or porch turned toward the mountains and the mosque whose slender minaret rises at the center of it all.

After a day of sharing the trail with more cows than people, passing by deserted villages, and hugging a gully’s edge on a heavily eroded and unpaved fire road, I eventually spill out of the forest onto asphalt that ends in Drelaj. My guesthouse, Konaku i Malsorit, is tucked just to the right of the minaret. An Albanian flag (this part of Kosovo is majority ethnic Albanian) whips in the breeze above the two-story home and its garden, ripe with peppers, tomatoes, onions, and maize.

Minarets dot the skyline in even small villages in Kosovo and Albania.

My host Blendi Lajqi tells me his family fled Drelaj during the 1998-1999 Kosovo War after their home was burned by Yugoslav and Serbian forces. He was six years old. After the war, the family moved to Peja, the nearest major city, and for around two decades, he says, the house and the land they left behind here were “dead, no longer a home.” The creation of the trail gave his family—and others in the village—a reason to return and reinvest in what they left behind. Looking around at it now, “dead” is hard to imagine.

The room I’m sleeping in, now completely redone into what could easily be a fully functioning apartment, once served as a makeshift hospital for the Kosovo Liberation Army (UÇK), the ethnic Albanian guerrilla force that fought the Yugoslav and Serbian forces during the war. Here, he tells me, Lajqi’s mother and aunt cared for the wounded.

Many hikers arrive knowing almost nothing about what happened here, he says. But for those who make a point to learn about it, the history of this region gives different weight to this trail—and the intention behind it. The guesthouses along the Peaks aren’t simply infrastructure for hikers. “It’s brought life back to the land and the house where my family lived until the beginning of the war,” Lajqi tells me. “When we opened the guesthouse, our home became a place where people from all over the world could come, stay, eat, talk with us, and experience our way of life. For me, there’s something special about that.”

Trails in this region include a great deal of altitude change—and the views that come with that.

The writer gathers around the dinner table with fellow trekkers at a local guesthouse.

Few people, however, have watched tourism reshape these mountains as long as Skender Selimaj of Hotel Rezidenca Quku i Valbones in Valbona, Albania. When he and his brother Alfred returned from the United Kingdom in the early 2000s, after leaving Albania during the period of communism, the high-walled valley hemmed in by jagged limestone peaks still revolved largely around subsistence farming. In 2004, they opened Restaurant Rilindja—meaning “rebirth” in Albanian—without knowing whether enough travelers would come to sustain it. Then, in 2009, Selimaj helped clear the passes toward Theth and Çerem and carried some of the first wooden trail signs into the mountains himself.

As in many locations along the Peaks of the Balkans route, the influx of tourism has since reshaped the Valbona Valley. The single-day hike over Valbona Pass to Theth has become one of Albania’s most popular mountain routes, which is also why my self-guided Zbulo itinerary intentionally bypassed it. Even with the trade-offs, Valbona has benefited. Farmers can now sell cheese, meat, eggs, and milk locally at better prices. Families have new income, while local children, Selimaj says, sometimes grow up speaking English simply from meeting travelers from around the world.

Selimaj, who spent years working as a mountain guide and in mountain rescue, still spends his free time exploring the terrain he grew up in, though he’s faced the fact that solitude is increasingly difficult to find. Where he once expected wild goats and empty mountains, “everywhere you go, you see somebody,” he says. He doesn’t wish tourism away; he has seen too clearly what it has done for local livelihoods. What he does want is a Valbona that remains clean, green, and recognizably local, where old stone houses and family-run businesses aren’t crowded out by large-scale outside development.

The Peaks of the Balkans trail passes through what’s called the Accursed Mountains—a name whose ominous origins supposedly lie either with the devil, war, or travelers cursing the range’s unforgiving terrain, depending on who you ask.

For Fahrig of Zbulo, the answer to the newfound business isn’t necessarily fewer trekkers. What he hopes to preserve on this trail are “living communities rather than places shaped entirely around visitors.” Doing that, he argues, means spreading trekkers more evenly: encouraging hikers to continue through Kosovo, directing some traffic toward quieter alternatives just beyond the busiest passes, and steering repeat or more adventurous trekkers toward newer alternative long-distance routes like the 225-mile High Scardus Trail that traverses the remote and mountainous borderlands of North Macedonia, Kosovo, and Albania.

In Kosovo, some of that work is already underway. Lajqi is part of a volunteer effort with other guesthouse owners and tourism businesses to create more natural alternatives around paved sections of the original route without cutting the villages themselves out of the trail—the other risk of making changes. “The best solution is not to completely change the original trail,” Lajqi says, “but to offer more choices, preserving the connection between the villages while also giving hikers the kind of mountain experience they came for.”

Over the days that follow, I keep moving west, circling back towards Theth. Each day brings with it another 3,000-foot pass to scale, another cucumber-and-tomato sandwich to enjoy once I get there, along with a steady mix of surprise, (some) stress, and plenty of solitude. Occasionally, I get lost when my GPS stops working or the orange dots and red-and-white striped trail markers disappear, and yet I always find my way. I walk, at times, with no one, and in other moments with dozens of travelers. Sometimes, it's just me and cowbell-clanging bovine. I keep going like this, collecting these little moments and memories, until, on the 10th day, I pass a bunker, the crumbling Cold War-era concrete mushrooms built by communist dictator Enver Hoxha, and realize I must be back in Albania.

By the time I approach Theth—the end of my route—I feel like I’ve walked through both versions of the Peaks: the one overwhelmed by its own success and the quieter version still there available alongside it.

The guesthouses along the Peaks aren’t simply infrastructure for hikers. “It’s brought life back to the land and the house where my family lived until the beginning of the war,” Blendi Lajqi of Konaku i Malsorit says.

For my final night on the trails, I hike into Bujtina Kometa, a guesthouse in the quiet hamlet of Okol situated roughly a mile-and-a-half from central Theth. A mezze spread of marinated chicken, seasoned potatoes, olives, tomatoes, soft cheese, and tzatziki for dipping lands on the table, all prepared by our host Ermira and her family. The thing about these trails is that even if you go your own way by day, you'll find yourself breaking bread with familiar faces by night. Every person around the table, I realize, is someone I've met somewhere along the trail—people I’ve shared miles with over the last 10 days as our paths kept crossing.

Ermira’s father tops up our water and hints at honey-soaked fruit for dessert; woodsmoke from a neighbor distilling homemade raki drifts through the low-lit dining room. Van Dam, seated across the table from me now, reaches for another forkful of potato dripping with tzatziki. The busy center of Theth, with its tour buses and day-trippers, still feels worlds away.

For one more night, these Accursed Mountains and all they carry—the besa, the borders, the beauty, and the stories etched into them—envelop us, proving that wide-open spaces and quiet still have their place in these mountains.

Most hikers spend about 10 to 13 days completing the full Peaks of the Balkans route.

The complete Peaks of the Balkans circuit covers roughly 119 miles (192 km) across Albania, Kosovo, and Montenegro. Most hikers spend about 10 to 13 days completing the full route, though shorter itineraries of 5 to 8 days often cut or bypass certain stages. Most routes involve 5 to 8 hours of hiking per day, typically covering 8 to 17 miles with significant elevation gain and loss.

Getting there: Fly into Podgorica in Montenegro or Tirana in Albania, transferring via shuttle or 4x4 to trailheads in Theth, Valbona, or Plav.

When to go: The core trekking season runs from June through September, but is increasingly stretching into October. Late June through August generally offers more reliable pass conditions, though the trail can get busy. Early June can still mean snow lingering on the highest passes, while September is the sweet spot for favorable hiking weather (peak traffic proves that everyone knows this). Early-to-mid October can be beautiful for experienced hikers willing to gamble on shorter days, colder nights, and the occasional burst of snow; later in the month, high-altitude guesthouses begin winding down, and do not reopen again until early May or June.

Who to go with: Albania-based Zbulo offers guided and self-guided trips (with logistics arranged, but no guide) ranging from 8 to 12 days. These include cross-border permits, guesthouse reservations, meals, luggage transfers, and route planning. If you're traveling independently, be sure to secure your date-locked cross-border permits at least two weeks before hiking, or have an agency like Zbulo secure them for you.

Where to stay: Accommodation ranges from family-run guesthouses and homestays to simple mountain huts, cabins, and small hotels. In remote sections, expect basic rooms—sometimes shared—along with hearty home-cooked dinners, breakfasts, and often a packed lunch for the following day. Budget roughly $25-55 USD per person per night depending on the room and whether meals are included. Book ahead in high season, and carry plenty of cash in Albanian lek or Euros in small denominations; card payments and ATMs are scarce in the mountains. In May and other shoulder-season periods, it is possible to arrange rooms on the fly, but from June through September—especially in bottlenecks like Dobërdol and popular stops such as Theth and Valbona—it’s smarter to book several weeks ahead. Camping is also possible on parts of the route, including at some guesthouses that allow trekkers to pitch a tent for a small fee and use facilities or buy meals. You can arrange your accommodations directly with hosts over WhatsApp using contacts found through Google Maps, social media, or the official Peaks of the Balkans App; many are now available on platforms like Booking.com as well.

#6193. Dreaming of Country Living? These Renovated Barn Airbnbs Got You Covered

Country living, with its beautiful nature, relaxing atmosphere, and stunning wildlife, makes it incredibly easy to forget your day-to-day stressors and embrace the slower path. And where better to enjoy this peace and quiet than from an Airbnb converted from a barn—provided, of course, you’re not actually sleeping next to a pitchfork and a pile of hay? Across the US, old dairy barns, horse stables, haylofts, and grain silos that once kept America’s farms running are finding dreamy second lives as vacation rentals. These sturdy structures are getting some very glamorous redesigns, but keeping the soaring ceilings, original timber beams, weathered wood, and old architectural details that no new build can quite replicate.

From sprawling farmhouses with enough room for the whole gang, to intimate hayloft hideaways made for a national park trip, to old grain silos that are surprisingly stylish places to sleep, there’s something interesting in every corner of the country. Expect modern interiors tucked behind century-old barn doors, outdoor soaking tubs overlooking rolling pastures, and properties where the resident animals are still very much part of the picture (morning coffee with a few curious goats, anyone?).

Whether you’re after a little farmyard nostalgia, a design-forward country escape, or simply a storied home just steps away from the wild, these barn Airbnbs make a pretty compelling case to trade your average stay for something with a little more hay-day history.

Number of guests: 2Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Proximity to Nashville, floor-to-ceiling windows, fully equipped kitchen, optional farm tours and event bookings

Bloomsbury Farm is a family-owned and -operated organic farm just outside Nashville. The 400-acre retreat is pastorally posh—the kind of place where wild turkeys and deer roam free, hawks swoop overhead, and coyotes howl in the night. The one-bedroom, one-bath rental is tastefully decorated: It’s where Martha Stewart meets Modern Farmer. That said, intentionality permeates every design choice, from the handsome leather headboard to the subway-tiled bath with Aesop hand soap. Guests are given farm-fresh eggs and a box of fruits and vegetables that are grown on-site; these come in handy when preparing meals on the kitchen’s professional gas range or grilling over the outdoor firepit.

City: Smyrna, TennesseeThings to do nearby: Brewer Farms, Cedar Stone Park, The Barn at Sycamore Farms, Arrington Vineyards

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1.5 bathsWhy we love it: Proximity to NYC, wood-burning fireplace, reading nooks, meadow and valley views, vintage arcade and board games

Just around a two-hour drive from NYC, this charmingly restored barn cottage awaits in the Hudson Valley. The space pairs a cozy wood-burning fireplace with expansive windows overlooking a meadow—one that the host notes becomes a “veritable bird sanctuary for most of the year.” It’s a harbor of hidden nooks made for cozying up with a book, and features a well-stocked kitchen and dining space for cooking, as well as a vintage arcade and board games for fun nights in with your crew. Previous guests have raved about its proximity to Hudson Valley hot spots: There’s no shortage of places to hike, ski, see art, or dine, as well as some fun local breweries and wineries. The property is within a 10- to 25-minute drive of six quaint Hudson Valley towns. (You can also request bikes from the hosts if you’re inclined to venture out on two wheels.)

City: Red Hook, New YorkThings to do nearby: Pine Plains, Stissing Mountain (and iconic restaurant Stissing House), Thompson Pond

Number of guests: 2Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Desert views, on-site animals, proximity to Zion National Park, fully equipped kitchen, firepit, sauna

With a classic red-barn build, friendly farm animals, and a sauna practically made for stargazing, this dreamy Airbnb is an oasis—especially if Zion National Park is on your itinerary. Just one hour from the park, you’ll find this whimsical base for two set between Utah’s red rock cliffs, sweeping canyons, and heaps of local hiking paths. Inside, enjoy tasteful touches everywhere. Sunlight pours through the studio; a vintage-style soaking tub sits on black-and-white checkered flooring, and the kitchenette has modern appliances as well as some plants and pastel green cabinets. You’ll have some company when walking outside, too: This farm stay comes with two adorable Highland cows as well as a chicken coop. There’s also a sauna and firepit, just in case you need another reason to visit.

City: Hildale, UtahThings to do nearby: Water Canyon Winery, Squirrel Canyon Trailhead, Coral Pink Sand Dunes, Zion National Park

Number of guests: 6Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 2 bathsWhy we love it: Outdoor firepit, central location, private stargazing deck, wood-burning fireplace, vinyl player

A silo in the Catskills? Now that's a fun place to spend a weekend. From the outside, this three-story converted tower is fairly understated, but step inside, and you'll find a surprisingly airy, thoughtfully designed little escape that makes every inch count. There's an open living room that flows into a stocked kitchen, two spacious (and stunningly modern) bathrooms, and a private deck for soaking up the quiet. The interiors have a cool, pared-back feel, with just the right amount of personality to make it feel like somewhere you'd actually want to hang out (board games and a puzzle marathon are very much encouraged). And while it feels nicely tucked away, Woodstock's galleries, shops, and restaurants are just 10 minutes down the road.

City: Willow, New YorkThings to do nearby: Mount Tremper, Emerson Kaleidoscope, Phoenicia Diner, Overlook Mountain

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 2 bathsWhy we love it: Ocean views, stereo system, heated floors, wood-burning stove, open and modern kitchen

What could be better—or more endearing—than this modern Northern California barn in a forest clearing? Renovated by San Francisco architect David Crimmins, this gem leans into its sleek agrarian style, with airy, open-beam ceilings, heated concrete floors, a redwood slab dining table, and windows on all sides, bringing the outside in. The house sits along a rocky coastline, primed for whale watching and trips to coastal wineries between the Redwoods and the Pacific. The high-design stay stands tall on Anchor Bay along the Mendocino Coast; you’ll have your very own one-acre yard amid the state’s dreamy Redwoods, and it’s just a 20-minute walk to the beach.

City: Gualala, CaliforniaThings to do nearby: Whale Watch Point, Gualala Arts Center, Point Arena Lighthouse, Bonham Trail to Cooks Beach

Number of guests: 3Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1 bathWhy we love it: Sauna, firepit, outdoor shower, proximity to Lake Michigan

Not every barn stay comes with Lake Michigan practically in its backyard. Tucked among 12 wooded acres in Leelanau County, this country base holds its former farm structure while offering its guests a fresh and pretty new lease. Once part of a 30-acre farm that stretched across both sides of the road, you can still appreciate a little of that history in its beautifully restored bones. These days, it's a two-bedroom hideaway that makes a wonderful home base for exploring Northern Michigan's wine country, with Northport's small-town charm and the peninsula's wineries and breweries just a hop and a skip away. There’s no need to leave your Airbnb for a fun day out: Spend the afternoon wandering out in nature, then make your way to the nearby secluded Lake Michigan beach. Peruse the guest reviews, and you’ll notice a telling pattern: Most travelers don't just stay once or twice—they return time and time again.

City: Northport, MichiganThings to do nearby: Cherry Basket Farm, Onomonee Road Beach, Fischer’s Happy Hour Tavern, Bay Front Park

Number of guests: 3Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Silo design, mountain views, fully equipped kitchenette, private patio, firepit, proximity to Glacier National Park

On an 80-acre family farm in Montana’s Flathead Valley, this converted grain silo is truly one of a kind. Alongside jaw-dropping mountain views, the structure itself is a treat—and happens to be more homey than one might think at first glance. Inside, the lofted king bedroom is spacious and comfy, the kitchenette is stocked with all you might need for a long weekend, and kid-friendly amenities are at your ready, from a pack-and-play to a portable high chair. That said, it’s best for one or two, or a couple traveling with a little one, since there aren’t full walls between the sleeping area.

Embrace the outdoors as much as you can here: According to previous guests, this barn puts you in a prime spot for stargazing around the firepit, jumping in the glittering Flathead Lake, and taking advantage of Glacier National Park—only 30 minutes away.

City: Kalispell, MontanaThings to do nearby: Glacier National Park, Conrad Mansion Museum, Flathead Lake, Wild Horse Island

#6192. Mayday At 33,000 Feet: Leaky Faucet Floods Frontier Airlines Airbus A321neo Cabin

Last week, a Frontier Airlines Airbus A321neo flying from Denver International Airport (DEN) to Detroit Metropolitan Wayne County Airport (DTW) had to divert to Chicago O'Hare International Airport (ORD) after a leaky faucet flooded the floor of the passenger cabin. The flight declared 'mayday' to air traffic control while cruising at 33,000 feet over eastern Iowa, and subsequently landed safely at Chicago O'Hare.

While there were no injuries as a result of the incident and the subsequent diversion and landing, the potentially serious nature of the leak meant that the situation had to be treated as a safety issue as opposed to just a mess that needed clearing up. This is because of the damage that water can cause to a jet's electronics. The aircraft, which is just two months old, has since re-entered commercial service.

Frontier Airlines flight F9-3566 is a daily scheduled flight from Denver to Detroit that typically takes between two and two-and-a-half hours to complete. On November 11, it took off at 11:02 AM, but, while cruising over Iowa at 33,000 feet, things took an eventful turn when a faucet in the forward lavatory of the A321neo operating the flight (N688FR) sprang a leak. The crew subsequently declared 'mayday.'

The flight subsequently descended through 24,000 feet as it made its way towards its requested diversion airport, Chicago O'Hare. According to View From The Wing, the pilots told ATC that they were "worried about electronics," with CBS reporting that the leak was so severe that the water spilled out of the bathroom and flooded the cabin, as seen above. Frontier told ABC7 Chicago in a statement that:

"The faucet in the forward lavatory sprung a leak, which caused water to flow along part of the aircraft floor."

The risks of water coming into contact with electronics are well known in all walks of life, but, in the world of commercial aviation, a situation such as this poses particular danger. This is because, on airliners like the Airbus A321neo, many of the jet's avionics and wiring systems are located below the floor of the main passenger cabin. As such, Wednesday's incident could have compromised them.

Aviation regulators are also all too aware of this threat, with the FAA having issued a relevant airworthiness directive, numbered as 2026-02-10. This replaced AD 2024-01-01, and it was issued after undetected leaks from Boeing 787 faucet modules seeped below the cabin floor and into the electronics bays. While this involves a different aircraft type to the Airbus A321neo, it highlights the relevant dangers.

It is also particularly noteworthy that N688FR, the Frontier Airlines Airbus A321neo involved in the diversion on November 11, is nearly brand-new. According to ch-aviation, it first flew just under three months ago, on August 21, and was delivered just over two months ago, on September 3. Frontier is an all-Airbus operator, with six A320-200s, 62 A320neos, 21 A321-200s, and 70 A321neos in its fleet today.

Two flight attendants were taken to hospital as the jet remains grounded and multiple flights were canceled.

After the flight landed in Chicago, a replacement A321neo registered as N655FR was dispatched to take the passengers of F9-3566 to Detroit. The Aviation Herald notes that their eventual arrival in the 'Motor City' took place around 4.5 hours behind schedule, just after 8:00 PM local time. As for N688FR, the first A321neo, the jet was grounded for the rest of the day before re-entering service on November 12.

Found an error? Send it info@simpleflying.com so it can be corrected.

This is the latest in a string of cabin incidents involving Frontier Airlines in recent months. As detailed in our coverage linked above, multiple flight attendants fell ill on one of the carrier's A321s in August, while, more recently, passengers rushed the exit door and clashed with crew after being kept on board with no air conditioning after a jet bridge failure. Ultimately, Wednesday's incident was a precautionary diversion with no injuries, and the aircraft has since re-entered regular service.

#6190. Which Hotel Credit Cards Offer Free Night Awards, And Are They Worth It?

Hotel credit cards are among the most underrated out there. Understandably a lot of people get cards like the Chase Sapphire Preferred® Card (learn more) and Chase Sapphire Reserve® Card (learn more) to maximize the rewards they’re earning for their spending, and that’s a great idea. These cards offer valuable bonus categories, no foreign transaction fees, great travel coverage, and more.

But I think supplementing one of those cards with hotel credit cards can make a lot of sense. That’s because hotel credit cards largely offer some incredible perks that more than justify the annual fee, including free hotel elite status, and even some free night certificates. So even if you’re not loyal to a hotel group, it’s easy to get outsized value.

In this post, I’d like to specifically look at which credit cards offer free nights as part of their rewards structure, how you can earn them, and if they’re worth it.

There are hotel credit cards issued by Hilton Honors, IHG One Rewards, Marriott Bonvoy, and World of Hyatt, which offer the opportunity to earn free night awards. To be clear, I’m not talking about the ability to earn points, but instead, the ability to earn free night awards that can be redeemed at a set of properties.

These free nights come in different forms — some free night awards are offered for spending a certain amount on a card, and some free night awards are offered as an annual benefit just for having a card, with no spending required.

So let’s take a look at the details of how these free night awards work, and then we’ll talk about whether they’re worth it. Note that I’m focusing specifically on cards that offer free night awards on an ongoing basis (rather than as part of a welcome offer), and am also limiting this to cards that are open to new applicants.

Hilton Honors has two credit cards that give cardmembers the ability to earn free night awards:

Hilton Honors free night awards are my single favorite hotel free night awards out there, given that they have no category caps, and they’re valid for 12 months from when they’re issued. I value Hilton points at 0.5 cents each.

Hilton free night awards can be redeemed for standard rooms at properties costing up to 250,000 points per night, and there’s only a small list of excluded properties. They’re even valid at Small Luxury Hotels of the World (SLH) properties that are part of the Hilton Honors partnership. It’s easy to redeem these at properties costing $1,000+ per night.

IHG One Rewards has three credit cards that give cardmembers the ability to earn free night awards:

IHG One Rewards free night awards are also potentially quite valuable, and they expire 12 months from when they’re issued. I value IHG points at 0.5 cents each.

While IHG free night awards are capped at properties costing a certain number of points, what I really like is how you can top them off with an unlimited number of points. So if a hotel requires 100,000 points, you could use a 60,000 point free night certificate, and then top it off with 40,000 points.

Marriott Bonvoy has four credit cards that give cardmembers the ability to earn free night awards:

Marriott Bonvoy free night awards are also extremely lucrative, and they expire 12 months from when they’re issued. I value Marriott points at 0.7 cents each.

While Marriott free night awards are capped at properties costing a certain number of points, you can top them each off with up to 25,000 points, to redeem at more expensive properties. So you could book a hotel costing 60,000 points per night by redeeming a 35,000 point free night award, and then redeeming 25,000 additional points.

World of Hyatt Honors has one credit card that give cardmembers the ability to earn free night awards:

World of Hyatt free night awards are valuable, but definitely the most restrictive of the bunch. Free night awards issued with the card expire 12 months after they’re issued. I value World of Hyatt points at 1.4 cents each.

Category 1-4 covers a lot of Hyatt properties (these can cost up to 25,000 points per night), but the catch is that you can’t use these certificates to redeem at more expensive properties by topping them off. Still, it should be very easy to get outsized value.

I’ll let my credit card portfolio speak for itself — I have quite the selection of hotel credit cards. They’re not necessarily cards that I spend a ton on, but instead, they’re cards I largely have because of the very strong perks that they offer, which to me, more than justify the annual fee. Let me just give a few direct examples…

I have the Hilton Honors Aspire Card, and it’s my single favorite hotel credit card. The card offers a massive number of perks, but in particular, the free night alone more than justifies the annual fee for me. I try to use this at properties that would retail for $1,000+ per night, so it’s pretty awesome to get that, along with all kinds of other perks, just for having the card.

I also think there’s merit to spending $60,000 per year on the card, if you can swing it. That spending would earn you a minimum of 180,000 points (since you earn at least 3x points per dollar spent with the card), plus two additional free night awards, potentially worth up to 500,000 points. So this is a great card to consider if you’re making a big purchase.

In the case of Marriott Bonvoy, I have both the Marriott Bonvoy Brilliant Card and Marriott Bonvoy Business Card, which get me free night awards worth 85,000 and 35,000 points, respectively. These also in and of themselves more than justify the annual fees on the cards. I generally redeem the larger free night award for a luxury hotel stay, while I redeem the lesser free night award for a stay at a mid-range property.

Lastly, I also have the World of Hyatt Credit Card, and that free night award also more than justifies the annual fee in and of itself. Admittedly I wish the free night award cap would be increased to reflect inflation, but even so, I get a ton of value out of this. At an absolute minimum, I use it when I have an overnight near JFK to stay at the Hyatt Regency JFK, which typically costs $300+ if paying cash.

There are potentially lots of great benefits to hotel credit cards, including big welcome bonuses, easy opportunities to earn hotel status, generous rewards structures for spending, and more.

The best part is that most issuers let you have multiple credit cards, meaning you can potentially earn more than one free night certificate per year. In the case of just about all of the above cards, I’d say the free night certificates more than justify the annual fees.

What’s your favorite hotel credit card free night certificate?

#6189. Thank You, Specialist Thomas Iglesias

The guard at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier didn’t hesitate to shout his admonition to a group of highfalutin visitors, a sterling example of duty and honor.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth awards Army Specialist Thomas Iglesias the Joint Service Commendation Medal at the Pentagon, November 12, 2026.

The secretary of defense visited the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier on Veterans Day, and yet the true voice of military authority on this occasion was an Army specialist.

When the group with Pete Hegseth laughed and began to chatter after taking a photo, the voice of Specialist Thomas Iglesias rang out, “All visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times!”

#6188. What Amenities Make An Airport Lounge Good? Here’s My Take…

I write a lot about airport lounges on the blog, ranging all the way from domestic lounges in the United States, to the best business class lounges, to the best first class lounges. When I rank the lounges that I like the most, some readers understandably have very different takes.

I thought it would be fun to start a discussion about basic expectations of airport lounges, and what makes them exceptional.

Obviously lounge standards should differ depending on whether you’re using Priority Pass to access a lounge or are traveling in international first class, so we’ll get into more detail on that below.

Broadly speaking, what I’m looking for in a lounge is a (relatively) quiet place to sit, connect to Wi-Fi, recharge electronics, use a clean bathroom, and maybe have some water or coffee. Other things are good to have, but not something I necessarily expect.

There are also some deal killers for me when it comes to airport lounges. Personally, if a lounge is packed, I have no interest in being there, and that largely reflects that over the years, terminals have become much better places to spend time:

I figured I’d share my expectations for lounges, and I’ll break it up into three tiers of lounges (admittedly some of the lines are blurred here):

I think it’s also important to note that everyone is looking for different things in lounges:

I think the two below videos from Cathay Pacific from several years ago oh-so-beautifully sum up what makes lounges great. The commentary in the videos is almost poetic.

With that out of the way, let me share my basic expectations of various types of lounges, and admittedly these reflect my preferences and biases.

My expectations for Priority Pass lounges, airport contract lounges, airline membership lounges, and credit card lounges, are pretty simple. I’m happy if I can actually consistently get in and have a quiet place to sit. Sadly that’s not as straightforward as it may sound, with so many stories of lounges denying entry to club members, Priority Pass members, etc.

What sets a “basic” lounge apart? I’d say showers, bathrooms that are significantly nicer than in the terminals, workstations, a good food selection (ideally with hot food), good coffee, and employees who actually make you feel welcome.

Just to give some examples of lounges in this category that I consider to be exceptional:

My expectations are a bit higher for purpose-built international business class lounges. In addition to what I expect from the more “standard” lounges above, I hope that international business class lounges will have hot food, a more premium drink selection, showers, and workstations.

What sets an international business class lounge apart? I’d say a la carte dining, nap rooms, barista-made coffee drinks, and generally elevated decor.

Just to give a few examples of lounges in this category that I consider to be quite good (we’re actually pretty lucky in North America):

International first class lounges are as premium as they get, so expectations should be high. In international first class lounges I expect a la carte dining, barista-made coffee, some sort of an area to rest, a truly tranquil environment, and staff who make you feel welcome.

What sets an international first class lounge apart? Dining that’s (high-end) restaurant quality, an amazing drink selection, individual nap rooms, spa treatments, and a ground experience that extends beyond the lounge. That’s to say either tarmac transfers or an escort to the gate, and that’s no doubt an area where many airlines fall short.

I’ve reviewed the world’s top first class lounges in detail, so it’s no secret what my favorite options are the Air France La Premiere Lounge Paris and Lufthansa First Class Terminal Frankfurt.

We’re all looking for different things from airport lounges, and I think that’s totally fair. Standards should differ based on what kind of a flight you’re taking, how you access the lounge, what you’re trying to accomplish by visiting a lounge, etc.

Everyone will have a different take on which lounges are great vs. just okay, and that’s fine. While I care about tranquility and good coffee, others care about great food and drinks.

I’m curious to hear from OMAAT readers — what makes a lounge great, in your book?

For applications through January 13, 2027, American Express and Hilton are offering increased welcome offers on their four co-branded credit cards, and these are among the best deals we’ve seen on the cards. With these lucrative welcome offers, you can earn both points and an uncapped free night award (valid at properties costing up to 250,000 points per night, which is Hilton’s highest award cost for standard room redemptions).

Not only are these great welcome offers, but these cards offer valuable benefits for those who stay at Hiltons with any frequency, so if you travel often, it’s worth having (at least) one of these cards in your wallet. In particular, I love the free night awards, given that they can even be redeemed at top Waldorf Astoria or Conrad hotels, or even Small Luxury Hotels of the World (SLH) properties.

Link: Learn more about the Hilton Honors American Express Card, Hilton Honors American Express Surpass® Card, Hilton Honors American Express Business Card, and Hilton Honors American Express Aspire Card

In addition to offering bonus points, three of the cards also include a free night award as part of the bonus (and the fourth card offers a free night award as an annual benefit, including the first year). For the purposes of framing the value of the points, based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Hilton Honors points to be worth 0.5 cents each.

I’m on the road about half the year on assignment for TPG and on any given week, you might find me browsing the jade market in Taipei, window-shopping through Galerie Vivienne in Paris or strolling through the San Telmo market in Buenos Aires on the hunt for collectibles.

I can’t tell you how many times I’ve seen a souvenir, piece of art, sweet treat or other little curio and thought, “Wouldn’t this make a great gift for so and so?”

The only trouble is, I travel light, so there’s nary a nook or cranny in my carry-on to fit a gift, let alone several.

I do, however, make a mental inventory of potential gifts I see so that I can order them for friends and family later. Here are a few of my favorite recent finds that might be perfect for someone on your holiday gift list, all inspired by my travels.

Best for: Armchair travelers who like to keep cozy

There’s a lot I love about 1 Hotels — their sustainable ethos, the Bamford bath amenities, in-room filtered water taps, the smattering of hyperlocal, destination-specific activities on offer to guests, bustling public spaces with unique dining concepts and…the bathrobes. I’m not usually a bathrobe kind of guy, but I can’t resist donning one of these ultracomfortable numbers anytime I’m a guest at one of these properties. Simple and soft, with a gray jersey-knit lining and a loose hoodie, they’re perfect for lounging with a cappuccino while you try to stave off jet lag.

TPG tip: You might want to make this purchase at an actual 1 Hotel boutique so you can earn more points per dollar with a credit card that offers a travel or hotel category bonus.

Best for: The Japanophile you want to impress

Like an unstoppable force meeting an immovable object, my delight in purchasing travel souvenirs is only impeded by the limited space in my small city apartment. That’s why I love the little lacquerware boxes and trays from Zohiko, a boutique in Kyoto’s Nakagyo Ward that traces its history back to the 17th century. I especially love the finely filigreed Kirikane style, where patterns or shapes are cut out in gold or silver leaf and pressed into place. I purchased a glossy black box with gold inlay of cherry blossoms and autumn leaves on my last visit, and I keep it on my nightstand to hold my wedding ring and watch.

TPG tip: Make a trip to Japan out of it and browse the physical Zohiko boutique (you can also enjoy tax-free purchases if you’re visiting) while checking out some of Kyoto’s exciting new hotels.

Best for: Folks who appreciate colorful, culturally significant crafts

Inevitably, every time I’m traipsing around Bogotá, I find myself drawn to this gorgeous little boutique in the city’s upscale Chapinero neighborhood, which sources fair-trade handcrafted pieces of art and decor from small communities around the country, including woven baskets starting at just $18. I am personally drawn to carefully carved wooden Tamo bowls from the coastal Nariño region, decorated with brightly dyed strands of wheat or barley fiber, but you can find everything from woven baskets to hammocks, jewelry and even pieces of furniture.

TPG tip: While you can often haggle for handicrafts in Colombia, prices in this boutique are as marked, so save your negotiating skills for street vendors.

Best for: Helping a friend spruce up their interior decor game

Although long popular with backpackers and river cruisers, Luang Prabang still feels like an under-the-radar find in mountainous Laos, sitting on the confluence of the Mekong and Nam Khan Rivers. It’s also a hotbed of fair-trade arts and crafts. A standout atelier in town is Ock Pop Tok, an art school, store and restaurant that aims to revive, support and teach traditional Lao artistic techniques. Visitors can take classes in silk-weaving, batik-dyeing and embroidery, among other offerings. I am always tempted to buy out the textile section of the boutique, but I usually limit myself to a vibrant wall hanging or two.

TPG tip: Don’t just make a purchase; spend a few days as a student at Ock Pop Tok to pick up a new craft yourself.

Best for: Travelers who like their perfumes with a hint of historical luxury

Of course, I’d suggest visiting the original Florence flagship of this bath and beauty purveyor, which dates back to 1221. It feels a little like visiting Ollivanders Wand Shop from “Harry Potter,” with antique cases bursting with all-natural unguents and elixirs whose formulas were originally developed by Dominican friars. But if you can’t get there, there are also locations around the U.S., including those in West Hollywood, California, Soho in New York City and Bal Harbour, Florida. I tend to keep it simple and go for the pure sweet almond oil, but you could also go regal and buy a bottle of the perfumery’s citrusy Acqua della Regina, created for Catherine de' Medici as a gift for her husband, the future king of France, back in 1533.

TPG tip: It can sometimes be less expensive to purchase these products from the original store in Florence, so why not make a trip out of it?

Best for: The fashionable cowboys at your rodeo

I love an eye-catching accessory, and belts are my statement pieces of choice. So on my last visit to Buenos Aires, I stopped by Arandu Talabarteria’s tony boutique in Recoleta. The whole store is inspired by a romanticized version of gaucho life on the pampas. You can find sturdy leather boots, billowy bombacha pants, cozy ponchos and my favorite: woven belts with intricate threadwork and high-quality leather. They start at $45 and can range into the hundreds of dollars, depending on the level of detail and craftsmanship. Best of all, you can ship to the U.S., so you don’t have to cross the equator to stock up.

TPG tip: They also have dog collars for your faithful canine companion.

Best for: The high-flying #avgeek in your life

If you’ve followed me for the past few years, you know I’m pretty much obsessed with KLM’s tile Delft houses, the little replicas of actual historical buildings around the Netherlands that the airline hands out to long-haul business-class passengers. I’ve attended the unveiling of each year’s new house for several years now, and my own collection has grown into a veritable village. If you have an equally #avgeeky member of your gifting circle and are looking for the perfect present, then you might want to consider buying one of these beauties for them. Historian Mark Zegeling’s “Little Kingdom by the Sea” book set, which delves into the history of all 107 of the houses, is a great accompanying gift as well.

TPG tip: Be sure to use a credit card that waives foreign transaction fees so you don’t get dinged with a 1-3% surcharge when buying your house.

Best for: Swanky sunseekers who want to make a splash

How do you tell me you summer on the French Riviera without telling me you summer on the French Riviera? You simply tote around a sunshiney yellow-and-white-striped beach bag from the iconic Carlton Cannes, the first luxury hotel to open in the city, way back in 1911. A lot has changed since then, but the simple design is meant to evoke the Côte d’Azur of yore, when you might have found Cary Grant and Grace Kelly sunbathing on the plage between scenes of “To Catch a Thief.”

TPG tip: Make your purchase in person and use an IHG One Rewards credit card to earn multiple points per dollar.

Best for: International imbibers with a sweet tooth

You might find it hard to remember your visit to Singapore, let alone pick up some souvenirs as gifts for friends, after you’ve had a few Singapore Slings at the Raffles Hotel’s iconic Long Bar. That’s why it might come in handy to pick up a keepsake Singapore Sling glass for your friends from the hotel’s online boutique. It’s like taking a sip of history with you. The nation’s signature drink was invented by Ngiam Tong Boon back in 1915 and is an intoxicating (and sweet!) mix of gin, grenadine, cherry liqueur, Benedictine, Curacao and both pineapple and lime juice. Even a sip can transport you back to a sultry Southeast Asian evening.

TPG tip: Pick a card that earns bonus rewards on everyday purchases, like the Capital One Venture Rewards Credit Card or Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card, so you’re making the most of your spending.

Best for: Your friends’ (or your own) globe-trotting tots

We can’t forget about the kids! In my experience, there are few better or more engaging (or educational) ways to get the tykes in your life interested in travel than Little Passports, a subscription membership where each month, your child is mailed a new box focusing on individual countries, animals, crafts and even DIY science experiments, depending on their specific subscription and age.

TPG tip: Don’t forget to choose the subscription length you want from the start, otherwise, these charges might sneak up on you month after month if you don’t cancel.

Best for: Your favorite skincare aficionado

I first came across Officine Universelle Buly’s sweet-smelling body products during a stay at the Rosewood Hotel de Crillon in Paris last year, and I promptly swiped several tubes of shampoo, conditioner and body lotion from my suite to use at home. On my next visit to the City of Light, though, I stopped by the enchanting store in the 6th arrondissement to sniff through various scents and balms tinged with exotic notes like Madagascar amber and Maltese iris. They also have fabulous tortoiseshell hair clips and combs that you can have monogrammed for even the most discerningly coiffed companions in your life.

TPG tip: If you’re purchasing liquid products and not checking a bag, make sure they comply with carry-on limits.

Best for: Yourself! This is the ultimate self-care splurge

In recent years, more and more hotel chains have started selling the mattresses they use directly to customers. And while you might be a Westin Heavenly Bed fan, or perhaps a devotee of DoubleTree’s signature Sweet Dreams mattress, I personally recommend a Four Seasons mattress, which has the plushest pillowtop of any hotel bed I’ve experienced. After staying at dozens of Four Seasons over the years, I finally took the plunge and purchased one for myself about six years ago and I’ve never slept better. It’s definitely a splurge, but you can’t put a price tag on a great night’s sleep. So make this one a gift for yourself.

TPG tip: Given the price tag, wait until you have a new credit card with a minimum spending requirement to meet to earn its welcome offer so you can put your splurge to good use.

#6184. Philippine Airlines Launches New U.S. Route

Philippine Airlines has landed in the U.S. Midwest.

The carrier on Monday operated its inaugural flight between Manila and Chicago O’Hare. The nonstop connection is the first ever between the Philippines and the Midwest.

“For Philippine Airlines, this is a strategic addition to our North American network,” PAL Executive Vice President and COO Carlos Luis Fernandez said in a news release. “It expands our presence to the Midwest and provides more convenient access to one of the largest regional economies in the United States. We know that many Filipinos and Filipino-Americans in Chicago, Illinois, and neighboring states have long looked forward to a direct and more convenient connection to the Philippines. We are proud to finally make this possible.”

Manila-Chicago service will operate three times weekly going forward.

PAL’s other U.S. destinations are New York-JFK, Los Angeles, San Francisco, Seattle, and Honolulu. It also serves Toronto and Vancouver in Canada.

#6182. How To Redeem World Of Hyatt Points For Best Value, Maximize Award Chart

I write a lot about the value of hotel loyalty programs, and in this post, I’d like to talk about World of Hyatt. What are the best ways to redeem World of Hyatt points, how many points do you need for a free night redemption, how does the award chart work, etc.?

Let’s start by talking about the basics of redeeming World of Hyatt points — how much should you expect to pay for free nights, are there blackout dates, how much are World of Hyatt points worth, etc.?

Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider World of Hyatt points to be worth 1.4 cents each. There’s no science to that, but rather I think that’s a fair, conservative valuation for what the points are worth. In other words, I won’t redeem points for a hotel stay with Hyatt unless I’m getting well over 1.4 cents of value per point (and that has to factor in the points I’m forgoing by redeeming rather than paying cash, etc.).

It’s important to come up with a points valuation for yourself (it can be different than mine), so that you can decide whether to pay cash or redeem points for a hotel stay.

I have lowered this valuation a little recently, in light of the World of Hyatt award chart devaluation we’ve seen, where Hyatt has gone from three tiers of pricing within each category to five.

World of Hyatt has no blackout dates, which is to say that if a standard room is available for sale with cash, it can also be booked with points.

Now, the important thing to keep in mind is that some hotels have a very small pool of “standard” rooms, and a vast majority of rooms at a hotel may be considered “premium.” If a hotel has 150 rooms, it’s possible that only 10 rooms are considered “standard,” so that’s the major issue you’ll run into when redeeming points at some properties.

Unfortunately in the hotel industry overall, we’ve seen a reduction in the number of standard rooms at many properties that are popular for redemptions, which is essentially a way for hotels to create indirect capacity controls.

Keep in mind that Hyatt has a great points availability calendar, which at least makes it easy to find the nights that are available with points, for those properties that are challenging.

Hopefully this isn’t an issue anyone runs into, but just keep in mind the World of Hyatt points expiration policy. World of Hyatt points expire after 24 months of inactivity. Any points earning or redemption activity resets the expiration of your points by a further 24 months.

Unlike Hilton Honors, IHG One Rewards, and Marriott Bonvoy, World of Hyatt continues to publish award charts for award redemptions (the exception is Mr & Mrs Smith properties, which I’ll talk more about in a bit).

The catch is that at this point, World of Hyatt has five tiers of award pricing for standard room redemptions — Lowest, Low, Moderate, Upper, and Top — and the variance within each category is huge. So while I appreciate that there’s not technically dynamic pricing, when a Category 1 hotel can cost 3,000 or 9,000 points, and a Category 8 hotel can cost 35,000 or 75,000 points, you’re not exactly getting a lot of assurance.

The standard award chart applies at a vast majority of properties globally, including most Hyatt branded properties. There are eight categories of hotels, and 40 different pricing tiers, given the five pricing bands within each tier. Pricing ranges from 3,000 points for a Category 1 property during the “Lowest” period, and 75,000 points for a Category 8 property during the “Top” period.

Next, World of Hyatt has an all-inclusive award chart, which applies to an ever-growing number of properties across Hyatt’s all-inclusive brands. Hotels fall into one of six categories, with the similar five bands of pricing, all based on double occupancy. Pricing ranges from 12,000 points for a Category A property during the “Lowest” period, to 85,000 points for a Category F property during the “Top” period.

Lastly, World of Hyatt has an award chart for Miraval properties, which are Hyatt’s super-luxurious wellness resorts. Pricing varies based on single or double occupancy, and then there’s also the five bands of pricing.

Note that unlike Hilton Honors and Marriott Bonvoy, World of Hyatt doesn’t offer a fifth night free on award redemptions. So you’ll pay the points that correspond to the number of nights you’re staying.

World of Hyatt is the only major hotel loyalty program that lets you efficiently redeem your points for suites. This can come in the form of free night redemptions, or in the form of an upgrade award. Unlike with standard room availability, there are capacity controls on suite redemptions, so these won’t always be available just because a suite is for sale.

You can find the standard suite award chart below, for the same Category 1-8 properties as above. As you can tell, the premium for a standard suite can range from around 20% to 100%, so there’s quite a bit of variance here. In many situations this could represent a good deal. Of course the ways that hotels choose to designate suites differs by property, so in some cases this can represent a huge upgrade, while in other cases it doesn’t.

You can find the premium suite award chart below, for the same Category 1-8 properties as above. As you can tell, there’s also quite a bit of variance here in terms of how much of a premium you’re paying.

World of Hyatt also lets you upgrade to club rooms, suites, and premium suites, using points. You can find the chart for that below, though note that this is only possible when booking a fully paid stay at the flexible rate directly with Hyatt. This requires a rate code, so it’s not even combinable with Hyatt Privé rates.

There are also more capacity controls here than you’d have if redeeming Hyatt suite upgrade awards, which are issued through the Milestone Rewards program.

World of Hyatt offers Points + Cash awards, whereby you can book a stay at a hotel using a combination of points and cash. This might sound appealing to those who want to reduce the cash cost of a stay using points, or those who don’t have quite enough points for a stay.

Points + Cash redemptions follow an award chart. The way this works, you can redeem 50% of the standard points required, plus you’ll receive around 50% off the cash component of a stay, in comparison to the flexible rate.

It’s always worth taking a look at this, though more often than not I don’t find this to be as good of a deal as just outright redeeming points. Also note that Points + Cash redemptions have capacity controls, unlike free night redemptions.

Hyatt acquired luxury travel company Mr & Mrs Smith, and you’ll find that many Mr & Mrs Smith properties are bookable through Hyatt channels. This is an opportunity to earn and redeem Hyatt points for stays at all kinds of independent luxury properties that you’d not otherwise have access to with a major loyalty program.

While the opportunity to earn points is potentially exciting, the catch is that points redemptions largely represent a bad value. Award pricing is fully dynamic, and you’ll find that in many cases, points only get you around a cent each toward a stay. That’s significantly less than I value them, so I wouldn’t recommend redeeming that way.

While I wouldn’t say it’s my favorite use of points, World of Hyatt offers Dining & Spa awards, whereby you can redeem points toward a folio credit that can be applied to on-property dining and spa awards. With this, you’ll get anywhere from 1.0 to 1.54 cents of value per point.

While there are some restrictions to be aware of, this is still something that has the potential to be useful for those with lots of points, who are looking to splurge on incidentals during a stay.

With the Milestone Rewards program, World of Hyatt members can earn Guest of Honor certificates. This extends World of Hyatt Globalist status benefits over the course of a stay, for up to seven nights. These can be applied to any eligible revenue stay or points stay, and offer lots of value.

Those booked with a Guest of Honor certificate receive the standard Globalist perks, including complimentary breakfast, suite upgrades subject to availability, and much more. This is one of my favorite loyalty perks out there.

World of Hyatt has a generous policy when it comes to letting members transfer or combine points between accounts. World of Hyatt members can transfer points between accounts at a 1:1 ratio.

Members can transfer a minimum of 1,000 points, and can transfer in increments of 500 points above that. Members can transfer up to 525,000 points per transaction, and may transfer or receive up to that many points across accounts per calendar year. World of Hyatt accounts must be at least 60 days old in order to send or receive points.

World of Hyatt members are also limited to making one free points transfer every calendar month, and six free points transfers every calendar year. Transfers generally happen within 24 hours, but in rare cases could require additional review, and could take up to 10 business days.

This can be a great way to combine points in order to have enough for a particular redemption, or even to transfer points in order to make a booking out of an elite member’s account, or using a Guest of Honor award.

Nowadays many properties charge resort fees or destination fees, which are essentially a money-grab. All World of Hyatt members don’t have to pay these when redeeming points, which can add significant value. Furthermore, World of Hyatt Globalist members don’t have to pay these even on revenue stays.

As a further perk, World of Hyatt Globalist members don’t have to pay for parking on award stays (however, non-Globalist members do have to pay for parking).

World of Hyatt has three elite tiers — Discoverist (10 elite nights), Explorist (30 elite nights), and Globalist (60 elite nights). While status isn’t quite as easy to earn as with some other hotel groups, there are still some opportunities to earn status with credit cards. World of Hyatt’s co-branded credit cards include the World of Hyatt Credit Card (learn more) and World of Hyatt Business Credit Card (learn more). You can earn elite qualifying nights and status with these cards:

Even if you’re not a Hyatt loyalist, the great news is that earning World of Hyatt points is pretty easy. However, the ratios aren’t as consistently good as in the past.

In addition to being able to earn World of Hyatt points with the World of Hyatt Credit Card and the World of Hyatt Business Credit Card, you can also transfer points from both Bilt Rewards and Chase Ultimate Rewards:

On top of that, World of Hyatt frequently has promotions for purchasing points. The reason this matters is because there are lots of situations where you could get outsized value simply by buying points from Hyatt and then immediately redeeming them for a hotel stay.

With the above basics out of the way about redeeming World of Hyatt points, how do you get the most value with your points? Let me share my approach to redeeming Hyatt points.

As a Hyatt Globalist member, I exclusively redeem my points for free night award redemptions in standard rooms. While I think there can be value in redeeming points for standard or premium suites, my general strategy is to redeem for standard rooms, and then use suite upgrade awards to confirm suites.

The reality is that I get huge value with my World of Hyatt points throughout the award chart, and not just at aspirational properties. Generally I decide to redeem points if I’m getting at least two cents of value per World of Hyatt point. There are several things I factor into that, though. When deciding whether to redeem points:

With World of Hyatt charging such vastly different amounts across the five bands of pricing, in some cases you’ll get the most value per point when redeeming during an off-peak period, while in other cases you’ll get the most value when redeeming during a peak period. You of course always want to compare the cash rates to the points redemption rates.

With a little bit of effort, I have no issues redeeming a vast majority of my Hyatt points for well over two cents each, in comparison to the cash cost.

Ultimately the reason I collect airline miles and hotel points is for aspirational redemptions. I try to redeem for things that I typically wouldn’t pay for in cash, where I’m getting outsized value.

So just as airline miles are best redeemed for first & business class travel, hotel points are often best redeemed for five-star properties that would cost a lot in cash. So the main reason I earn Hyatt points is to be able to redeem at properties belonging to brands like Alila and Park Hyatt. From Alila Napa Valley, to Alila Ventana Big Sur, to Alila Jabal Akhdar, to Park Hyatt Kyoto, to Park Hyatt Milan, to Park Hyatt Paris, I’ve had some amazing award redemptions over the years.

World of Hyatt is my all-around favorite hotel loyalty program. I greatly value the elite perks I receive as a Globalist member, and I also consistently get great value with my points, especially for aspirational properties. I also love how World of Hyatt points can efficiently be transferred from Chase Ultimate Rewards, providing an easy pathway to racking up this currency.

Personally my favorite use of World of Hyatt points is for stays at Hyatt’s top luxury hotels, where you’ll almost consistently get the best value, assuming you can find award availability. However, I’ve gotten great value at lower end properties as well.

Now, in fairness, the value of Hyatt points is definitely decreasing a bit at the moment, and on top of that, the reduced transfer ratio from other currencies is frustrating, and definitely eats into the value a bit. That being said, that’s true of the industry at large, as we’ve also seen endless devaluations with Hilton Honors and Marriott Bonvoy. I do still get the most value with Hyatt.

What has your experience been with redeeming World of Hyatt points?

#6181. Report: Google Accepts Privacy Safeguards for Spirit Data

The Wall Street Journal reported Monday that the proposed sale will exclude personnel records, including medical files, results of drug and alcohol tests, performance reviews, payroll information, and grievance and arbitration filings.

Unions representing former Spirit pilots and flight attendants had objected to the inclusion of that data, noting Google’s plans to use the information to train its artificial intelligence models. The agreement reached this week resolves the unions’ concerns, the Journal said.

Google and Spirit initially planned to have an outside company “deidentify” the airline’s records. That process will still take place, though at a higher standard than Spirit intended to use, and Google will be prohibited from attempting to “reidentify” the data.

Spirit went out of business in May following a dramatic rise in jet fuel prices. The decision to auction off its internal records for use by AI was a first for the airline industry and opened up a new realm of contestation for workers and employers.

#6180. FAA Issues Nationwide Ground Stop, Shuts Down The Skies: What’s Going On?

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has issued a nationwide ground stop, which is pretty unprecedented. Admittedly we’ve had our fair share of air traffic control issues in the United States over the years. But this is really on a different level, unlike anything we’ve seen since 9/11, in terms of operational disruptions. I guess it’s fitting that this is happening on Friday the 13th.

At 3:54PM ET today (Friday, November 13, 2026), the FAA issued a ground stop for flights across the country, as pilots received the following message:

DUE TO EXTRAORDINARY CIRCUMSTANCES AND FOR REASONS OF SAFETY. ATTENTION ALL AIRCRAFT OPERATORS, BY ORDER OF THE FEDERAL AVIATION COMMAND CENTER ALL AIRPORTS ARE GROUND STOPPED. ALL DEPARTING TRAFFIC SHOULD REMAIN GROUND STOPPED UNTIL FURTHER NOTICE. INBOUND INTERNATIONAL FLIGHTS WILL BE MANAGED ON A CASE BY CASE BASIS.

As of now, the ground stop is through 11:30PM ET, though it’s possible that it’s lifted before then. That timeline clearly reflects the extent to which the current situation is a complete mess, and this won’t be an easy fix.

As usual, JonNYC was among the first to break the news, and he even reported on this before the official ground stop was issued, when airports in the Northeast started having issues, prior to this going nationwide.

Kind of major, started at approx 3:15pmBoston Center, New York Center, Chicago Center, New York Approach have all lost numerous frequencies. All facilities are in ATC Alert. Some sectors in New York Center are unable any traffic currently. Numerous— I mean NUMEROUS frequencies…

“All airspace is currently being sterilized and centers are preparing for ATC Zero operations. Airborne’s should NOT be majorly effected— i.e, at least for now, this is not a “9/11 type of event” where airbornes are being forced to land at the closest airport available. All…

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy confirmed this development a while later, sharing that there were “communication issues impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers,” and he stated that “FAA technicians are investigating the issue.”

The @FAAnews issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers. FAA technicians are investigating the issue. We will provide immediate updates as we have them.

As of now, there’s no timeline for this ground stop ending. To my knowledge, I believe this is now the most significant ground stop we’ve seen in the United States in over 25 years (since 9/11).

If you’re flying this weekend, expect that things will be a mess. To those flying right now, good luck. Ford is on a flight that was supposed to depart at 3:59PM, so suffice it to say that he had some pretty bad luck here, as they pushed back, and then this happened. I hope not too many others are in the same situation.

There’s a major issue when you have flights landing but flights can’t depart, since you have way more planes than gates. So get ready to be patient if you’re onboard a flight, given the complicated logistics.

What could explain an air traffic outage of this scale? As of now, all we can do is speculate, though there are a few interesting things to point out.

First, it remains to be seen if this is related, but the FAA reportedly began its rollout of the new AI-powered air traffic management tool this week, known as SMART (which stands for “Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories”).

Timing-wise, it seems like there’s a possibility this could be related. At the same time, you wouldn’t assume this leads to communication issues, which is what seems to be going on here. So it’s worth pointing out the timing, but we have no reason to believe the two things are related.

Yes the FAA began its nationwide rollout of the SMART AI for ARTCCs to use this week. It’s not clear at this time if the rollout is related to this outage, but if it’s a rolling communications issue, it’s much more likely it’s within already established equipment pilots-ATC use https://t.co/PXqSFdOA1q

One can’t help but wonder if a cyber attack might be to blame. Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin insists that there are no indications of this being a cyber attack. However, if they’re still investigating the cause, it seems hard to rule anything out.

Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin said the agency had no indications of outages being tied to a cyberattack or potential terror threat, adding that the nationwide ground stop was “just a telecommunications outage." https://t.co/cb8xON9Xrz

If this is truly “just a telecommunications outage,” then that represents a major failure. How can air traffic control nationwide have that issue, rather than it just being isolated to one region? Are there no redundancies?

I don’t want to be a conspiracy theorist, but it sure feels to me like some very unusual things are going on. We just saw a huge Microsoft outage, and it has been a very strange week in general. Those two things can of course be completely unrelated, but you can’t help but point it out.

The FAA has grounded flights nationwide, “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.” For nearly two hours now, no flights have taken off in the United States, making this the largest outage since 9/11, to my knowledge.

It remains to be seen what the cause of this was, and whether this is a tech glitch, a cyber attack, or what. To those flying now (or this weekend), good luck… you’re going to need it!

What do you make of this strange ATC outage?

#6179. Alaska Adds Service to Four New U.S. Cities

Alaska Airlines will bring four new destinations into its domestic network next summer.

The carrier announced Thursday that it will serve Charlotte, North Carolina, Jacksonville, Florida, Norfolk, Virginia, and Des Moines, Iowa, from Seattle. Three of the four cities – Jacksonville, Norfolk, and Des Moines – have never had nonstop flights to Seattle.

Currently, only American Airlines connects Charlotte and Seattle.

The Des Moines service will also mark Alaska’s debut in Iowa.

All four connections will operate daily, year-round. Flights to Charlotte and Norfolk will begin June 10, 2027, with Jacksonville and Des Moines launching later that month, on June 24.

Alaska will also offer seasonal service from Seattle to Guadalajara, Mexico, from March 18, 2027, to Aug. 9. Flights will operate three times weekly, using Boeing 737 aircraft.
