Any time I get overwhelmed these days, the first thought I have is: I need to go touch grass. And I really mean it — the great outdoors is exactly where I go to unwind, relax, challenge myself and have a good think. In fact, for many of us at TPG, it's a big part of the reason we love to travel.

This holiday season, you might find yourself shopping for someone who plans their entire winter travel schedule around where to ski the best powder on the planet, or maybe for someone whose traveling around the world bagging peak after peak. Maybe you're close with a national park enthusiast, or you need a really good stocking stuffer for a dedicated marathon runner. Or maybe someone in your life loves nothing more than cozying up at the perfect camping spot for a long weekend.

No matter what type of outdoor adventure their passion might be, this gift guide (though non-exhaustive; I had to cut myself off at some point!) compiles some of my absolute favorite, go-to items for those who simply love to spend time outside. Have a scroll, and let us know in the comments what your dream outdoor gift would be.

It goes without saying that anyone who skis or snowboards throughout the winter season can benefit from a pass. My personal favorite in recent years has been the Ikon pass, which has taken me to mountains like Mammoth, Steamboat Springs and Killington. But the opportunity to get your turns in certainly doesn't stop at the U.S.; the Ikon pass famously gets passholders access to all four major ski resorts in Niseko, Japan, known for having some of the best (if not the best) powder in the world.

TPG tip: With a purchase as hefty as this one, you'll want to ensure you use a card that will maximize rewards. I'd recommend a card that earns an elevated, flat rate across all purchases — like the Capital One Venture Rewards Credit Card.

Best for: The sustainability-minded gourmand

While I've taken Pataognia Provisions tinned fish on the trail before, I have to admit I eat it at home all the time, too. Anyone with an affinity for tinned fish — and for sustainably sourced seafood — will love this variety pack that gives you a taste of everything from lemon herb mussels to sardines in coconut curry.

TPG tip: American Express often has valuable Patagonia deals for cardholders, so check your Amex offers during the holiday season to see if you'll get a statement credit for spending a certain amount at Patagonia.

Shop Patagonia Provisions Tinned Fish Variety Pack

Not all hiking socks are created equal, and after many a mile spent scrambling up the granite of the White Mountains, I've found that Darn Tough are true to their name in every sense. I'm partial to the micro crew cushion sock — they provide just enough cushion without taking up too much space in my boot, they're breathable and they hold up well on multi-day trips. But pick any Darn Tough style and it's pretty tough to go wrong.

TPG tip: Darn Tough is often eligible for Capital One Shopping Rewards via several online retailers like Cabela's and Shoebacca. If you're a cardholder, make sure you're shopping with the Capital One portal Chrome extension to make sure you're getting the best deal.

Cozy is the primary concept with Outerknown's Blanket Shirt (available for men and women in a wide array of colors and patterns). The first time I put one of these on about a decade ago, I knew it would become a staple in my everyday wardrobe, but especially for shoulder season camping trips and cabin getaways, when evenings and early mornings are cold and crisp.

TPG tip: Outerknown is available at Nordstrom, so Nordstrom cardholders and Nordy Club members can consider cashing in their valuable awards for this item — or even earn cash back on top of your Nordy Club rewards by starting your online Nordstrom purchases via Rakuten.

Anyone who goes out into the backcountry regularly knows that having a plan for hydration is a necessity — and having a dependable, safe way to filter water is simply nonnegotiable. Sawyer makes some of the most popular and reliable water filtration systems for those hitting the trail — I recently used my Sawyer Squeeze on a four day backpacking and was blown away by how simple and functional it is. It removes 99.99999% of bacteria — that's a lot of nines. Whether its used while camping, hiking, backpacking, hunting, fishing or just packed for an outdoor-centric travel excursion, this is a valuable tool for any outdoor enthusiast to carry with them.

TPG tip: You can buy a Sawyer water filtration system on Amazon to get Amazon Prime benefits like free two-day shipping. Just make sure to use a card that's great for Amazon purchases.

If you know someone who loves to backpack — or maybe they're a first timer and you're helping them round out their backpacking setup — the MSR Pocket Rocket is the camp stove I come back to again and again (and I think many, if not most, backpackers would say the same). It's famously lightweight and foldable, boils water very quickly, has a sturdy base for excellent pot support  and is super easy to use and set up (this is coming from someone who lit a camp stove on fire once — I've never had that issue with this one).

#6177. Beond Airlines Suspends Flights For The Rest Of The Year: Better Luck In 2027?

Back in April 2026, we saw Beond Airlines suspend all scheduled operations for the summer, as the airline claimed it would resume flights as of late October. Then in October, it announced it would return in December. There’s now another update, as the airline has just announced that it will resume flights in January. That doesn’t sound so good, does it?

Beond Airlines launched operations in 2023, and it brands itself as the world’s first premium leisure airline. The company is headquartered in Dubai, but primarily operates flights to and from the Maldives. I reviewed the airline in 2024, and the onboard product was super pleasant. The airline currently has a fleet of two aircraft, including one A319 and one A321.

Anyway, in mid-April 2026, the company announced that it would suspend its scheduled operations for the entire summer. The airline promised to resume flights in October, for the winter season.

Then in October, the airline announced that it would suspend operations through November 30, 2026, meaning it will resume flights as of December 1, 2026. Then just yesterday, the airline announced that it would suspend operations through December 31, 2026, meaning it will resume flights as of January 1, 2027.

So I guess it remains to be seen if we actually see a resumption of flights as of January, or if the timeline will get pushed back again. If you can’t make all-business class flights to the Maldives work for the festive season, then prospects seem pretty grim.

Beond Airlines does have its “commitment” to customers when plans change, which includes the ability to change destinations or travel dates, receive a travel credit valid for 18 months, or to receive a full refund. A change of destinations or dates, plus a travel credit, isn’t worth a whole lot for an airline that keeps pushing back its relaunch.

Interestingly, but perhaps not surprisingly, earlier this year the airline deleted its customer promise webpage, which used to guarantee rebooking on another airline in business class in the event a flight is canceled, or else the airline would offer a free flight. That page is now gone, and there’s no mention of rebooking on another airline.

So the airline will “support you every step of the way,” unless you actually want to take the vacation you booked, in which case you’re out of luck (which is less than ideal, given that many Maldives properties have very strict cancelation policies).

While Beond Airlines’ business plan was questionable under the best of circumstances, the crisis of this year makes matters worse:

So I feel bad for Beond, and I’m not trying to do a “told you so, I was right” thing, because these are of course exceptional circumstances. The thing that made me suspicious about Beond for so long is that the airline would repeatedly make outlandish growth announcements, only to rarely follow through on them. That’s neither here nor there, though.

Keep in mind that since operations were initially suspended in April, we’ve seen some interesting developments:

My assumption is that Saudi Arabia is to some extent funding the Red Sea flights, given how the country is throwing money at any airline willing to fly there. However, one wonders if that’s enough money to make the math work, or if Beond even has the general funding right now to keep things operating.

It’s just all so strange, because it feels like half of the announcements from Beond Airlines are really targeting prospective investors, constantly promoting how it’s going to open new subsidiaries all over the world, launch dozens of new routes, etc.

As I said in April, I didn’t think it was a sure bet that flights would resume in October. Now we’ll see if flights actually resume in January. I wouldn’t count on it. One bizarre angle to this is that Beond has claimed it will launch flights to London Heathrow (LHR). Best I can tell, there’s no public record of the airline getting slots for that. And if the airline did have slots, it would be under a “use it or lose it” clause, so not operating the route would make the airline lose them.

In the spring of 2026, all-business class airline Beond suspended scheduled operations through October 2026. Then the airline announced it would resume flights in December 2026. Now the airline claims it will relaunch flights in January 2027. Over the summer, we learned that the airline wasn’t paying many staff for months, and the airline is now pivoting to operating service via Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea Airport.

We’ll see what happens in the coming weeks. Presumably the Red Sea service gets the airline some money from the Saudi government, but it remains to be seen if that’s enough to keep this operation afloat.

It’s understandable that the current situation is really challenging, between the price of jet fuel, plus overall sentiment about the Middle East. However, I have to imagine the airline didn’t have great financial health before this whole mess started, and suspending flights in some ways only makes things even worse.

How do you see this playing out for Beond?

#6176. How Much Do A Pair Of Boeing 777X Wings Cost?

The Boeing 777X has some of the largest and most technologically advanced wings ever fitted to a commercial airliner. Its enormous carbon-fiber structure combines greater aerodynamic efficiency with folding wingtips, allowing the aircraft to use existing airport gates despite its impressive wingspan. Developing such an ambitious design, however, comes at a considerable price, and Boeing has never disclosed exactly how much a finished pair costs.

Boeing does not sell 777X wings separately, and the company has never published a unit price for a finished pair. That leaves no simple price tag to quote and forces us to look elsewhere for clues. Aircraft values, development spending, factory investment, and industry estimates can all help narrow the range, but they do not point to exactly the same number. So what can they actually tell us about the cost of the 777X's wings?

The most defensible estimate for a pair of Boeing 777X wings is roughly $35 million to $55 million. That is an inference rather than an official Boeing figure. It comes from applying a commonly cited aerospace benchmark, which places advanced composite wings at roughly 15% to 25% of an aircraft's value, to an estimated Boeing 777-9 street price of approximately $190 million to $230 million.

That calculation produces a much wider theoretical range of about $29 million to $58 million, making $35 million to $55 million a reasonable middle ground. The comparison becomes even more striking when the aircraft's official pricing is considered. The 777-9's last published list price was about $442 million, but airlines generally negotiate substantial discounts from published prices. That difference is why using the list price directly would produce a very different wing estimate.

There are also estimates that go considerably higher. A BlackJet pricing guide puts the cost of each 777X wing at around $50 million. Taken literally, that would mean approximately $100 million for a pair. The problem is that the source does not make sufficiently clear whether the figure represents one wing, a complete wing set, or another valuation measure.

The bigger numbers associated with the 777X belong to a different category altogether. Boeing reportedly spent at least $2 billion on research, engineering, and testing for the wing, although that figure is widely repeated rather than officially disclosed by the company. The manufacturer also invested more than $1 billion in the facility where the wings are produced. As reported by Reuters through The National, Boeing has taken about $15 billion in losses related to the 777X program as delays, higher costs, and other problems have pushed the price of developing and building the aircraft far beyond the original expectations.

That figure helps show how expensive the program has become, but it cannot be used to calculate the price of a pair of wings.

The first reason the 777X wing is expensive is impossible to miss: it is enormous. With its folding tips extended, the wing spans 235 feet, 5 inches (71.8 meters), which the Herald of Everett noted makes it the longest wing Boeing has ever built.

Its size is not simply a matter of appearance. According to Simple Flying, the carbon-fiber wing has roughly 18% more area than the wing fitted to the 777-300ER. On the ground, the folding tips reduce the span to 212 feet, 9 inches (64.8 meters), allowing the aircraft to remain compatible with airport infrastructure designed around smaller wings. That mechanism adds another layer of engineering to an already large structure.

Material requirements are only part of the equation. Boeing also needed a dedicated manufacturing system capable of producing the wing at the required scale. Unlike the 787, whose composite wing was outsourced to Mitsubishi Heavy Industries, Boeing decided to manufacture the 777X wing itself. The Seattle Times reported that the Everett wing center represented an investment of about $1 billion.

The facility itself illustrates why the wing cannot be compared with a conventional aluminum structure simply by looking at raw material prices. Boeing said at the facility's opening that the building contains three of the world's largest autoclaves, each large enough to accommodate two 737 fuselages. According to The Seattle Times, each autoclave measures 120 feet (37 meters) long and 28 feet (8.5 meters) in diameter.

The production process adds another layer of cost. The Seattle Times described automated equipment laying carbon-fiber tape across the wing's spars and skins, while a single wing skin requires about 300 separately programmed robot runs. The folding wingtip system then adds actuators, locks, sensors, and associated certification work that a conventional fixed wing does not need.

There is another problem for Boeing: production volume. The company is not building hundreds of 777X wing sets every month. When a program produces relatively small numbers of a highly complex component, the cost of specialized tooling, robotics, autoclaves, engineering, and inspection has to be spread across fewer aircraft. That does not necessarily make every wing physically expensive to manufacture, but it makes recovering the enormous upfront investment much harder.

A visually striking feature, the folding wingtips on the 777X are critical to its operation.

Michelangelo DeSantis | Shutterstock, Simple Flying

The factory investment therefore tells only part of the story. Boeing's spending on the wing began long before the first production-standard aircraft could fly, and much of that money cannot be recovered simply by producing another wing.

Boeing's clearest public figure came in 2016, when the company said it had invested more than $1 billion in the Everett site for the new composite wings. Since then, Boeing has focused publicly on the aircraft's certification and delivery schedule rather than disclosing a detailed unit-cost breakdown. In October 2025, AP reported that CEO Kelly Ortberg moved the first 777X delivery target to 2027 and that Boeing took a $4.9 billion charge during the quarter.

Ortberg said the delay was related to certification rather than newly discovered technical problems. That distinction matters because the financial consequences of a delayed program can become much larger than the cost of the physical hardware itself. A factory can continue to incur expenses while aircraft wait for certification, production can become inefficient, and engineering teams can remain committed to a program for years longer than originally planned.

Aircraft valuation provides another way to estimate the underlying economics. According to the BlackJet guide, valuation firm Avitas placed the 777-9's discounted purchase price at approximately $200 million in 2018 dollars. Airlines have nevertheless continued to commit to the aircraft. AP noted that Qatar Airways was waiting for 124 aircraft and Emirates had ordered 205 at the time.

That demand matters because the wing's development cost ultimately has to be recovered across the aircraft Boeing sells. As Simple Flying reported, the roughly $15 billion in 777X charges largely reflects accounting costs associated with delays, production inefficiencies, and certification problems rather than the entire development bill. The same report cites BlackJet's view that final development costs could approach $20 billion.

That puts the $35 million to $55 million wing estimate into perspective. The physical cost of carbon fiber, labor, machinery, and assembly is only one part of what Boeing ultimately has to recover. For the early aircraft, program-level costs and years of development can have a much larger effect on the economics of each delivered jet.

The 777X wing becomes easier to understand when compared with the alternatives Boeing and Airbus have chosen. The closest Boeing comparison is the Boeing 787, which also uses a carbon-fiber wing but has a different production model. Boeing outsourced the 787 wing to Mitsubishi Heavy Industries, while the larger 777X structure is produced internally at Everett.

The older 777-300ER offers a different benchmark. Its aluminum wing spans roughly 212 feet (64.8 meters) and does not require folding tips. It is therefore less complex from both a structural and manufacturing perspective, even though the 777X wing has to provide a considerably larger aerodynamic surface.

Carbon fiber gives Boeing advantages that help explain the investment. The material is lighter and stiffer than aluminum, allowing the manufacturer to increase wing span and fuel-carrying capability without accepting the same weight penalty that a comparable aluminum structure would impose. The 777X therefore uses a much more expensive production system to obtain an aerodynamic advantage that would have been difficult to achieve through a simple evolution of the previous-generation wing.

Airbus followed a more conservative path with the A330neo. Instead of developing an entirely new carbon-fiber wing, Airbus lengthened the existing aluminum structure from 197.8 feet (60.3 meters) to 210 feet (64 meters), with composite elements incorporated into the design. The approach is less revolutionary and requires less specialized manufacturing infrastructure, although it also delivers a smaller aerodynamic step. Boeing is paying for a much larger and more complex structure, but the purpose is to reduce fuel consumption over thousands of flights. The relevant question is whether the additional cost produces enough efficiency over the aircraft's service life to justify the investment.

A percentage of an aircraft's purchase price is not necessarily a reliable measure of what it costs to manufacture a particular component. Aircraft pricing reflects far more than the sum of its individual parts, including commercial negotiations, customer support, equipment options, and the manufacturer's own financial position. Applying a percentage to the 777-9's estimated selling price therefore provides a useful comparison, but it does not reveal the actual resources required to build its wings.

The distinction becomes even more important when comparing different generations of aircraft. The 777X's composite structure, folding tips, and dedicated production infrastructure have little in common with the manufacturing economics of an older aluminum wing. Even another composite-wing aircraft, such as the 787, follows a different production model. A percentage that might be reasonable for one aircraft cannot automatically be transferred to another.

Ultimately, there is no publicly available breakdown showing how much of a 777-9's selling price can be attributed to its wings. The $35 million to $55 million range is therefore a way of illustrating their potential economic scale, not a figure that can be independently verified against Boeing's manufacturing accounts.

For now, $35 million to $55 million remains a defensible estimate for a pair of Boeing 777X wings, based on a 15% to 25% share of a $190 million to $230 million aircraft value. Boeing has not confirmed that figure, and the higher estimates circulating online demonstrate just how uncertain the calculation remains.

The more firmly established numbers tell a different story. Boeing invested more than $1 billion in the factory, reportedly spent at least $2 billion on wing development, and has accumulated roughly $15 billion in 777X program charges. Those figures show that the real economic burden of the wing is not contained in its carbon-fiber materials or assembly labor. A large share of the cost was created before the first airline could operate the aircraft.

That distinction will become increasingly important once the 777X enters airline service. Boeing is targeting first delivery in 2027, with the production-standard aircraft now flying while certification hurdles remain. Once airlines begin accumulating operational experience, fuel-burn and maintenance data will provide something current estimates cannot: evidence of whether the enormous investment behind the 777X wing produces enough real-world savings to justify its cost.

Until then, the $35 million to $55 million range is best treated as a calculated estimate, not a price tag. The first years of airline service should reveal whether Boeing's most ambitious commercial-airliner wing has become an expensive engineering achievement, a worthwhile investment, or some combination of both.

#6175. Duffy And Mullin’s FAA Ground Stop Press Conference: Self-Praise, A $50 Billion Ask, And Conflicting Stories

Yesterday, we saw the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issue a nationwide ground stop, which wasn’t fully lifted for over four hours. This represents the single biggest grounding of flights in the United States since 9/11, so the scale of whatever happened is pretty wild.

At around 8PM last night, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin held a press conference to update people on the state of things. I can’t help but cover this, because it felt like something between an SNL skit and a shakedown, and they couldn’t even keep their story straight… all while praising themselves for doing an unprecedented job!

Below you can find the press conference last night regarding the FAA shutdown, which happened around the time that the ground stop was lifted. First Mullin and Duffy spoke for around 10 minutes, and then they took questions for around 20 minutes.

The gist of the story is that they claim there were no signs of this being a cyber attack, and basically they broadly blame the outdated air traffic control system.

Mullin didn’t speak for long, and his primary comment was this:

“This is what the leadership of President Trump looks like, by the organization and team he has put together. We are built to handle crises like this, and that’s exactly what we’re doing. We’re moving at an unprecedented pace, as a whole of government, to make sure we’re doing the public justice by making sure everyone is safe, which everyone is.”

Isn’t this a little self-congratulatory, especially while he’s also claiming that they don’t fully know the cause here? Just objectively, the pace was indeed unprecedented… it was the longest ground stop since 9/11!

Then you have Duffy speak, and this basically just turned into a demand for Congress to give him $50 billion to modernize our aviation infrastructure, while not actually being honest about the state of things:

“The President, for the last year, has been asking Congress to fully fund a full build of a new air traffic control system.”

That’s just not accurate at all. In July 2025, Congress authorized $12.5 billion for modernizing air traffic control, which Duffy described as a “down payment.” Since then, the size of the request kept changing, and the formal ask only went to Congress this week, when Duffy asked lawmakers for $30.1 billion for air traffic control and airport upgrades.

So it’s a bit rich to claim that Congress has been uncooperative over the past year, especially when you consider Republicans have controlled the White House, House, and Senate.

He then tried to explain what happened, which just feels like a complete deflection to me, as it’s about an overall need to modernize ATC, rather than what actually went wrong here:

“What happened is that our switches, actually got overloaded with data, and they went down… I shouldn’t say they went down… they started to give us inconsistency with the data from those routers, and because of that, we shut the system down. Now, I have already replaced some of those switches with President Trump, and our new IP switches did not go down. It’s the old hardware that went down, and I think the question for the American people is, ‘do you want your Congress to fund this?'”

“I think the Congress at a point looked at the history of the FAA, and said ‘we don’t trust you.’ Well with President Trump, and what we’ve done, I think they do trust, because what we’ve done with that first tranche of money.”

“I’ve asked the President to ask for $30 billion. I want $50 billion.”

Obviously our air traffic control technology is really outdated and does need updating, there are no two ways about it. However, what was different yesterday, and caused an outage to this scale?

You can see I quoted Duffy above as saying that he claimed that “what happened is that our switches, actually got overloaded with data,” and that this caused the shutdown. I’m not a tech expert, but how exactly does that happen and cause the systems nationwide to have issues? At most, you’d assume it would be regionalized, no?

So this is where the questions from reporters come in handy. Mullin seemingly threw Duffy under the bus, saying:

“What it appears to be right now is that as Secretary Duffy and FAA was going in and putting patches in the system, they were putting new equipment, and new technology, and that new equipment and new technology was overwhelming the older system.”

You can see Secretary Duffy’s reaction as Secretary Mullin says the newer technology was overwhelming the system. pic.twitter.com/IeoW5nM4aY

Duffy was then asked what was different yesterday, given that the system had been in place for years. As you’d expect, there was no good answer.

Initially Duffy made it sound like they knew exactly what happened, but then he backtracked on that, and said “we’re still working on the details of what went wrong, I’ll be happy to give you more information, but I don’t want to give you the wrong information.”

Very good set of questions from Luke Radel for Secretary Duffy and Secretary Mullin. pic.twitter.com/f6tlfDtbJG

I also appreciate how someone actually asked the question about this being blamed on Congress, given that the Republicans have had full control for the past two years. As you’d expect, Duffy’s response was first to ask what network the person was from.

DUFFY: How many times does this have to happen before congress gives the money to fix it?R: You’ve been in office almost two years now, Republicans controlled both chambers of congress and still do.DUFFY: What your network are you from? pic.twitter.com/xuX5arTwjl

What’s amazing to me is the overall tone of the press conference. They feel bad for themselves, with Duffy pointing out that he hopes he doesn’t have to give another press conference after 8PM. You know what’s not mentioned once, though? Thanking travelers for their patience throughout all of this, or apologizing to the public for the disruption. Not once.

I’m 100% in support of funding and modernizing air traffic control. But when you have the biggest outage you’ve had in over 25 years, it seems a bit rich to say “give us $50 billion” and “we’re doing an unprecedented job.” And again, if Mullin is to be believed, the system updates that were put in place were to blame.

Breaking – All flights nationwide have beengrounded – the #FAA is facing a computer outage.Yet another major blow to incompetent Transportation Sect Mayor Pete and people who get important jobs with no experience to check some identity politics boxes.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin held a press conference last night about the nationwide ground stop, and it just struck me as being incredibly tone deaf and off base.

You had Mullin congratulating the Trump administration for their “unprecedented” response, you had Duffy claiming the outage was due to switches getting overloaded with data, and you had Mullin then claim this happened because of the system updates that Duffy put in place. Oh, and the focus was also on demanding that Congress give them $50 billion, suggesting they’ve been dragging their feet for the past year.

There was zero tone of accountability or apology. There was no “thanks to everyone traveling for their patience,” but instead, self-pity for the fact that they had to be there after 8PM on a Friday, when they’d probably rather be at home… or a bar, maybe.

What do you make of this press conference?

#6174. Delta 360: Benefits & How To Earn This Invitation-Only Status

All of the “big three” carriers in the United States have invitation-only elite status. I’ve written about how American has Concierge Key and United has Global Services, and in this post, I’d like to take a look at Delta 360, which is Delta’s invitation-only elite status. I’d argue it’s the most mysterious, least talked about, and perhaps the rarest, of the three.

What is Delta 360 status, how do you earn it, what are the benefits, and how many members are there? I’ll share everything I know…

Delta 360 is Delta Air Lines’ invitation-only elite status. It’s my understanding that this is the most exclusive of the invitation-only elite tiers, in the sense that there are the fewest members. Despite that, the benefits are actually pretty weak, at least on paper. For that matter, Delta 360 isn’t even a formal elite tier, which is to say that you separately still have to qualify for status in the Delta SkyMiles Medallion program.

For what it’s worth, here’s how Delta describes Delta 360 status on its website:

Delta 360° is an annual, invitation-only membership for our most loyal SkyMiles Members. A Delta 360° Membership offers Delta’s most premium suite of benefits and services exclusive to our top SkyMiles Members. Entry into Delta 360° will be extended to a very small percentage of Diamond Medallion Members. Considerations include, but are not limited to: overall Delta flight activity, premium product purchases (Delta One, Delta Premium Select, Delta First) and spending on Delta SkyMiles American Express Cards.

As is the case with the invitation-only status of American and United, the requirements to earn Delta 360 status aren’t published. However, based on the data points I’ve seen, the criteria are even more confusing. With American and United, as a general rule, you need to spend well over $50,000 per year to have a shot at the status. In the case of Delta, you probably need to spend even more.

As Delta officially states, getting an invitation to Delta 360 is for the “most loyal SkyMiles members.” Generally speaking:

Some suggest that you’d have to spend $100,000 per year on Delta flights to be invited as a Delta 360 member at major hubs, while the number could be much lower if you’re not based at a hub.

Note that qualification for Delta 360 is annual (so it expires at the end of the elite year), and criteria could change year-to-year. So it’s possible you have the same activity in two years, and earn Delta 360 one year, but not the other. There’s also no way to ask for or request the status (at least not in a way that will achieve the intended result). Instead, you’ll be contacted if you’re eligible, and you’ll see your account updated to reflect that.

There’s one other way to earn Delta 360 status. As part of the SkyMiles lifetime elite status program, you can receive Delta 360 status for life if you rack up five million lifetime miles. This metric is based on the number of eligible miles flown on Delta.

Just for some context on all of this, Delta’s top published tier is Diamond Medallion, and that requires earning 28,000 Medallion Qualifying Dollars (MQDs) in a program year. That would require $28,000 in spending on Delta tickets, or $280,000 to $560,000 in spending on select co-branded Delta credit cards.

Interestingly, Delta 360 isn’t a separate tier in the SkyMiles program. That’s to say that Delta 360 members still have to earn status in the SkyMiles Medallion program. Most Delta 360 members are also Diamond Medallion members, but in theory it’s possible to earn Delta 360 without being a Diamond Medallion member.

This is different than American AAdvantage and United MileagePlus, where Concierge Key and Global Services are separate tiers, above the published top tier levels.

What are the benefits of Delta 360 status?

Those are all the Delta 360 benefits that I’m aware of. There’s no upgrade priority for Delta 360 members beyond their standard Diamond Medallion status, so Delta 360 doesn’t factor into upgrade priority. Furthermore, any confirmed upgrades would be earned through the standard Choice Benefits program, as this is how you can earn Global Upgrade Certificates (GUCs) and Regional Upgrade Certificates (RUCs).

So the benefits of Delta 360 are weak, though I’d imagine that the “soft” treatment is very good — Delta has great service to begin with, and I imagine it’s even better for Delta’s best customers.

I also think it’s noteworthy how Delta is much quieter about this status than American and United. There’s just not as much public acknowledgement of invitation only status at Delta as at American and United (and that might be by design).

This is a real mystery, and all I can do is speculate. For context, I’ve speculated that there are 10,000-20,000 American Concierge Key members, and I’ve speculated that there are 15,000-25,000 United Global Services members.

This is purely a guess on my part, but I think the number of Delta 360 members is probably in the 5,000-10,000 range. That’s simply because the status seems to be more difficult to earn. Like I said, this is purely a guess on my part, and I could be wrong. If anyone has any data or info, I’d love to hear it.

It’s hard to say whether something like Delta 360 is “worth it.” For one, the qualification requirements aren’t even published, so how can one say whether it’s worth it when you don’t know what it will take? Second, I’d say the value of something like Delta 360 varies greatly based on the type of traveler you are.

If you’re a domestic road warrior doing 200 segments per year, you might actually get significant upside from the improved assistance during irregular operations, the Delta One Lounge access, etc. Meanwhile if you take a handful of international long haul business class trips per year, the upside will likely be very minimal, above and beyond what you’d otherwise get.

So I absolutely don’t think it’s worth going out of your way to try to earn something that doesn’t even have published qualification requirements. But if you earn it anyway, of course, it’s a nice thing to have!

The “big three” US carriers all have their own invitation-only elite status, with other programs including American Concierge Key and United Global Services. So how do they all compare?

The reality is that all three tiers are primarily about better improved “soft” treatment, including during irregular operations. On paper, I’d say Delta 360 probably offers the fewest official perks of the three tiers. The one exception is that Delta One Lounge access is an absolutely awesome benefit, given the quality of lounges (though the lack of free guests limits the usefulness for those not usually traveling alone).

Here are a couple of thoughts on the comparable status tiers at American and United:

Delta 360 is Delta Air Lines’ invitation-only elite tier. It’s the US airline status that’s probably hardest to earn. Historically the benefits have been weaker than comparable status with American and United, though with access to Delta One Lounges, that’s perhaps no longer the case. Delta 360 offers dedicated customer support, a Sky Club membership, Delta One Lounge access, good odds of tarmac transfers, and more.

To earn Delta 360, be prepared to spend a lot on Delta flights, especially if you’re based out of a Delta hub.

Are any OMAAT readers Delta 360 members? If so, what has your experience been like?

#6173. The Selective Persecution of Nathan Cofnas

What happened to free expression in academia?

A Ku Klux Klan hood placed by activist group Led By Donkeys covers the Cecil Rhodes statue at Oriel College in Oxford, Britain, November 12, 2026, ahead of a scheduled talk by U.S. academic Nathan Cofnas.

T he organization Led By Donkeys pulled off a stunt at Oxford University: Two activists dressed as construction workers used a cherry-picker truck to place a Ku Klux Klan hood over the head of the Cecil Rhodes statue at Oriel College around 5 a.m. on Thursday, and they placed a sign saying “RACISTS WELCOME HERE” in its hands. Why? “Next week, this college will host a talk by the white supremacist Nathan Cofnas, who stated that in a fair meritocratic system, black people like me would ‘disappear from almost all high-profile positions outside of sport and entertainment,’” Kehinde Andrews said. Andrews is the first professor of black studies in the United Kingdom and author of, among other books, The Psychosis of Whiteness.

Cofnas is no stranger to controversy. He’s currently under fire for previous writings about IQ differences across racial groups and for exposing the extensive academic misconduct committed by Cambridge professor Jason Arday, who was found dead amid the ensuing controversy. “It was a media lynching,” Andrews claimed. The organization repeatedly suggested on social media that, by hosting Cofnas, the college is “staying true to form” because “it continues to display this statue of Cecil Rhodes, the notorious imperialist who created brutally racist colonies in southern Africa.”

The Brand New IHG One Rewards Premier Select Credit Card

Earn up to $4,300 in travel value when you spend $120,000 in your first 4 months as a cardholder

As High As 175,000 points. Find Out Your Offer.

I've never flown with Hawaiian Airlines, yet the Hawaiian Airlines® World Elite Mastercard® is the latest addition to my wallet. With Hawaiian and Alaska Airlines sharing the same loyalty program, Atmos Rewards, the Hawaiian Airlines Mastercard is an attractive option for anyone who regularly flies with either airline.

This card offers common airline-associated perks, but like many cobranded airline cards, it will likely prove hard to justify if you aren't flying at least a couple of times each year with Alaska or Hawaiian. That said, if you're able to properly take advantage of its perks, it can offer a lot to boost your travels. Card rating*: ⭐⭐⭐

The information for the Hawaiian Airlines World Elite Mastercard has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

The $99-per-year Hawaiian Airlines Mastercard comes with some of the benefits you'd expect out of a mid-tier airline card, including:

You won't find lounge access or statement credits on this card, but that simplicity may be welcome for those tired of needing a spreadsheet to help them justify a card's annual fee.

Living in the Pacific Northwest, I often fly Alaska Airlines domestically. As someone who unsuccessfully tried to get the earlier this year, I'm happy that my Hawaiian Airlines Mastercard offers perks on both Hawaiian and Alaska. They may not be as comprehensive as those offered by the Summit, but this card is substantially cheaper.

Receiving two free checked bags isn't too common for a mid-tier card, so I appreciate this perk. But it's important to note that free checked bags with this card are subject to a few restrictions:

If you're traveling with a companion, you could check their bag as your own bag to navigate around this card only allowing the primary cardholder free checked bags.

I face a $45 checked bag fee for my first bag and a $55 fee for my second when flying Alaska within the continental U.S. and Alaska. Even as someone who usually only checks one bag, I just need to do so on one round-trip with Alaska to almost entirely cover this card's annual fee.

Aside from that, using the full $100 annual companion discount on a trip you’d otherwise book can offset the $99 annual fee. New cardholders also receive a one-time 50%-off companion discount. Both discounts can be used on eligible round-trip Main Cabin travel between Hawaii and North America on either airline.

I wish the Hawaiian Airlines card had priority boarding, since overhead bin space can be hard to come by and I'm not a fan of gate-checking my bag. Still, it isn't a deal-breaker for me given this card's annual fee is easy to at least break even on.

This card has no foreign transaction fees and offers standard travel protections like trip cancellation/interruption and travel accident insurance.

The Hawaiian Airlines Mastercard earns Atmos Rewards points, which is the loyalty currency both Hawaiian Airlines and Alaska Airlines use. It earns:

Through Dec. 31, you'll earn 50% bonus points on every dollar spent if you're a resident of Hawaii (up to 5,000 points).

With this card, you'll also earn 1 Atmos Rewards status point per $3 spent, with no cap. You won't get an elite status boost at the start of the qualification year, but this card can help you close the gap to elite status if you're close.

The best way to use your Atmos Rewards points is for flights on Hawaiian and Alaska or with partner airlines, such as American Airlines. Alaska Airlines in particular offers a lot of value for your points, especially on short-haul domestic flights.

Recently, I redeemed 5,000 Atmos Rewards points (plus $5.60 in taxes and fees) for a flight between Portland International Airport (PDX) and Spokane International Airport (GEG). Given the cash price was $184, I received over 3.5 cents per point in value (after taking taxes and fees into consideration). That's more than double TPG's November 2026 valuation of Atmos Rewards points at 1.6 cents per point.

It's this combined loyalty program that allows me to justify holding this card despite never setting foot on a Hawaiian flight and having no current plans to do so. It's hard to earn Atmos Rewards points, since they currently only partner with Bilt as a transfer partner. Without an Alaska Airlines-associated card, the Hawaiian Airlines Mastercard is my best bet for earning points I can use with this program.

As an alternative to redeeming your points for flights, you can also use them for Alaska Vacations packages and Alaska Airlines-curated experiences.

As I mentioned previously, the Hawaiian Airlines card lacks priority boarding and a comprehensive elite status boost at the start of the year. In ways like this, it's clear this card hasn't received a refresh recently, unlike many other popular airline cards.

That means this card may fall short of expectations if you're anticipating a card with well-rounded airline perks. The inability to use this card's free checked bag perk with companions is a non-issue if you're only traveling with one person and two bags, but it becomes a larger limitation if you're traveling with many bags or a group.

If you fly at least a couple of times each year with Hawaiian or Alaska and don't have a cobranded Atmos Rewards card, I believe this card is more than likely worth it. Despite lacking several perks we've come to expect from airline cards these days, it's still quite easy to get outsize value from the $99 annual fee.

Currently, new Hawaiian Airlines Mastercard cardholders can earn up to 70,000 bonus points:

According to TPG's valuations, this welcome offer is worth up to $1,120. In an era when many welcome offers ask for thousands in spending, it's refreshing to see a valuable one that only requires $2,000 in total spending.

Even if you're on a limited budget, this should be an attainable welcome offer. I recommend applying now, given how much this bonus is worth and how easy it is to earn.

Just remember that Barclays can be inquiry-sensitive. If you've opened six or more cards in the past 24 months, you may have a hard time getting approved.

If this card isn't a good fit for you, consider one of these alternatives:

For additional options, check out our picks for the best airline cards.

I'm happy I chose to add the Hawaiian Airlines Mastercard to my wallet. Between two free checked bags and the annual $100 companion discount, I expect I'll be able to easily get outsize value against the $99 annual fee each year.

While this card offers significant value to the right traveler, if you don't fly with either Alaska or Hawaiian at least a couple of times each year, you will likely struggle to find a lot of value in this card. If you're an Alaska Airlines loyalist and you qualify for a Bank of America card, I'd suggest the instead.

That said, if you fly at least occasionally with Hawaiian or Alaska, or you want to earn Atmos Rewards points to use with partner airlines, I recommend giving this card serious consideration.

#6171. Lufthansa Abruptly Cancels This 13-Hour Boeing 747 Route: See Map Now

The Boeing 747 has become a rare sight these days, as only a handful of airlines still operate the Queen of the Skies. Lufthansa is one of them and remains the largest operator of scheduled passenger flights using the type. According to data from aviation analytics company Cirium, 15,061 Boeing 747 flights are scheduled worldwide between December 2026 and October next year.

Of these, Lufthansa accounts for more than 60% of the flights, around 9,673. The German flag carrier continues to deploy the aircraft on several routes from Frankfurt Airport (FRA) to destinations across North America and Asia, including Singapore Changi Airport (SIN). But in its latest schedule update, the carrier has removed the 747 from its Frankfurt-Singapore route next summer.

Lufthansa currently operates one daily flight between Frankfurt and Singapore using the Boeing 747-400, and the aircraft will remain on the route until March 27, 2027, when the northern winter scheduling season ends. The airline had originally planned to continue using the jumbo jet during the summer 2027 season, but that is no longer the case.

Instead, the German airline will deploy its 293-seat Airbus A350-900 on the route. The aircraft features the airline's new Allegris cabin, comprising 48 business class seats, 21 premium economy seats and 224 economy seats. By comparison, the 747-400 currently operating the route accommodates 371 passengers, including 67 business class seats, 32 premium economy seats and 272 economy seats.

The aircraft change will therefore result in a reduction of 78 seats per flight, or approximately 21%. However, the change appears to be temporary, as the airline's current schedule indicates that the 364-seater Boeing 747-8 will take over the route next winter.

The changes come as Singapore Airlines has also decided to remove the Airbus A380 from the route next summer. The aircraft has not operated scheduled flights to Frankfurt since the northern winter season began on October 25, but was originally due to return on March 28, 2027, with daily flights from Singapore.

However, the airline now plans to use the four-class Boeing 777-300ER throughout the summer season, rather than splitting operations between the 777 and A380 as previously scheduled. Singapore Airlines’ 777-300ER accommodates 264 passengers, including four in first class, 48 in business class, 28 in premium economy and 184 in economy.

By comparison, its A380 has 471 seats, comprising six first-class suites, 78 business-class seats, 44 premium economy seats and 343 economy seats. The changes will reduce the airline's weekly seat capacity from 5,145 in summer 2026 to 3,696 next summer, a reduction of approximately 28%.

The carrier has previously operated three daily flights to Frankfurt on certain dates during the summer seasons of 2023 and 2024, but a third daily service is not scheduled for next summer. This means that the Frankfurt-Singapore route will not see double-decker passenger aircraft during summer 2027.

The handful of remaining 747-400s are set for a packed schedule as retirement looms.

While airlines have increasingly retired their 747 fleets, Lufthansa remains one of the largest operators of the type. According to ch-aviation, the German flag carrier has eight 747-400s in its fleet, although only five remain active, alongside 17 Boeing 747-8s.

These aircraft continue to help the airline maintain capacity across its long-haul network. Cirium data shows that Lufthansa has scheduled around 6,820 Boeing 747 flights for summer 2027, covering a total of 16 routes. All of these destinations will see a daily 747 flight.

Half of these serve destinations in the United States, including Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR), George Bush Intercontinental Airport (IAH) in Houston, Los Angeles International Airport (LAX), Miami International Airport (MIA), and New York (JFK). Multiple South American and Asian destinations are also scheduled to receive the aircraft, as shown in the table above.
